records.rec_Title: Angela Varnbühler, St. Gallen, Female, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), Main sections

value.title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch")

details.value:
This manuscript, which in earlier scholarship was often referred to as a “Chronicle,” is in fact the Konventsbuch (Convent Book) of St Katharina in St Gall (61r: “…und sol dis also in des convents buoch gesetz werden…”).

It contains chronological entries concerning the economic interests of the convent. The manuscript was compiled during the reform period, at a time when the convent was transitioning from private ownership to communal property. As such, the book enabled the leadership of St Katharina to account to the community for the management of its assets. It also allowed the sisters to keep track of the property they had originally brought into the convent.

The manuscript includes records relating to building activities, furnishings, the scriptorium, legal disputes, and donations, as well as entries concerning individual sisters, confessors, or workers, and—more sporadically—notes on the history of the convent.

The chronicle contains reports and notes from a wide variety of areas of contemporary convent history: Angela Varnbühler 's investing hand begins (ex post) with her election as prioress in 1476, and continues with a list of the conventuals as well as reports from the implementation of the first Steps to reform the monastery. The other entries, in chronological order, concern a wide variety of events from everyday convent life: entry of novices and their later profession; News of death (from conventuals, relatives and friends); Endowments (of seasons and interest) and gifts; Book production in the scriptorium; Economy of the monastery (conductor's annual accounts, administration, land acquisition [fields, forests, vineyards]); Expansion and conversion as well as artistic furnishings of the monastery buildings; Contemporary events from the history of the monastery and order - even the event of the solar eclipse in 1485 found its way into the chronicle with an entry by the prioress (f.45r ).

Stockholm, Kungliga Biblioteket, A82a, Anna Karlsdotter (d. before 1450), anglicized as Anna Charles in the Syon Martyrology (London, British Library, MS Additional 22285), who was responsible for a Latin and Swedish prayer-book (Stockholm, Kungliga bibliotheket, MS A82a), as brought to light by Claes Gejrot.6 Given that she was one of the four professed sisters who came from Vadstena to help establish Syon, it would be easy to conclude that later English postulants learnt something about manuscripts from Anna and perhaps her fellow Swedes, but there is no proof.

details.value:
Approximately 20 hands or textual sections can be distinguished. Various forms of Bastarda script are used. Since some scripts resemble each other closely, the number of hands may in fact be smaller, and some differences may be explained by different writing phases or circumstances.

The hands are identified as follows:
	•	Hand 1: 1r–7r (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 2: 8r–43v; Sister Regina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect with influences from Middle Bavarian).
	•	Hand 3: 44r–54v (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, probably with Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 4: 55r–v; identical with Hand 6 (75r–77v) and/or Hand 17 (242v–244v)?
	•	Hand 5: 56r–75v (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, probably with Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 6: 75v–77v; identical with Hand 4 (55r–v) and/or Hand 17 (242v–244v)?
	•	Hand 7: 78r–136v; Sister Rossina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, possibly with Alemannic influences).
	•	Hand 8: 137v–170v; Sister Veronica Hoffman(in) (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 9: 171r–193v; possibly identical with Hand 15 (231r–232v).
	•	Hand 10: 193v; identical with Hand 12 (195r–199v) and Hand 14 (200v–230r)?
	•	Hand 11: 194r–v; identical with Hand 13 (200r).
	•	Hand 12: 195r–199v; identical with Hand 10 (193v) and Hand 14 (200v–230v), i.e. with Sister Birgitta?
	•	Hand 13: 231r–232v; identical with Hand 11 (194r–v).
	•	Hand 14: 200v–230r; Sister Birgitta; identical with Hand 10 (193v) and Hand 12 (195r–199v)? (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 15: 231r–232v; possibly identical with Hand 9 (171r–193v).
	•	Hand 16: 233r–242r.
	•	Hand 17: 242v–244v; Susana; possibly identical with Hand 4 (55r–v) and/or Hand 6 (75r–77v).
	•	Hand 18: 245r–256v; Sister Eufrosina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, possibly with Upper Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 19: 257r–275v; Sister Justine (writing language: Nuremberg dialect?).
	•	Hand 20: 276r; Sister Apollonia Kastner (?; this is suggested at least by the entry das buͤchlin gehert muͤter Clara layin von s. Appolonia Kastner ewer getrewe s. in Christo).

details.value:
Writer of the main parts: Sister Barbara von Rottenburg in the Dominican monastery Maria-Reut(h)in (Fiala/Irtenkauf p. 84)
Based on the documents used for binding, this (collective) manuscript originates from the Dominican convent of Reutin. According to G. Piccard’s watermark analysis, it was not begun before 1515 and was completed by around 1529.
The main scribe of its primary sections is Sister Barbara von Rottenburg of Reutin (Gand No. 175), who identifies herself in a manuscript she authored (Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 31, f.64r). She is considered the primary scribe of Reutin from around 1488 to 1534. Her works include:
 • Cod. theol. et phil. qu. 77 (1488-1492),
 • Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 31 (1492),
 • Cod. brev. 27 (1511),
 • Cod. brev. 73 (1521),
 • Cod. theol. et phil. qu. 49a-b (1524),
 • Cod. brev. 49 (1529),
 • Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 33 (1534).

Stuttgart, Württembergische Landesbibliothek, Brev. 73, several hands: Hd. 2 = Barbara von Rottenburg
The manuscript is composed of partially incomplete prayer booklets written by various hands at different times. The initial section was written in 1496 at the Benedictine Monastery of Lorch: “56v Written in Lorch in the year 1496 by Clemens of the convent brothers of Lorch” (likely Clemens Aurifabri, prior in 1490; see Württembergische Geschichtsquellen, Vol. 12, 1910, p. 86).
The second hand is attributed to Sister Barbara of Rottenburg from Reutin (see Cod.brev.63), suggesting Reutin as the manuscript’s library of origin. Her work is dated to 1521 (83v).

Provenance
The manuscript was written by a certain Beatris Dircs Bonen dochter for a convent of Canonesses Regular, dedicated to St. Nicholas and St. Mary Magdalene. According to the Database BNM, the formula on f.17r-17v suggests that the manuscript was made for the Canonesses Regular of St. Mary Magdalene (Op het Spui), Amsterdam. According to Stooker & Verbeij (1997), the formula could have also been for the Canonesses Regular of St. Mary Magdalene, Zaltbommel.

Würzburg Universitätsbibliothek, M.ch.f.4, A collection of manuscripts, written primarily on paper, which can be localized to Bamberg. The first part of the manuscript contains a German mirror of salvation. Erasmus Sternhals is identified as its writer in a colophon. The work was probably made for the Bamberg canon Georg von Löwenstein. This is indicated by the depiction of a kneeling canon and several coats of arms on f.56r. The German-language biography of the Holy Bishop Otto, which is bound in afterwards, also refers to Bamberg. It was written down by two Bamberg Poor Clares and completed in 1483. The third work in the collection is a life of Saint Catherine, dated 1488 and also written by a woman.

Written in North-east France or possibly Cologne, as script and ornamentation in the type developed by the nuns of Chelles suggest; the MS has close affinity with the group of three MSS of St Augustine (Cologne, Dombibliothek 63, 65, 67) written by nuns for Hildebald, Archbishop of Cologne (785–819). Belonged to St Faron, Meaux, till the French Revolution, then to Gosselin, later to Remusat, at whose sale it was bought by Messrs Payne, the London booksellers, in 1833.

details.value:
ff. 1a–21d. Cent balades : «Aucunes gens me prient que je face / Aucuns beaulx diz et que je leur envoye ... - ... non pour tant derrenierement / En escrit y ay mis mon nom.Explicit C balades».
ff. 21bis a -24c.Virelays : «Virelays. I.Je chante par couverture / Mais mieulx pleurassent my oeil ... - ... Pour leur estas / mais a quoy que l'en tende/ On doit croire ce que la loy commande».
ff. 24c-25b. Les balades d'estrange façon : «Doulçour, bonté, gentillesce / Noblesce, beauté, grant honnour ... - ... Paine y mettray, c'est le devoir/ Voué aux loyaux. Tu as dit voir».
ff. 25b-32d.Ballades de divers propos : «Assez acquiert tresor & sengourie/ Tres noble avoir grant richesce amasse ... - ... A du tout en vo demaine/ D' entreprendre armes et paine».
ff. 33a-34d. Complainte amoureuse II : «Doulce dame, veulliez oïr la plainte / De ma clamour / Car pensee destrainte ... - ... Tous voz desirs et longue vie preste/ A vo beau corps/ Et puis a l'ame appreste / Legiere amende.Explicit etc.».
ff. 37a-39a. Lays : «... y a qui charge / d'avoir fausse et fainte cointise ... - ... Et vous serez surhaussez / Sur tous bons sans contredire. Explicit».
ff. 39b-45b. Rondeaux : «Com turtre suis sans per toute seulete/ Et com brebis sans pastour esgaree ... - ... Plaist/ Dieux. Explicit etc.».
ff. 45c-48d. Jeux a vendre [Incomplet] : «Je vous vens la passe Rose/ Belle dire ne vous ose ... - ... Quant vous me faictes bonne chiere/ Ma gracieuse dame chiere».
ff. 50a - 65b. Débat de deux amants [Incomplet] : «Un grant debat dont J'oÿ fort tencier / A deux amans ... - ... S'il le cerche trouver me puet enté / En tous les lieux ou es crestienté. Explicit le debat des deux amants».
ff. 65c- 71d. Epistre au dieu d'Amours : «Cupido par la grace de lui / Dieu des amans sanz aide de nullui ... - ... Cupido le dieu d'amours/ cui amans font leurs clamours. Explicit».
ff.72a - 77a. Dit de la Rose : « A Tous les princes amoureux/ Et aux nobles chevalereux …- … Se il disoit un yne / Il sauroit le nom bel et digne. Explicit le dit de la rose ».
ff. 77c - 89c. Livre des trois jugements : « Bon seneschal de hainaut preux et sage / Vaillant en fais et de gentil lignaige/ Loyal courtois de fait et de courage ... -... Que vous ottroit Joye parfaitte et fine / Pry Jhesucrist qui ne fault ne ne fine. Explicit le dit des .iii. jugemens ».
ff.90a - 106b. Dit de Poissy : « Bon chevalier vaillant plain de savoir / Puis qu'il vous plaist a de mes diz avoir / Et le m'avez par escript fait savoir …- … Vrays fins amans loyaux et non faintis / Que vraye amour tient subgiez et creintis. Explicit le Dit de Poyssy».
ff. 106c - 141b. Epître Othéa  : « Treshaulte flour par le monde louee / A tout plaisant/ Et de dieu advouee …- … Ad ce propos dit le saige. Auris bona audiet cum omni concupiscencia sapienciam. Ecclesiastici. iii. Capitulo. Explicit l'Epistre Othea ».
ff. 141c - 149a. Epîtres sur le Roman de la Rose : « A tresexcellent/ treshaulte et tres redoubtee princesse …-… et gens de honneste et salvable vie/ La tienne cristine de pizan. Explicit les epistres sus le Rommant de la Rose ».
ff. 149c - 153d. Enseignement à son fils : « Filz je n'ai mie grant tresor / Pour t'enrichir pour ce tres or ... -… Car biens mondains vont a deffin / Et l'ame durera sans fin. Explicit les diz moraux ».
ff. 154a -155d. Oraison Notre Dame : « O vierge pure Incomparable / Pleine de grace inextimable …-… A ceulx qui ont pechié remis/ Nous ottroit et grace pleniere. Amen ».
ff. 156a -156c. Les quinze joies de Notre Dame : « Glorieuse dame Je te salue / Treshumblement d'icelle .xv. Joyes…-… Que ou ciel montas de pechié la Racine/ Ostes de moy et met devocion. Amen. Explicit le livre de christine. Deo gracias ».
ff. 157a- 174d. Dit de la Pastoure : « Moy de sagece pou duite / Ja par mainteffoiz deduite …-… De vivre/ c'est pasture/ Sans qui de vivre n'ai cure ».

details.value:
To the most excellent, revered, powerful, and most noble princess,
My lady Isabel, Queen of France…

Written on the eve of October, in the year of grace 1405.

Your most humble and obedient servant,
Christine de Pizan.

Please accept this writing, if it pleases you,
Made by my own hand after midnight, at one o’clock.
Noble lord, for whom I have written it,
Please accept it.
When it pleases you, it can be copied more finely.
But I had no other clerk at the time—
Please accept it…”

Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, BnF Français 835, Les manuscrits de Christine de Pizan ont été écrits par trois mains bien reconnaissables : P, R et X (Christine de Pizan elle-même). Le ms Français 835 a été transcrit, dans sa majeure partie par R, identifié à P. de Cruce : cf.Delsaux, « Profil d’un copiste des manuscrits originaux de Christine de Pisan : P. de La Croix, alias la main R », article à paraître dans Scriptorium. P a copié les ff.441vb, l. 26 à 44vb. La main X a fait quelques corrections : mouche ou restauration sur laquelle l’auteur a réécrit, à l’encre noire, les mots manquants au f.100 : cf.G. Ouy et C. Reno, « Identification des autographes de Christine de Pizan », dans Scriptorium, 34, 1980, p. 221-238.

records.rec_Title: Cordula von Schönau, St. Gallen, Female, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), f.70v - 71v

value.title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch")

details.value:
This manuscript, which in earlier scholarship was often referred to as a “Chronicle,” is in fact the Konventsbuch (Convent Book) of St Katharina in St Gall (61r: “…und sol dis also in des convents buoch gesetz werden…”).

It contains chronological entries concerning the economic interests of the convent. The manuscript was compiled during the reform period, at a time when the convent was transitioning from private ownership to communal property. As such, the book enabled the leadership of St Katharina to account to the community for the management of its assets. It also allowed the sisters to keep track of the property they had originally brought into the convent.

The manuscript includes records relating to building activities, furnishings, the scriptorium, legal disputes, and donations, as well as entries concerning individual sisters, confessors, or workers, and—more sporadically—notes on the history of the convent.

The chronicle contains reports and notes from a wide variety of areas of contemporary convent history: Angela Varnbühler 's investing hand begins (ex post) with her election as prioress in 1476, and continues with a list of the conventuals as well as reports from the implementation of the first Steps to reform the monastery. The other entries, in chronological order, concern a wide variety of events from everyday convent life: entry of novices and their later profession; News of death (from conventuals, relatives and friends); Endowments (of seasons and interest) and gifts; Book production in the scriptorium; Economy of the monastery (conductor's annual accounts, administration, land acquisition [fields, forests, vineyards]); Expansion and conversion as well as artistic furnishings of the monastery buildings; Contemporary events from the history of the monastery and order - even the event of the solar eclipse in 1485 found its way into the chronicle with an entry by the prioress (f.45r ).

Ipse namque scripserunt mo/nasteriensibus dominis quatinus deum pro eis rogent ut a pe/nis eas liberet & in paradyso collocet. Quisquis eis ab/stulerit anatematizatus sit': (a) ff.1v-29v; (b) ff.30r-50v; ff.51r-63v; ff.64r-93v; ff.94r-119v; ff.120r-145v; ff.146r-153r; ff.154r-167v.

London, British Library, Harley 3099, The date '1134' at the end of the note is a post-medieval addition, but the names of five of the nuns are found at the end of a manuscript dated 1130 and produced in the same abbey. Moreover, four among them are mentioned in the mid-12th-century necrology of the same house (see Thoma 1951).

records.rec_Title: Dorothea Marchionissa, Bamberg, Female, Bamberg, Staatsbibliothek, Lit. 18, Proofs

details.value: This present work, along with twelve other volumes, was begun by Brother Franciscus Mathie of the Observant branch of the Friars Minor, under the provincial vicar, the reverend Father Johannes of Lindefelcz, at St. Clare’s in Bamberg, in the small monastery or residence of the confessor of the virgins and sisters of St. Clare, under Abbess Katharina Sensenschmid, with the worthy confessor Jodocus Cutzenbach, whose soul may rest in peace. In the year of the Incarnation 1498, around the feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, it was happily completed by the same Brother Franciscus, the least of priests, with his own hand. The work was not (!) illuminated, bound, or corrected under the reverend Father Johannes Keller, provincial vicar, the noble Abbess Dorothea Marchioness, and Father Frederico Gerberstorfer, the well-known confessor at that time, in the year of salvation 1501, on the eve of the feast of the Purification of the Immaculate Virgin Mary (etc.).

value.title: Bamberg, Staatsbibliothek, Lit. 18

details.value: Presens opus cum alijs XII voluminibus incepit fr. Franciscus Mathie de observantia O.Min. sub vicario provinciali patre utique rev. Iohanne de Lindefelcz apud s. details.value:
In the year of our Lord’s birth 1483, on St. Sylvester’s Day, I, Dorothea von Hof, wrote out this book. And in the previous autumn, on St. Fridolin’s Day in the year 1482, I was 24 years old. And it was nine years since St. Paul’s Conversion Day in the year ’83 that Jörg and I were joined together in marriage. Love overcomes all things. Deo gratias.

Also, when I was 19 years old on St. Verena’s Day, I went, on the following Holy Cross Day, on pilgrimage to Einsiedeln with an “angel’s garment,” and there I cast down my worldly clothing and finery, which I no longer wore thereafter.

Dorothea von Hof (1458-1501), née Ehingerin
From the possession of Margarete Ehingerin, née Neidhart (died 1513), married since 1482 to the Constance patrician Hans Ehinger (1456–1505), son of Heinrich Ehinger and Margarete von Kappel; cf.the alliance coat of arms Ehinger/Neidhart 2r and the ownership entry 357r: This book belongs to Margreth Ehingerjn in Mergstat. Contrary to earlier opinions, it was therefore not the older Margarete Ehinger, née von Kappel (died 1490?), but rather her daughter-in-law who owned this manuscript (cf.Gebauer [2010] p. 37 f.[with family tree]); she was thus likely also the sister-in-law of the scribe, Dorothea von Hof, née Ehingerin. Regarding three other manuscripts from the possession of the older Ehinger generation, see Nos. 36.0.2. (Einsiedeln Stiftsbibliothek, Codex 710), No. 43.1.55. (Einsiedeln, Stiftsbibliothek, Codex 283), and No. 59.2.5. (St. Gallen, Kantonsbibliothek, VadSlg. Ms. 343 c–d).

f.57ra-138rb = Konrad Bischoff : Legend of St. Otto (Wü)
f.138rb-164ra = 'Catherine of Alexandria' (prose legend), French, East French

A collection of manuscripts, written primarily on paper, which can be localized to Bamberg. The first part of the manuscript contains a German mirror of salvation. Erasmus Sternhals is identified as its writer in a colophon. The work was probably made for the Bamberg canon Georg von Löwenstein. This is indicated by the depiction of a kneeling canon and several coats of arms on f.56r. The German-language biography of the Holy Bishop Otto, which is bound in afterwards, also refers to Bamberg. It was written down by two Bamberg Poor Clares and completed in 1483. The third work in the collection is a life of Saint Catherine, dated 1488 and also written by a woman.

records.rec_Title: Elisabeth Muntprat, St. Gallen, Female, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), Unclear

value.title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch")

details.value:
This manuscript, which in earlier scholarship was often referred to as a “Chronicle,” is in fact the Konventsbuch (Convent Book) of St Katharina in St Gall (61r: “…und sol dis also in des convents buoch gesetz werden…”).

It contains chronological entries concerning the economic interests of the convent. The manuscript was compiled during the reform period, at a time when the convent was transitioning from private ownership to communal property. As such, the book enabled the leadership of St Katharina to account to the community for the management of its assets. It also allowed the sisters to keep track of the property they had originally brought into the convent.

The manuscript includes records relating to building activities, furnishings, the scriptorium, legal disputes, and donations, as well as entries concerning individual sisters, confessors, or workers, and—more sporadically—notes on the history of the convent.

The chronicle contains reports and notes from a wide variety of areas of contemporary convent history: Angela Varnbühler 's investing hand begins (ex post) with her election as prioress in 1476, and continues with a list of the conventuals as well as reports from the implementation of the first Steps to reform the monastery. The other entries, in chronological order, concern a wide variety of events from everyday convent life: entry of novices and their later profession; News of death (from conventuals, relatives and friends); Endowments (of seasons and interest) and gifts; Book production in the scriptorium; Economy of the monastery (conductor's annual accounts, administration, land acquisition [fields, forests, vineyards]); Expansion and conversion as well as artistic furnishings of the monastery buildings; Contemporary events from the history of the monastery and order - even the event of the solar eclipse in 1485 found its way into the chronicle with an entry by the prioress (f.45r ).

details.value: Here is completed the legend of Saint Francis. It was written by Elspet of Amberg in the year when one counted from Christ’s birth one thousand three hundred and in the thirty-seventh year [i.e. 1337]. And Katerina of Burghausen wrote the legend of Saint Anthony, and she was sixty-seven years old when she wrote the legend. And the legends were both written and illuminated and fully completed on the day after the feast of Saint Bartholomew. Whoever reads the legends, let him pray to God for them, and also for those who carried out the parchment-making and the binding, that God may help us all to the honourable company of the beloved lord Saint Francis and the worthy lady Saint Clare. Amen.

details.value: Here ends the legend of Saint Francis. This was written by Elspet von Amberk in the year counted from Christ's birth as one thousand three hundred and thirty-seven. Then Katerina von Purchhausen wrote the legend of Saint Anthony. She was sixty-seven years old when she wrote the legend. The legends were completed, illuminated, and perfected after Saint Bartholomew's day at night. Whoever reads the legend, pray to God for her, and for [crossed out] also for those who have sponsored and arranged it, may God help us all to the honorable company of the beloved Saint Francis and the venerable lady Saint Clare. Amen.

value.title: Lucerne, Provincial Archives of the Swiss Capuchins, PAL L

details.value:
(f.126r) Hie ist volendet di legend von sand Franciscen. Die hat geschriben Elspet von Amberk in den iar, do man zalt von Chistes geburt tausent und driuhundert und in dem xxxvij iar. So hat Katerina von Purchhausen geschriben di legend von sancto Antonio. Und diu was in den lxvij iar alt, da si di legend schreip. Und di legend wurden peid geschriben vnd erleuht und volpraht nah sand Bartholomeus des na’htes tages. Amen.

records.rec_Title: Elizabeth von Winsen, Medingen, Female, Hildesheim, Cathedral Library, Hs. J 27, Full manuscript

details.value: Here ends what the deepest thoughts of the heart reveal, written by hand and with the full use of the body, as will be clearly seen by the eye that examines all. Written with flowers, so let us join illustration with text. All this was done and completed by the servant alone in the cloister of Meding, situated near Luneburg. I confess that I belong to the Cistercian order and use the name known to all, called Elisabeth of Winsen. To my own glory and to the glory of Christ, in the year one thousand, four hundred, and ten, with ten added and sixty-three with five combined, on the venerable feast day of Christ, by the command of the venerable Lord Provost Tylemann of Bavensted, and for the sake of ministering to the needs, for the love of my beloved friend, Elisabeth of Bavensted.

value.title: Hildesheim, Cathedral Library, Hs. J 27

Würzburg Universitätsbibliothek, M.ch.f.4, A collection of manuscripts, written primarily on paper, which can be localized to Bamberg. The first part of the manuscript contains a German mirror of salvation. Erasmus Sternhals is identified as its writer in a colophon. The work was probably made for the Bamberg canon Georg von Löwenstein. This is indicated by the depiction of a kneeling canon and several coats of arms on f.56r. The German-language biography of the Holy Bishop Otto, which is bound in afterwards, also refers to Bamberg. It was written down by two Bamberg Poor Clares and completed in 1483. The third work in the collection is a life of Saint Catherine, dated 1488 and also written by a woman.

records.rec_Title: Eugenia, France, Female, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 7560, Full manuscript

value.title: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 7560

details.value:
Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, BnF Latin 7560, Des annotations et corrections interlinéaires sans doute de la main de la copiste : f.4r, 5r, 33r-34r, 39r, 42r, 44r, 46v-54r ; et d’autres mains : f.41r-43v, 47r-47v. Des annotations marginales de diverses mains : au f.1r, la cote Colbert, la cote Regius répétée deux fois, la cote actuelle, une ligne d’un chant religieux (« Nunctio uere quia misit dominus angelimi »), et des neumes (orisci catalans et neumes aquitains ; on en trouve aussi au f.54v) ; d’autres annotations à connotation religieuse sont à noter aux f.6r, 42v et 54v ; un certain nombre d’annotations sont illisibles ou effacées (f.11r, 22r, 40r et 54r) ; on peut également mentionner un astérisque au f.45r, un « y » au f.49r et, d’une main moderne, « 307 » sur le f.54v. 
Comme l’indiquent C. Jeudy (1974, p. 129-130) et B. Bischoff (2014, p. 128-129) dans leur notice respective, le manuscrit a été copié dans le troisième quart du IXe siècle en France, dans un scriptorium d’influence insulaire, par une copiste du nom d’Eugenia, qui donne son nom dans une souscription rédigée en lettres grecques (mais en langue latine) au f.54r (voir H. OMONT, 1905, p. 15 pour la transposition). Il a peut-être été copié dans le Sud de la France ou en Catalogne, ou du moins s’y est trouvé très vite après sa copie, car la main légèrement postérieure à la première (fin du IXe siècle) qui ajoute les carmina des f.54r et 54v est caractérisée par des traits wisigothiques et des neumes d’Aquitaine et orisci catalans ont été notés sur les f.1r et 54v vers la même période.

Item diit boeck is volscreven int jaer ons heren vijftien hondert ende xxx ende heeft geeynt op sante antonys avont ende heeft gescreven suster foelsken hoeymans diet uut mynnen om gods wil int sieck huys gescreven heeft in hoeren enen tachtichsten jaren een Ave maria uut mynnen om gods wil.

This Middle Dutch prayer-book was partially copied (ff. 121r-210v) by a religious woman named ‘Foelsken Hoeymans’. Her identity is known from another manuscript that originates from the female Franciscan tertiaries of Hessenberg in Nijmegen (Nijmegen, Regionaal Archief, MS I a 29). The female scribe, according to a colophon (f. 210v), copied the manuscript in the convent’s hospital at the age of 81. The manuscript appears to have been written for use in the hospital as well, since the majority of its texts concern prayers for the ill, dying and deceased, Ars moriendi-treatises, and a treatise on patient suffering.

details.value: This present work, along with twelve other volumes, was begun by Brother Franciscus Mathie of the Observant branch of the Friars Minor, under the provincial vicar, the reverend Father Johannes of Lindefelcz, at St. Clare’s in Bamberg, in the small monastery or residence of the confessor of the virgins and sisters of St. Clare, under Abbess Katharina Sensenschmid, with the worthy confessor Jodocus Cutzenbach, whose soul may rest in peace. In the year of the Incarnation 1498, around the feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, it was happily completed by the same Brother Franciscus, the least of priests, with his own hand. The work was not (!) illuminated, bound, or corrected under the reverend Father Johannes Keller, provincial vicar, the noble Abbess Dorothea Marchioness, and Father Frederico Gerberstorfer, the well-known confessor at that time, in the year of salvation 1501, on the eve of the feast of the Purification of the Immaculate Virgin Mary (etc.).

details.value: f. 42v-55v, almost every entry is by a different hand, including the two first and probably two further hands.

Hamersleben group, Script comparison
In f. 42v-55v, almost every entry is by a different hand, including the two first and probably two further hands.

Main text in carolino-gothica by at least five hands of the so-called “Hamersleben group”:
 • Hand 1 (main hand): 1v–23v, 26r–41r, 42v–43v, 56r–70v (also occasional interlinear corrections and additions on some leaves written by the other hands).
 • Hand 2: 24r–25v, 35v (only an insertion), 41r–42v.
 • Then, from 42v–55v, almost every entry is by a different hand, including the two first and probably two further hands.
 • Hand 5: 70v–79v.
The additional notes and verses inserted on 2r–3r, 4v–6v, 7v–9r, 10v, 12r–v, 14v–15r, 16r–v, 17v–18r, 25r, 27r, and 68r–70v are by a hand of the so-called “Scriptrix group.”

Latin

Carolino-Gothica by four different hands.
 • The main hand (Hand 1) is associated with the Scriptrix group (a network of identified female scribes at Lamspringe).
 • Hands 2–4 show affinities with the Hamersleben group.
Hand 1 (main hand): 1r line 4 – 200v line 10.
Hand 2: 1v, line 4 – end of page.
Hand 3: 24v, lines 19–20 (on erasure).
Hand 4: 189r, lines 20–23.

Hand 1 (main hand) is, according to Cohen-Mushlin, identical in script to the Augustinus text in 903 Helmst., fols. 1r–75r, which Härtel assigns to the Scriptrix group (Cohen-Mushlin, 165; Härtel Geschrieben und gemalt, 85).
	•	Hand 2 has, according to Cohen-Mushlin, similarities to both hands of 204 Helmst., to 903 Helmst., fols. 75v–142v (Hand 2 – the hand of the Gregory text), and to 480 Helmst., fol. 1v (Cohen-Mushlin, 165).

 • Cohen-Mushlin attributes several image captions and possibly much of the artwork to the scribe/artist Ermengard, active in other Lamspringe codices (e.g., 204 Helmst.). Two principal artist-hands:
 • Hand A (Ermengard?): 102r, 148v, and most historiated initials.
 • Hand B: 164r, showing slightly different proportions and palette.
 • Stylistic links to other Lamspringe manuscripts and to Cologne workshop influences.

Explicit compendium theologice virtutis (sic). Deo dicimus gratias. Scriptum per Henrietam anno Domini M°CCCLVI.
Perscriptum a Henrieta de Lathilliaco, anno LV (not a clear reading), iovis post festum beati Luce (22 October 1355).

Hugo Ripelin, Compendium theologicae veritatis, written between the lines and on the margins of a codex containing biblical texts from the 12th century. The space intended for the gloss, which was left blank, was occupied by the new text. The dimensions of the manuscript (ff.195) are 320x215 mm, the space for the original text is 208x90 mm for 18 lines on a full page. Many of the sheets were partially cut, presumably to make parchment. In 1354, before the new text was added, the codex had belonged to Nicasius, curate of 'Casiacum' (Chezy-sur-Marne, Aisne), as can be deduced from the ex libris on f.195v.The manuscript was later transferred to Saint-Germain-des-Prés (ex libris of the 16th century on f.195v and of the 18th century, with the signature 116, on the unnumbered sheet preceding f.1).

details.value: Two Merovingian saints from Hesbaye, who were successively abbesses of Aldeneik on the Meuse. According to their Vita, the two sisters had received a careful education: they had learned to read, to sing, to paint, and to write—activities which, their biographer notes, even strong men would have found arduous. They later settled in the family monastery, where they devoted themselves, among other things, to passementerie work to embellish ritual garments. They also copied, again according to their biographer, the Gospels, a psalter, and other sacred writings.

According to their Vita, the two sisters had received a careful education: they had learned to read, to sing, to paint, and to write—activities which, their biographer notes, even strong men would have found arduous. They later settled in the family monastery, where they devoted themselves, among other things, to passementerie work to embellish ritual garments. They also copied, again according to their biographer, the Gospels, a psalter, and other sacred writings.

details.value:
2. fols. 204ra–228vb - Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas: De beatitudine. Translated by Thomas Finck
Ends with colophon stating completion at the Benedictine house in Ehingen, on St Kilian’s day, 1489.
3. fols. 229rb–260ra - Jacob of Paradise: On the apparitions of separated souls (German translation, probably by Thomas Finck). Text dated internally to 1482.
4. fols. 260rb–271ra - Thomas Finck (?): Sayings of the holy teachers. A collection of moral and spiritual maxims, addressed to women religious.
5. fols. 271va–292ra - Pelagius (Pseudo-Jerome): Letter to Demetrias (German)
6. fols. 292va–302va - Johannes Gerson: On spiritual mendicancy (German translation, probably by Thomas Finck)
7. fols. 303ra–315vb - Johannes of Kastl: On the goal of religious perfection (formerly De adhaerendo Deo). Translated by Thomas Finck, explicitly for devout women.
8. fols. 316va–329ar - The “42 Golden Rules”. A reform text for spiritual life.
9. fols. 330ra–336rb - Bonaventure: Letter containing 25 memorials (German translation, probably by Thomas Finck)
10. fols. 336va–342rb - Pseudo-Augustine (Guigo II the Carthusian): Scala paradisi. Translated by Thomas Finck, dated 1485.
11. fols. 342va–345va - Ludolf of Saxony: Vita Christi, Book II, ch. 41 (German translation, probably by Thomas Finck)
12. fols. 345vb–347va - Fourteen causes by which a person may recognize their imperfection
13. fols. 347va–348rb - Mass prayer (“Trina oratio”), attributed to Pope Gregory the Great
14. fol. 348va–b - Collection of sayings on penance
15. fols. 349ra–350rb - On temptation among members of religious orders
16. fols. 351va–381vb - Thomas Finck: Treatise on the Canonical Hours
17. fols. 381vb–387vb - Instruction for proper conduct during the Divine Office

details.value: Jouarre Laud 1, Ascribed to Chelles by Bischoff, to Jouarre by McKitterick., Low

1. (f.1r) Charlemagne, De litteris colendis - Added in German Anglo-Saxon minuscule, c. 800.
2. (fols. 2r-259v) - Augustine, De trinitate (CPL 329) - Preceded by ep. 174 (Ad Aurelium de trinitate), f.2r.

Most recently edited by M. J. Lapidge, The Anglo-Saxon Library, 148–51., Latin, Fols. 1r, 260r: additions in German Anglo-Saxon minuscule.,

Oxford, Bodleian Library, Laud misc 126, Can't be consulted (restricted)
At least fifteen hands.
(note: Jouarre was a double monastery, so these scribes could be women or men)
Origin North France, doubtless Chelles. The peculiar uncial and the decoration connect this MS with the group represented by the famous Sacramentary, Vatic. Regin. Lat. 316 (CLA 1.105). On f.1 is added in Anglo-Saxon script saec. VIII–IX Charlemagne's Letter to Abbot Baugulf of Fulda, and on f.260 a library catalogue, perhaps of Würzburg (see CLA plate). Belonged to St Kilian's of Würzburg certainly by the ninth century, as is shown by the entry on f.1v ('. . . faciat eum sancto Kiliano restitui'). The same page has the Würzburg ex-libris saec. XIII. Acquired by Archbishop Laud before 1638.

records.rec_Title: Justina Blarer, St. Gallen, Female, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), f.86r, f.87r, f.87v - 88v, f.96v - 97r, f.111v - 114v and passim em

value.title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch")

details.value: f.86r , f.87r , f.87v - 88v , f.96v - 97r , f.111v - 114v and passim em

This manuscript, which in earlier scholarship was often referred to as a “Chronicle,” is in fact the Konventsbuch (Convent Book) of St Katharina in St Gall (61r: “…und sol dis also in des convents buoch gesetz werden…”).

It contains chronological entries concerning the economic interests of the convent. The manuscript was compiled during the reform period, at a time when the convent was transitioning from private ownership to communal property. As such, the book enabled the leadership of St Katharina to account to the community for the management of its assets. It also allowed the sisters to keep track of the property they had originally brought into the convent.

The manuscript includes records relating to building activities, furnishings, the scriptorium, legal disputes, and donations, as well as entries concerning individual sisters, confessors, or workers, and—more sporadically—notes on the history of the convent.

The chronicle contains reports and notes from a wide variety of areas of contemporary convent history: Angela Varnbühler 's investing hand begins (ex post) with her election as prioress in 1476, and continues with a list of the conventuals as well as reports from the implementation of the first Steps to reform the monastery. The other entries, in chronological order, concern a wide variety of events from everyday convent life: entry of novices and their later profession; News of death (from conventuals, relatives and friends); Endowments (of seasons and interest) and gifts; Book production in the scriptorium; Economy of the monastery (conductor's annual accounts, administration, land acquisition [fields, forests, vineyards]); Expansion and conversion as well as artistic furnishings of the monastery buildings; Contemporary events from the history of the monastery and order - even the event of the solar eclipse in 1485 found its way into the chronicle with an entry by the prioress (f.45r ).

Illumination(s) in Directorium chorii, Cantus sororum, Latin; Swedish,

This manuscript was written in Vadstena Abbey, in the nuns scriptorium. The parchment was payed by sr Birgitta Gudmundi and it was completed at S Michaels eve 1517. It was written by one of the nuns, keeping her identity secret in the colophon on f.37v. It contained music and was intended for use in the church. There are closely related manuscripts in both Uppsala and Stockholm Libraries, either written or decorated by the same nun/nuns. The nuns had taken influence from their sisters i the Netherlands in the design of the large pen-flourished initials. One of the nuns who most frequently painted her large decorated initials in the same style as here was Christina Hansdotter Brask, but she seem to have hade successors. A very similar design can be found in KB A 12, UUB C 431, C 443, C 484, RA E 9002. Some of these are by Christina Hansdotter Brask and from the same period as this manuscript. The present mss is however executed by a much more stable hand than the Brask mss from the same period. A more suitable candidate is Katarina Gudmundsdotter, whose palaeography is in accordance with the scribe of this mss.

This book was commissioned by Sister Elseby, the daughter of Gyrd, for the convent when she was serving as the cantor. It was written on parchment purchased with the silver belt gifted by her maternal aunt, Mistress Kristin Björn Nielson, which was valued at 24 marks. This book was written by a sister of the convent in the year of our Lord 1502, during the time when our beloved Mother Sister Anna Fickonis was abbess, to the honor of God and for the spiritual benefit of all my dear sisters.

records.rec_Title: Katerina of Burghausen, Female, Lucerne, Provincial Archives of the Swiss Capuchins, PAL B1, f. 126-175

details.value: Here is completed the legend of Saint Francis. It was written by Elspet of Amberg in the year when one counted from Christ’s birth one thousand three hundred and in the thirty-seventh year [i.e. 1337]. And Katerina of Burghausen wrote the legend of Saint Anthony, and she was sixty-seven years old when she wrote the legend. And the legends were both written and illuminated and fully completed on the day after the feast of Saint Bartholomew. Whoever reads the legends, let him pray to God for them, and also for those who carried out the parchment-making and the binding, that God may help us all to the honourable company of the beloved lord Saint Francis and the worthy lady Saint Clare. Amen.

records.rec_Title: Katherina van Ghiseghem, Brussels, Female, Brussels, Bibliothèque royale Albert Ier, Ms.15136, Full manuscript

details.value: In the year of our Lord one thousand four hundred seventy-two. On the feast day of Saints Peter and Paul in June, Sister Katherina van Ghiseghem, professed nun in our cloister at Jericho, began to write this book on the tabernacle. And she completed it in the same year, on the fourth day of April, on the feast day of Saint Ambrose, which fell on a Sunday. She did this in honor of God and for the common edification with great diligence, working on it diligently at all chosen times when she was not engaged in communal work. She was twenty-six years old at the time. Pray for her eternal salvation out of love for God. This book belongs to the cloister of Our Lady Rose-planted in Jericho, within Brussels, near Saint Catherine's, of the Augustinian order. Whoever finds it, return it to the religious ladies for the love of God.

details.value: Here ends the legend of Saint Francis. This was written by Elspet von Amberk in the year counted from Christ's birth as one thousand three hundred and thirty-seven. Then Katerina von Purchhausen wrote the legend of Saint Anthony. She was sixty-seven years old when she wrote the legend. The legends were completed, illuminated, and perfected after Saint Bartholomew's day at night. Whoever reads the legend, pray to God for her, and for [crossed out] also for those who have sponsored and arranged it, may God help us all to the honorable company of the beloved Saint Francis and the venerable lady Saint Clare. Amen.

Cursive book script by three different hands:
 1. f.s 7r-145v, 164r-225v, 227r-257v by Kunigund Niklasin.
 2. f.s 2r-4v, 148r-158r, 171r-v, 226r-v, 230r-v, 258r-281v, and fragments at 5r and 289r by Klara Keiperin.
 3. Later additions at the end of the 15th or early 16th century (282r after the text).

Copied by Kunigund Niklasin and Klara Keiperin from a book borrowed from the convent by a virgin named Anna Winterin, which was later passed to Margareta Scheurerin in Pforzheim.

Of the original three-volume work (previously signed E I–III), only this second volume has survived.

Part of C08 was written in the years 1473–1486, when Margareta Claesdotter was abbess. The name of the scribe cannot be determined here in a fully objective manner. In the second part, the name of the scribe is certain, but the dating is not sufficiently precise. However, in 1486 Anna Fickesdotter became prioress, and this would probably have been mentioned in some way if the manuscript had been written after that year. There is, however, no doubt that the hand is the same in both parts. Kristina Johansdotter Brask wrote the directorium chori.

Cursive book script by three different hands:
 1. f.s 7r-145v, 164r-225v, 227r-257v by Kunigund Niklasin.
 2. f.s 2r-4v, 148r-158r, 171r-v, 226r-v, 230r-v, 258r-281v, and fragments at 5r and 289r by Klara Keiperin.
 3. Later additions at the end of the 15th or early 16th century (282r after the text).

Copied by Kunigund Niklasin and Klara Keiperin from a book borrowed from the convent by a virgin named Anna Winterin, which was later passed to Margareta Scheurerin in Pforzheim.

Of the original three-volume work (previously signed E I–III), only this second volume has survived.

Dice sancto Tomaso de Aquino: obediencia è virtù, ff.85r-113r); Orazioni (in latino e volgare, ff.114r-115v); Regula perfecte religionis (in volgare, inc. Audi filia et vide et inclina aurem tuam ... Al nome de Dio ... et del beato glorioso miser sancto Iovany Batista del quale vogliamo dire alcuna cosa, ff.143r-218r), Italian,

Rome, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Varia 24 (574), Lana dei Galvagni is not self-identified as a nun – but the contents of the ms. point to that conclusion – especially the “Regula perfecte religionis”. It was sent to a “Fra Giustino romano cappuccino predicatore” from Venice (f.218r). Lana states her name as “Lana de Galvagni fiola che fu de miser zan Bertolameo” (f.219v) – is this the Venetian Zuan? If so, this would again point to its production as Venetian. Lana wrote “Franciscus et Claram” on f.219v – was she possibly from a house of Clarissans? The ms. came from the Augustinian convent of Gesù e Maria in Rome

value.title: London, British Library, Egerton Ms.2849/1

details.value:
The mortuary roll of Lucy of Hedingham was produced c.1225-1230 to mark the death of the foundress and first prioress of the Benedictine nunnery of Castle Hedingham in Essex. The prioress is only identified as Lucy, and her identity is uncertain; she was probably a noblewoman connected to the de Vere family, as Aubrey de Vere (b. c. 1115, d. 1194), 1st earl of Oxford, founded the nunnery in 1191. The roll is believed to be the oldest intact English illuminated mortuary roll. The roll was sent to 122 religious houses in the southern half of England, each writing an answer to a request for prayers made by Agnes, Prioress of Hedingham, for the soul of her predecessor Lucy. The respondants include the Cambridge Franciscans, established there in 1226, hence the dating of the roll to approximately 1225-1230.

The roll comprises two parts, which are now stored separately: Egerton MS 2849/1 is the first part of the roll, including the heading, illumination and tituli (responsive prayers added by various houses) 1-6, and Egerton MS 2849/2, which is the second part of the roll, including tituli 7-122.

records.rec_Title: Loppa von Spiegel, Cologne, Female, London, Victoria and Albert Museum, Inv.-Nr. 8997 I, Full manuscript

details.value: Loppa von Spiegel, Cologne, Script comparison, Medium
, Leaf from an Antiphoner from the Franciscan Convent of St Klara, Cologne, Latin,

London, Victoria and Albert Museum, Inv.-Nr. 8997 I, An Antiphonal contains the choral parts sung during the celebration of the Divine Office or Mass celebrated by a monastic or other community. This type of choirbook was usually written in large format so that the whole choir could read the music at once. This example was made at the convent of St Klara in Cologne by one of the nuns, Sister Loppa de Speculo. Another surviving leaf records that Sister Jutta paid for the book while Loppa carried out the writing, lining (putting in the staves for the music), notation and illumination 'in the year 1350, when there was a great plague everywhere'. This was one of a series of books produced in the convent. The Abbess, Heylwigis von Beechoven, who had ruled the convent since 1344, is portrayed kneeling by the historiated initial of the Descent of the Holy Ghost on the Virgin and Apostles associating her prayer with this crucial event, when the Holy Spirit came to earth and the mission of the Apostles to spread the Christian revelation began. The prayer of her convent was thus part of the mission.

In the year 1494 the venerable mother Margreta Grundtherrin died in the convent of St Clare; she had been prioress there for 43 years and died in the 56th year of her age. This venerable Margreta Grundtherrin wrote this little book herself on parchment; she lies buried there in the church of St Clare.

Karlsruhe, Badische Landesbibliothek, Lichtent. 69, Written in a bastarda script predominantly by Sister Regula, except for:
 • f.46ra (7 lines)
 • f.222vb–223rb (two contemporary hands)
 • f.51v (an addition around 1500).
Corrections and additions, mostly by the original scribe, are present.

Book of Holy Maidens and Women (f.1ra–223rb)
 • Introduction: Discusses the four cardinal virtues symbolized by the four rivers of paradise (Ortus voluptatis).
 • Legends: A collection of 57 legends of female saints, beginning with St. Mary Magdalene (Maria stabat ad monumentum foris plorans).
 • Provenance: Compiled by Sister Regula, as noted in secondary literature (e.g., K. Kunze).
 • Literature: The legend of Mary of Egypt has been edited by K. Kunze (1978).
 2. Pseudo-Eusebius, Epistola ad Damasum de Morte Hieronymi, German Translation (f.223va–228rb, 267va–278rb)
 • A medieval German adaptation of the Latin text (BHL 3866), attributed to Pseudo-Eusebius, concerning the death of St. Jerome.
 • The German translation does not match other known Middle High German versions.
 3. Pseudo-Jerome, Letter to His Mother on Virtues (f.229ra–240rb)
 • An instructional and exhortative letter, in which “Jerome” advises his mother on virtuous living.
 • The manuscript’s version is not mentioned in key reference works.
 4. The Golden Pater Noster (f.240rb–243rb)
 • An expanded meditation on the Pater Noster (Our Father) prayer, reflecting on its theological implications.
 • Includes parallels with Patrologia Latina (PL 149, 569–576).
 5. A Short Gloss on the Pater Noster (f.243rb–244ra)
 • A brief guide on the meaning and spiritual significance of the prayer.
 6. The School of Virtues (f.244ra–252vb)
 • A didactic dialogue between a master and a novice (later referred to as a novitiate), discussing ascetic virtues and leading to eternal life.
 7. Epistola ad Moniales (f.252vb–255ra)
 • An exhortative letter to nuns, urging them to heed divine inspiration and embrace the love of Christ.
 8. Dicta on the Gift of Tears and Prayer (f.255ra–255vb)
 • Spiritual reflections and teachings attributed to Augustine, Basil, Paschasius, and Bernard.
 9. An Epistle to an Abbess (f.255va–259ra)
 • A letter emphasizing love and obedience, comparing divine love to the strength of death, and exalting Christ as the bridegroom of virgins.
Ascetic Instructions (f.259ra–262va)
 • A text composed for the “entertainment of young cloistered nuns” by a learned priest.
 • Focuses on ascetic ideals and encouragement, referring to the nuns as Christ’s chosen spouses.
 • Likely written specifically for the Lichtenthal convent.
 2. Another Epistle on Five Virtues (f.262va–264vb)
 • Opens with Ponite corda vestra in virtute eius (Ps 47,14), emphasizing the virtues that adorn a faithful life.
 • Encourages the practice of virtues to achieve eternal blessedness.
 • Ends with a devotional note from the scribe, requesting a recitation of one Ave Maria.
 • Mentions Liber Monasterii Lucida Vallis, linking it to Lichtenthal Abbey (often called Lucida Vallis in Latin).
 3. On True Poverty (f.265ra–266ra)
 • Draws on Matthew 12:1 to explore the virtue of poverty in imitation of Christ and his disciples.
 • Provides a theological framework for embracing material poverty as a spiritual ideal.
 4. A Consolatory Sermon by St. Bernard (f.266ra–267ra)
 • Begins with Bonum est nos hic esse (Mt 17:4), using Bernard of Clairvaux’s alleged reflections to address monastic audiences.
 • Discusses the joys and trials of cloistered life and the ultimate reward of eternal glory.
 5. Poem on the Meaning of Suffering (f.267ra)
 • A six-stanza poem offering solace to those enduring hardships, linking suffering to the promise of the Kingdom of Heaven.
 • Contains irregularities in verse and stanza structure, reflecting its devotional rather than literary focus.
 6. Return to Pseudo-Eusebius, Epistola ad Damasum (f.267va–278rb)
 • This section resumes from f.223va, completing the translation of Pseudo-Eusebius’s text on the death of St. Jerome.

details.value: In the name of God, on the 4th day of April 1484. This I have copied for my consolation from the sermons of Master Mariano the Roman, preached during Lent in Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence. If there are errors, it would be my fault: I did not keep them well in memory. I, Margherita, daughter of Messer Tommaso Soderini, wrote this with my own hand. Whoever reads it, pray to God for me. If it is written well, it was a gift of God, and I thank Him. All good comes from God; all evil is from me.

value.title: Florence, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze, Magl. XXXV 98

details.value: Margherita’s hand, free from formal constraints, is an outstanding example of personal, highly cursive writing, with clear mercantile influences—notably the ligatures of d with the following vowel and the widely splayed form of r.

f. 3v: Al nome di Dio, a dì 4 d'aprile 1484. Questo o ritrato a mia chonsolatione delle prediche di maestro Mariano romano, di quaresima, in Santa Maria del Fiore in Firenze. Se ci fusi manchamento, sarebe mio difetto: non arei tenuto bene a mente. Io Margherita figliuola di meser Tommaso Soderini o scritto questo di mia mano. Chi lo legie prieghi Idio per me. Se gli è scritto bene, è stato dono di Dio e Lui ringratio. Tutto el bene vien da Dio, tutto el male son io.

details.value:
Completed in praise and honor / Of Mary and God the Lord /
And in deepest devotion above all / Margreten Vesslerin is her name. /
A worthy and praiseworthy sister / From Wilperg, in the little town nearby, /
Who confirmed God’s power / With all her sisters, young and old. /
When they offer their prayers during Mass, / Let them not forget the scribe of this book, /
Which was written in truth in the year / One thousand five hundred and fourteen, /
On the eve of tender Magdalene / Who was forgiven all her sins. /
May she secure for us God’s blessing / Here and there, eternal life. /
Amen. / 1514.

Maria Dies de Oña, Burgos, Colophon, High
, Gradual for Cistercian Use, part I, Latin,

Dallas, Bridwell Library, Southern Methodist University, BRMS 155, Produced, signed, and dated by the Spanish nun Maria Dies de Oña, this early sixteenth-century Spanish manuscript gradual contains the “propers” and choral chants for the Mass for Cistercian Use, according to the pre-Tridentine liturgical calendar. Although a complete volume, it is not a complete work as it contains approximately only the first third of the liturgical year, from the first Sunday in Advent to Palm Sunday. Given the size and format of this volume, the complete gradual for the entire liturgical year would have been represented by three or four volumes.

Produced by a female religious copyist for use by the female monastery of San Salvador de Oña in Burgos, this substantial volume is almost entirely composed of chant and does not include the long spoken portions of the Mass. Minor leaf repairs, occasional corrections, marginal additions, and instructions for following the text indicate that this manuscript was used on a regular basis.

Fulda, Landesbibliothek, Ms. Aa 125, The origin in a Franciscan convent is evidenced by:
	•	The feast of the stigmatization of St. Francis (135r) and the rubric on f.150r referring to von unßerm werdigen vader Franciscus (“our worthy Father Francis”).
	•	The suffrage for Severus, unserm Patrone (“our patron”) on f.162r, situated within the liturgical year sequence between November 11 and November 21, suggesting Boppard (Archdiocese of Trier).
In 1489, Franciscan sisters from Besselich settled in Boppard, known for their manuscript production (cf.J. Marx, Geschichte des Erzstifts Trier, vol. 2, part 2, 1862, p. 423, and K. Schlegel, Besselich am Mittelrhein, 1980, p. 19).

details.value: Here begins the prologue to the following sermons which our venerable father, Brother Jan Storm, preached in our monastery in Jericho when he was both our commissary and rector. These sermons, our esteemed mother, while she was not yet in the state of prelature, considering the heavy burden and labor of the said Honorable father, received the inspiration and devotion to transcribe these sermons, so that the labor of the preacher might be rewarded with eternal glory as often as anyone's devotion is moved to listen or study these sermons. Let us faithfully pray for our venerable father who has labored in preaching, and for our beloved mother, Sister Marie van Pee, may God grant her eternal peace, who has labored to transcribe this... So, I have endeavored to gather this following book from many sermons preached in our monastery over five years...

Here end the sermons of our Venerable fathers, which I have gathered a few of for my own edification and for those who wish to study. And they were completed in the year of our Lord, 1366, on the feast of Saint Laurence, the glorious martyr, before vespers.
This book was completed in the year of our Lord when it was written. Fourteen hundred and sixty-seven, on the sixth day of September, on a Sunday.

details.value:
Approximately 20 hands or textual sections can be distinguished. Various forms of Bastarda script are used. Since some scripts resemble each other closely, the number of hands may in fact be smaller, and some differences may be explained by different writing phases or circumstances.

The hands are identified as follows:
	•	Hand 1: 1r–7r (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 2: 8r–43v; Sister Regina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect with influences from Middle Bavarian).
	•	Hand 3: 44r–54v (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, probably with Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 4: 55r–v; identical with Hand 6 (75r–77v) and/or Hand 17 (242v–244v)?
	•	Hand 5: 56r–75v (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, probably with Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 6: 75v–77v; identical with Hand 4 (55r–v) and/or Hand 17 (242v–244v)?
	•	Hand 7: 78r–136v; Sister Rossina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, possibly with Alemannic influences).
	•	Hand 8: 137v–170v; Sister Veronica Hoffman(in) (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 9: 171r–193v; possibly identical with Hand 15 (231r–232v).
	•	Hand 10: 193v; identical with Hand 12 (195r–199v) and Hand 14 (200v–230r)?
	•	Hand 11: 194r–v; identical with Hand 13 (200r).
	•	Hand 12: 195r–199v; identical with Hand 10 (193v) and Hand 14 (200v–230v), i.e. with Sister Birgitta?
	•	Hand 13: 231r–232v; identical with Hand 11 (194r–v).
	•	Hand 14: 200v–230r; Sister Birgitta; identical with Hand 10 (193v) and Hand 12 (195r–199v)? (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 15: 231r–232v; possibly identical with Hand 9 (171r–193v).
	•	Hand 16: 233r–242r.
	•	Hand 17: 242v–244v; Susana; possibly identical with Hand 4 (55r–v) and/or Hand 6 (75r–77v).
	•	Hand 18: 245r–256v; Sister Eufrosina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, possibly with Upper Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 19: 257r–275v; Sister Justine (writing language: Nuremberg dialect?).
	•	Hand 20: 276r; Sister Apollonia Kastner (?; this is suggested at least by the entry das buͤchlin gehert muͤter Clara layin von s. Appolonia Kastner ewer getrewe s. in Christo).

value.title: Karlsruhe, Badische Landesbibliothek, Donaueschingen 365

details.value: ms. 425, f. 1r–2v, fol. 3v line 8 – fol. 79v; ms. 365, f. 1r–85v, line 5

Bastarda with slightly right-leaning ductus; individual letters hardly connected; letters d and a strongly angular; d both with and without loop, predominantly with loop; in loopless d (e.g. fol. 1r line 25; fol. 4r lines 3, 5–6; fol. 64r line 6) the d-bow forms a rhombus standing on a corner. Headstroke and beginning of the g shaft intersect; the lower g loop is not closed; lower shaft end of k broken and extended to the right; in double s and double f the shaft of the first s or f is strongly shortened. In the first line the ascenders are somewhat more extended and furnished with cadels.
H1 is probably identical with H1 in Don. 365

value.title: Karlsruhe, Badische Landesbibliothek, Donaueschingen 365

details.value: Strongly angular Bastarda of a high calligraphic standard with upright ductus; d consistently without loops, while most other letter forms show loops; the lower g loop is open and convexly curved. The scribe shows similarities to Hand 13 among the hands listed by Schneider for the writing school of the Nuremberg convent of St Catherine; cf. Karin Schneider, Die deutschen mittelalterlichen Handschriften. Beschreibung des Buchschmucks: Heinz Zirnbauer (Die Handschriften der Stadtbibliothek Nürnberg I), Wiesbaden 1965, p. XXXIII, with fig. 27; however, the two hands are not identical.

Stockholm, Kungliga Biblioteket, A82a, Anna Karlsdotter (d. before 1450), anglicized as Anna Charles in the Syon Martyrology (London, British Library, MS Additional 22285), who was responsible for a Latin and Swedish prayer-book (Stockholm, Kungliga bibliotheket, MS A82a), as brought to light by Claes Gejrot.6 Given that she was one of the four professed sisters who came from Vadstena to help establish Syon, it would be easy to conclude that later English postulants learnt something about manuscripts from Anna and perhaps her fellow Swedes, but there is no proof.


 1. Hand 1: (Later addition?) Schedula in cursive script.
 2. Hand 2: (Later addition?) Schedula in cursive script, f.5v (textualis).
 
3. Hand 3: Fols. 1r–3v, likely also 6r–13v, and possibly 53r–103r (textualis).
 4. Hand 4: Likely 13v–25r and possibly 53r–103r (textualis).
 5. Hand 5: Likely 25r–53r and possibly 53r–103r (textualis).
 6. Hand 6: Fols. 103r–108r (textualis).
 7. Hand 7: Fols. 108v–124v (textualis).
 8. Hand 8: f.125v (cursive).
 9. Hand 9: Fols. 125v–131r (cursive).
 10. Hand 10: Fols. 131r–138v (cursive).
 
11. Hand 11: (Later addition?) f.140v (cursive).

(Reference: Gejrot 1994, pp. 18–19.)

Scribe: A. K. [Anna Karlsdotter], Vadstena, f.140v.

London, Lambeth Palace Library, Ms. 546, Lambeth Palace Library MS 546 is a collection of devotional material written by a number of late fifteenth- or early sixteenth-century hands. The main contents are 'The xv Sorowes of oure lady' (fos 7v-20v) and the 'golden letany' (fos 34r-51v, with a preface on fos 29r-33v),4 with devotions in English, and prayers in English and Latin making up the rest of the volume. It is with one of these devotions, specifically its colophon, that the present note is concerned.

Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 29400 / 8, Written in Northeast France in the centre which produced the Cologne manuscripts of Augustine for Archbishop Hildebald (795–819), apparently the convent of Chelles. The fragment was used as a fly-leaf in a printed book (Asc. 837) which probably belonged to the small Augustinian house at Bernried in Bavaria: an entry saec. XVI referring to the obit of 'Johan Ducziner Brobst zu Berñriedt' (†15 August 1535) is seen on the recto.

details.value: ...Deo gracias. Dicz puch ist aussgeschriben worden do man czalt von vnsers lieben herren Jhesu Cristi gepurt M CCCC vnd yn dem XXXVII jar an vnsers lieben herren fronleichnams abent (29. May). Pytt got fu/e/r die schreyberin die dycz puch geschriben hat.

Three volumes of a Bible that was originally four volumes, but was originally planned to be six volumes or six volumes ( MBK III,3, p. 599f.): Cent. III,40 is referred to in old entries (1 r , 285 v ) as daz ander puch der bibel , Cent. III,41 (front cover, 258 va ) as Daz dritt puch der bibel, Cent. III,43 (front cover, 354 v ) as Daz VI puch der bibel. In the city library since 1538.
two hands: Kunigund Niklasin (1 ra –5 vb , 19 ra –109 rb , 135 ra –258 rb ) and another scribe (7 ra –18 vb , 109 va –134 rb )
corrections by another hand

20 slips of paper sewn to the lower margins contain instructions for illustrations, which are repeated on a sheet pasted to the inside front cover.

value.title: Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Cent. IV 30

details.value:
The ms. bore the signature E LXIII in Nuremberg's St. Catherine's Monastery .
Continuation in Nuremberg, Stadtbibl., Cod. Cent. V, 5
written in book cursive by the hand of Ursula Geiselherin; a second hand appears on f.s 185rb-189ra, 217vb-219rb; corrections and additions by a third hand.

Written by Ursula Geiselherin based on an exemplar from the Klarakloster (Poor Clares) in Nuremberg.

The exemplar is preserved in Berlin, germ. f.1276 (see Degering I, p. 171), formerly Cheltenham, Phillipps 19491 (see Priebsch, Deutsche Handschriften in England I (1896), p. 127, no. 131).

The copy made at the Katharinenkloster is in two volumes; Volume II = Cent. V, 5.

records.rec_Title: Ms. Oxford, Bodleian Library, Canon. Misc. 278, Unidentified Hand 1, Female, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Canon. Misc. 278, f. 97-128

details.value: ‘This was written in the year of Our Lord 1467, the 17th day of February. Pray for her who wrote this, per me SR’

value.title: Oxford, Bodleian Library, Canon. Misc. 278

details.value:
f. 128.
The colophon in red ink is written in the feminine form and can be found on the last folio of the second of three booklets that together make up Can. misc. 278.
‘Dit was ghescreven int jaer ons heeren / 1467 den 17sten dach van februarius / bit voor haer die dit heeft ghescreven / Per me SR’
It is the only known colophon from a Middle Dutch manuscript attributed to a secular female scribe and one of the rare examples of such attribution to female scribes in the late Middle Ages.

Collection of moralising verses
1. (fols 97–112)
Disticha Catonis (with Middle French translation by Jehan Le Fèvre)
Language(s): Middle French and Latin
Incipit: (prologue) Chaton fu preu chevalier e sage homme Mains bons consaulx en la cite de Romme
Incipit: (text) Si deus est animus nobis ut carmina dicunt
Incipit: (text) Soyes certain que dieu est et dois croire
Explicit: hec breuitas fecit coniungere binos
Explicit: En ce dittier en ay fait de doux quatre
2. (fol. 113r)
Prayer to the Virgin Mary
Language(s): Middle French
Incipit: Doulce vierge plaisant et coye Par qui vient tout honeur e joye
Explicit: Que jaye vraie contricion Et en la fin confession Amen
3. (fol. 113v)
Proverbs
Language(s): Middle French
Incipit: Qui a des pois en sa maison Du pain fetiz et du boillon
Explicit: Qui se souffit de ce que dieu luy donne Plus a asses que tel qui porte couronne
Fol. 114r blank.

4. (fols 115–118r)
Moralising poem
Language(s): Middle Dutch
Rubric: O menschen wilt dit lesen. Op dat ghij helich ende zalich moghet wesen. (added at the bottom of the otherwise blank fol. 114v)
Incipit: O mensche oft ghij docht ende wist den tijt
Explicit: Dat wij dan en wich met hem moeten leuen. Amen
5. (fols 118v–124)
Proverbs
Language(s): Middle Dutch
Incipit: Boetius seit. Alre wijsheyt fundament. Es dat men gode mint ende kent.
Explicit: In mijn enden moet ic \willic/ verblijden. Ende mijn ghebaren oft in mij gheen lijden en ware.
6. (fol. 125)
Poem on death
Language(s): Middle Dutch
Incipit: Ic wil leuen ende ic moet steruen. Dat ic hebbe des moet ic dernen.
Explicit: Want Jeghen die doot en es ghenen scilt. Elc leue also hij steruen wilt.
7. (fols 125v–126r)
Den gheesteliken A.B.C.
Language(s): Middle Dutch
Incipit: (prologue) Messe te hooren en laet met om gode te ghenen en aermt niet
Incipit: (text) Aen siet wanen ghij commen sijt.
Explicit: Z goet so sluut hier vp hu slot.
8. (fols 126r–128)
Moralising prose
Language(s): Middle Dutch
Incipit: Meester du leeres my vremde consten.
Explicit: Ende Jeghen die doot en es gheene scilt: Elc leue also hij steruen wilt:
Colophon: Dit was ghescreuven int Jaer ons heeren. .1467. den .17.sten dach van februarius bit voor h haer die dit heeft ghescreuen per me S. R.

Burgos, Santa María la Real de Las Huelgas, Ms. 6, The Consueta was compiled and copied by a single scribe (scribe A), who wrote the seven senions, in collaboration with another scribe who wrote the chapter headings in red ink (Rubricator A). According to Catalunya, “we can be sure that the two main scribes of Huelgas 6 (Scribe A &Rubricator A) were women. The Consueta was written entirely from the nuns’ perspective, but the clearest evidence that confirms the female identity is the use of verbs in first person to refer to the activities performed by the nuns (Catalunya, 2016, p. 110)
Later a secondary scribe (Scribe B) added three f.s at the beginning of the codex with a table of contents for all seven senions and annexed two consecutive bif.s at the end of the codex, on which the scribe B copied commentaries to the Rule of St Benedict. This scribe also corrected the text and the rubrics of certain chapters in the main body of the manuscript and added a foliation in red roman numerals on the right side of the upper margin of each recto. Written above it is a modern foliation in Arabic numerals, in pencil.
Many other secondary hands contributed with further corrections throughout the entire manuscript. This suggests that the codex was in use for some time after its compilation.

Part of C08 was written in the years 1473–1486, when Margareta Claesdotter was abbess. The name of the scribe cannot be determined here in a fully objective manner. In the second part, the name of the scribe is certain, but the dating is not sufficiently precise. However, in 1486 Anna Fickesdotter became prioress, and this would probably have been mentioned in some way if the manuscript had been written after that year. There is, however, no doubt that the hand is the same in both parts. Kristina Johansdotter Brask wrote the directorium chori.

fols. 1r–36v Epistola de vita et passione domini nostri Jesu Christi, translated by Johannes Busch, Latin.

This is the Latin translation, by the reformer and chronicler Johannes Busch, of an anonymous Middle Dutch meditation text; see C. C. de Bruin, De dietse oertekst van de anonieme ‘Epistola de vita et passione domini nostri Ihesu Christi et aliis devotis exercitiis’, in Nederlandsch archief voor kerkgeschiedenis NS 34 (1944/45), 1–23. It is the only known copy explicitly intended for a women’s convent, as the original form of address frater has been replaced with soror.

details.value: f. 1v-23v, 26r-41r, 42v-43v, 56r-70v (also occasional interlinear corrections and additions on some leaves written by the other hands).

Main text in carolino-gothica by at least five hands of the so-called “Hamersleben group”:
 • Hand 1 (main hand): 1v–23v, 26r–41r, 42v–43v, 56r–70v (also occasional interlinear corrections and additions on some leaves written by the other hands).
 • Hand 2: 24r–25v, 35v (only an insertion), 41r–42v.
 • Then, from 42v–55v, almost every entry is by a different hand, including the two first and probably two further hands.
 • Hand 5: 70v–79v.
The additional notes and verses inserted on 2r–3r, 4v–6v, 7v–9r, 10v, 12r–v, 14v–15r, 16r–v, 17v–18r, 25r, 27r, and 68r–70v are by a hand of the so-called “Scriptrix group.”

value.title: Wolfenbüttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, Cod. Guelf. 480 Helmst.

details.value: Carolino-gothica by numerous hands (probably eleven); exact differentiation impossible, since many contributions consist of only a few consecutive pages. At least one hand (1v), and probably more, belongs to the so-called “Hamersleben group” (cf. Cod. Guelf. 475 Helmst.; Härtel, p. 20 passim; Cohen-Mushlin, pp. 165–167, on this MS). Marginalia and nota marks by the original scribes.

1r–12r — Quodvultdeus of Carthage: Contra Iudaeos, Paganos et Arrianos. 
12v–24v — Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Verba seniorum) drawn from Vitas patrum III, V, VI, VII and other sources. 
25v–87r — Bede the Venerable: De templo Salomonis.
88r–106r — Hugh of Saint Victor: De institutione novitiorum.
106r–125v — Hugh of Saint Victor: De tribus diebus.
126r–151v — Hugh of Saint Victor: De vanitate mundi. 
Latin

Ms. Württembergische Landesbibliothek Brev. 73, Unidentified Hand 1, Stuttgart Low

, Prayer book;
1r–1v: Rubric for prayers of Pope Urban IV.
 • 2r–55r: Daily prayers from Sunday to Saturday: “Almighty Father, eternal God, whose power enables the mind to comprehend …” These prayers follow a fixed sequence: God the Father, God the Son, Holy Spirit, Trinity, Mary, Angels, John.
 • 56v: Scribe’s colophon
 • 102r–111r: “A short teaching of the devout father Bonagratia (Bonaventure) of the Franciscan Order,” a spiritual guide: “Dearest brothers, at your request and desire, I have compiled for you a brief teaching…”, German,

Stuttgart, Württembergische Landesbibliothek, Brev. 73, several hands: Hd. 2 = Barbara von Rottenburg
The manuscript is composed of partially incomplete prayer booklets written by various hands at different times. 
The initial section was written in 1496 at the Benedictine Monastery of Lorch: “56v Written in Lorch in the year 1496 by Clemens of the convent brothers of Lorch” (likely Clemens Aurifabri, prior in 1490; see Württembergische Geschichtsquellen, Vol. 12, 1910, p. 86).

The second hand is attributed to Sister Barbara of Rottenburg from Reutin (see Cod.brev.63), suggesting Reutin as the manuscript’s library of origin. Her work is dated to 1521 (83v).

Origin North France, doubtless Chelles. The peculiar uncial and the decoration connect this MS with the group represented by the famous Sacramentary, Vatic. Regin. Lat. 316 (CLA 1.105). On f.1 is added in Anglo-Saxon script saec. VIII–IX Charlemagne's Letter to Abbot Baugulf of Fulda, and on f.260 a library catalogue, perhaps of Würzburg (see CLA plate). Belonged to St Kilian's of Würzburg certainly by the ninth century, as is shown by the entry on f.1v ('. . . faciat eum sancto Kiliano restitui'). The same page has the Würzburg ex-libris saec. XIII. Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, BnF Français 835, Les manuscrits de Christine de Pizan ont été écrits par trois mains bien reconnaissables : P, R et X (Christine de Pizan elle-même). Le ms Français 835 a été transcrit, dans sa majeure partie par R, identifié à P. de Cruce : cf.Delsaux, « Profil d’un copiste des manuscrits originaux de Christine de Pisan : P. de La Croix, alias la main R », article à paraître dans Scriptorium. P a copié les ff.441vb, l. 26 à 44vb. La main X a fait quelques corrections : mouche ou restauration sur laquelle l’auteur a réécrit, à l’encre noire, les mots manquants au f.100 : cf.G. Ouy et C. Reno, « Identification des autographes de Christine de Pizan », dans Scriptorium, 34, 1980, p. 221-238.

details.value: In the name of Lord (Jesus) (Christ) [then 'ella' crossed out] and of the glorious Virgin Mary, mother of God, and of Lord Saint John the Baptist, on the day of whose conception this book was begun, the 24th day of September 1488.

This book belongs to the nuns of the Paradiso, copied by me Sister Raffaella with much effort and hardship. And it is the eighth that I have copied, all for the spiritual consolation of my sisters in (Christ), and I do not believe I will copy more except for the Corona of the monks, which I have started in another volume. And if the letter is rustic, the author and the words are worthy, and therefore it should be regarded.
Amen. Finished on the 23rd day of June 1496

Finito fu questo libro a dì primo di giugno nell’anno del giubileo 1500” (See photo) (the ‘aforewritten sermon’ would be Book VI of Anselm of Canterbury’s Meditations which she copied in the blank space left in the quire (on ff.90r-92v) after finishing the pseudo-Jerome’s Exortation to the Monks which ends on f.90rA. But she also adds two more short sermons on the last f.of the quire (f.92v) - Giovanni Dominici’s Regola del governo di cura familiare and Giannozzo Sacchetti’s Esortazione morale. The next recto f.(f.93r) begins Iacopo da Varazze’s Legenda aurea.)

details.value:
, fol. 1r — Ownership inscription.
	•	fols. 1v–107r — Gregory I, Pope: Dialogorum libri IV (ed. CPL 1713; CALMA 4, 413–415, no. 1).
	•	fol. 107v — Anathema., Latin,

, Carolino-gothic script by the hand of the nun known as “Scriptrix” (on the scribe see 943 Helmst.; other manuscripts from the group: 443 Helmst., 447 Helmst., 482a [1r–81v], 510 Helmst., 511 Helmst., 718 Helmst. [10v–97r], 723 Helmst., 903 Helmst. [1r–75r], 943 Helmst., 1030 Helmst.).

This Gregory manuscript is assigned by Härtel to the Lamspringe nun who calls herself Scriptrix (for the scribe group see 943 Helmst.; Härtel, Geschrieben und gemalt, 21f.). It shows the type of decorated display and initial majuscules common in this group, also found in 510 Helmst., 943 Helmst., and 723 Helmst. (cf. Härtel, Geschrieben und gemalt, p. 23, figs. 1–3). The initial ornament is closely related to that in 510 Helmst., 511 Helmst., 1030 Helmst., and 943 Helmst., with 510 Helmst. and 1030 Helmst. representing a slightly later stage with more three-dimensional vine forks and with elements overlapping or entwining the initial shaft. Close parallels to 519 Helmst. are shown by the composite manuscript 511 Helmst., with its coloured backgrounds and narrow leaf shapes (for stylistic parallels see 511 Helmst.). As in 511 Helmst., direct Cologne influences can increasingly be traced, no longer filtered through Lippoldsberg (on Lippoldsberg see 943 Helmst.). The vine/bud type with integrated palmettes and the backwards-curving terminal bud (fol. 1v), as well as the dragon tailpiece with indented and notched outer edges, occur in Cologne manuscripts, particularly from St. Pantaleon (Cologne Cathedral Library, Hs. 162 and Hs. 163, both Cologne [?], 3rd quarter of the 12th c., Glaube und Wissen, cat. no. 72; and Cologne Cathedral Library, Hs. 31, St. Pantaleon, Glaube und Wissen, cat. no. 31).
