records.rec_Title: Regula Keller, St. Gallen, Female, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), f.102r - v, f.115v f., f.152r, 152v, f.154r - 157r, f.158r - 161r, f.160r (bottom)-v, f.162v - 164r, f.169r ff., f.175v, f.185r

value.title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch")

details.value:
This manuscript, which in earlier scholarship was often referred to as a “Chronicle,” is in fact the Konventsbuch (Convent Book) of St Katharina in St Gall (61r: “…und sol dis also in des convents buoch gesetz werden…”).

It contains chronological entries concerning the economic interests of the convent. The manuscript was compiled during the reform period, at a time when the convent was transitioning from private ownership to communal property. As such, the book enabled the leadership of St Katharina to account to the community for the management of its assets. It also allowed the sisters to keep track of the property they had originally brought into the convent.

The manuscript includes records relating to building activities, furnishings, the scriptorium, legal disputes, and donations, as well as entries concerning individual sisters, confessors, or workers, and—more sporadically—notes on the history of the convent.

The chronicle contains reports and notes from a wide variety of areas of contemporary convent history: Angela Varnbühler 's investing hand begins (ex post) with her election as prioress in 1476, and continues with a list of the conventuals as well as reports from the implementation of the first Steps to reform the monastery. The other entries, in chronological order, concern a wide variety of events from everyday convent life: entry of novices and their later profession; News of death (from conventuals, relatives and friends); Endowments (of seasons and interest) and gifts; Book production in the scriptorium; Economy of the monastery (conductor's annual accounts, administration, land acquisition [fields, forests, vineyards]); Expansion and conversion as well as artistic furnishings of the monastery buildings; Contemporary events from the history of the monastery and order - even the event of the solar eclipse in 1485 found its way into the chronicle with an entry by the prioress (f.45r ).

After the council of the city of St. Gallen lifted the enclosure of the Dominican monastery of St. Catherine on May 2, 1528, and the convent gradually dissolved, only Regula Keller and two sisters remained in the monastery buildings, where she continued to copy the Rule of Augustine and the Constitutions of the Order of Preachers until 1543. The reading of the Rule and Constitutions was emphasized more strongly in Reformed monasteries, in keeping with the nature of the Observance. (men)

records.rec_Title: Sapientia Wirt, St. Gallen, Female, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), Unclear

value.title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch")

details.value:
This manuscript, which in earlier scholarship was often referred to as a “Chronicle,” is in fact the Konventsbuch (Convent Book) of St Katharina in St Gall (61r: “…und sol dis also in des convents buoch gesetz werden…”).

It contains chronological entries concerning the economic interests of the convent. The manuscript was compiled during the reform period, at a time when the convent was transitioning from private ownership to communal property. As such, the book enabled the leadership of St Katharina to account to the community for the management of its assets. It also allowed the sisters to keep track of the property they had originally brought into the convent.

The manuscript includes records relating to building activities, furnishings, the scriptorium, legal disputes, and donations, as well as entries concerning individual sisters, confessors, or workers, and—more sporadically—notes on the history of the convent.

The chronicle contains reports and notes from a wide variety of areas of contemporary convent history: Angela Varnbühler 's investing hand begins (ex post) with her election as prioress in 1476, and continues with a list of the conventuals as well as reports from the implementation of the first Steps to reform the monastery. The other entries, in chronological order, concern a wide variety of events from everyday convent life: entry of novices and their later profession; News of death (from conventuals, relatives and friends); Endowments (of seasons and interest) and gifts; Book production in the scriptorium; Economy of the monastery (conductor's annual accounts, administration, land acquisition [fields, forests, vineyards]); Expansion and conversion as well as artistic furnishings of the monastery buildings; Contemporary events from the history of the monastery and order - even the event of the solar eclipse in 1485 found its way into the chronicle with an entry by the prioress (f.45r ).

Carolino-Gothica by four different hands.
The main hand (Hand 1) is associated with the Scriptrix group (a network of identified female scribes at Lamspringe).
Hands 2–4 show affinities with the Hamersleben group.
Hand 1 (main hand): 1r line 4 – 200v line 10.

Hand 2: 1v, line 4 – end of page.
Hand 3: 24v, lines 19–20 (on erasure).
Hand 4: 189r, lines 20–23.

Hand 1 (main hand) is, according to Cohen-Mushlin, identical in script to the Augustinus text in 903 Helmst., fols. 1r–75r, which Härtel assigns to the Scriptrix group (Cohen-Mushlin, 165; Härtel Geschrieben und gemalt, 85).
	•	Hand 2 has, according to Cohen-Mushlin, similarities to both hands of 204 Helmst., to 903 Helmst., fols. 75v–142v (Hand 2 – the hand of the Gregory text), and to 480 Helmst., fol. 1v (Cohen-Mushlin, 165).

 • Cohen-Mushlin attributes several image captions and possibly much of the artwork to the scribe/artist Ermengard, active in other Lamspringe codices (e.g., 204 Helmst.). Two principal artist-hands:
 • Hand A (Ermengard?): 102r, 148v, and most historiated initials.
 • Hand B: 164r, showing slightly different proportions and palette.
 • Stylistic links to other Lamspringe manuscripts and to Cologne workshop influences.

Härtel assigns this Origen commentary to the Lamspringe nun who identifies herself as “Scriptrix”; the decorated initial majuscules with leaf and flower motifs support this identification (for the scribe group see 943 Helmst.; Härtel, Geschrieben und gemalt, pp. 21f.). As B. Lesser has demonstrated, the text was prepared with consultation of the Georgenberg manuscript of Origen’s homilies, Cod. Guelf. 100 Helmst., providing further evidence of collaboration between the two houses, also visible in book decoration (cf. Cod. Guelf. 510 Helmst.).

Approximately 20 hands or textual sections can be distinguished. Various forms of Bastarda script are used. Since some scripts resemble each other closely, the number of hands may in fact be smaller, and some differences may be explained by different writing phases or circumstances.

details.value: “One Ave Maria, for God’s sake, for the scribe, as it was often difficult for her. This book is completed in the year of our Lord, when one wrote 1526, on St. Ambrose’s Day in Lent at eight in the morning, and may God be eternally praised for it. This book was written by Sister Gertken Opten Koeten for her ancestors in their yearly remembrance, particularly for St. Kilian, Henrick Opten Koete, and Else his wife, and for their children. details.value:
The inside of the front cover and the endpaper contain fragments of a manuscript similar to the Graduale, the back dirt page belonged to a lectionario or breviario from the 14th century and the inside of the back cover is covered with a fragment of a liturgical parchment manuscript, also from the 14th century. At the foot of this fragment is written:
Qui scripsit, scribat et longo tempore vivat. Amen.
Que me scribebat, Sophia nomen habebat. Explicitly liber iste.

Qui scripsit, scribat et longo tempore vivat. Amen.
Que me scribebat, Sophia nomen habebat. Explicitly liber iste.

In the period when the manuscript was produced, four bearers of this name are recorded among the canonesses of Marienberg: the sacristan Sophia Barnstorf and the conventuals Sophia of Brunswick, Sophia of Werle, and Sophia of Meinersen.

During the period in which the Hs. was created, four bearers of this name have been handed down among the Marienberg choir women: the sexton Sophia Barnstorf and the conventual nuns Sophia von Braunschweig , Sophia von Werle and Sophia von Meinersen 
Around 1510, the Graduale was supplemented (Part II) and then re-bound after identifying the scribe's hand and the binding stamp in the Benedictine monastery of Clus in accordance with the requirements of the reformed liturgy of the Bursfeld Benedictine Congregation. 

In the catalogue of Colophons of the Bouveret, noted as wolfenbüttel 542.

Würzburg Universitätsbibliothek, M.ch.f.4, A collection of manuscripts, written primarily on paper, which can be localized to Bamberg. The first part of the manuscript contains a German mirror of salvation. Erasmus Sternhals is identified as its writer in a colophon. The work was probably made for the Bamberg canon Georg von Löwenstein. This is indicated by the depiction of a kneeling canon and several coats of arms on f.56r. The German-language biography of the Holy Bishop Otto, which is bound in afterwards, also refers to Bamberg. It was written down by two Bamberg Poor Clares and completed in 1483. The third work in the collection is a life of Saint Catherine, dated 1488 and also written by a woman.

Written by Ursula Geiselherin based on an exemplar from the Klarakloster (Poor Clares) in Nuremberg.

The exemplar is preserved in Berlin, germ. f.1276 (see Degering I, p. 171), formerly Cheltenham, Phillipps 19491 (see Priebsch, Deutsche Handschriften in England I (1896), p. 127, no. 131).

The copy made at the Katharinenkloster is in two volumes; Volume II = Cent. V, 5.

records.rec_Title: Veronica Hoffman, Female, Göttingen University Library, 8° Ms. Ms. theol. 292, f. 137v–170v

value.title: Göttingen University Library, 8° Ms. Ms. theol. 292

details.value:
Approximately 20 hands or textual sections can be distinguished. Various forms of Bastarda script are used. Since some scripts resemble each other closely, the number of hands may in fact be smaller, and some differences may be explained by different writing phases or circumstances.

The hands are identified as follows:
	•	Hand 1: 1r–7r (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 2: 8r–43v; Sister Regina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect with influences from Middle Bavarian).
	•	Hand 3: 44r–54v (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, probably with Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 4: 55r–v; identical with Hand 6 (75r–77v) and/or Hand 17 (242v–244v)?
	•	Hand 5: 56r–75v (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, probably with Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 6: 75v–77v; identical with Hand 4 (55r–v) and/or Hand 17 (242v–244v)?
	•	Hand 7: 78r–136v; Sister Rossina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, possibly with Alemannic influences).
	•	Hand 8: 137v–170v; Sister Veronica Hoffman(in) (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 9: 171r–193v; possibly identical with Hand 15 (231r–232v).
	•	Hand 10: 193v; identical with Hand 12 (195r–199v) and Hand 14 (200v–230r)?
	•	Hand 11: 194r–v; identical with Hand 13 (200r).
	•	Hand 12: 195r–199v; identical with Hand 10 (193v) and Hand 14 (200v–230v), i.e. with Sister Birgitta?
	•	Hand 13: 231r–232v; identical with Hand 11 (194r–v).
	•	Hand 14: 200v–230r; Sister Birgitta; identical with Hand 10 (193v) and Hand 12 (195r–199v)? (writing language: Nuremberg dialect).
	•	Hand 15: 231r–232v; possibly identical with Hand 9 (171r–193v).
	•	Hand 16: 233r–242r.
	•	Hand 17: 242v–244v; Susana; possibly identical with Hand 4 (55r–v) and/or Hand 6 (75r–77v).
	•	Hand 18: 245r–256v; Sister Eufrosina (writing language: Nuremberg dialect, possibly with Upper Swabian influences).
	•	Hand 19: 257r–275v; Sister Justine (writing language: Nuremberg dialect?).
	•	Hand 20: 276r; Sister Apollonia Kastner (?; this is suggested at least by the entry das buͤchlin gehert muͤter Clara layin von s. Appolonia Kastner ewer getrewe s. in Christo).

details.value: This little prayer book was completed in the year of our Lord 1478, on the very day of Saint Ambrose the Bishop. It was written by Sister Wendelmodis Roltemans at the request of her dear niece Leve Ter Bruggen, an honorable matron. And Sister Agnes Martini illuminated it. The holy nuns of the monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict at Saint Catherine in Syloe, near the renowned and prosperous city of Groningen in Friesland. The aforementioned Leve Ter Bruggen, as a memorable gift, gave this prayer book to the illustrious and honorable man John of the Valley of Roses, also known as Vanden Roesendael."

In the year of our Lord one thousand four hundred and eighty-six, Sister Beatris Dircs, daughter of Bonen, wrote this little book when she was sixty-two years old and had lived in the cloister for forty-five years. Pray for her for God's sake, and recite a Our Father and three Hail Marys.

details.value: f.111v: "Inden jaer ons heren doemen screef M iiii[c] ende lxxxvi soe heeft suster beatris dircs bonen dochter dit boecskijn ghescreven Doe si out was lxii jaer Ende ghewoent hadde in den cloester xlv jaer Bidt voer hoer om godswille Ende leest een pater noster ende iii ave maria."

Whereas according to the Byvanck database, this manuscript may have been made in the eastern part of the Northern Netherlands, according the Database BNM, it was made in Amstelland
Provenance
The manuscript was written by a certain Beatris Dircs Bonen dochter for a convent of Canonesses Regular, dedicated to St. Nicholas and St. Mary Magdalene. According to the Database BNM, the formula on f.17r-17v suggests that the manuscript was made for the Canonesses Regular of St. Mary Magdalene (Op het Spui), Amsterdam. According to Stooker & Verbeij (1997), the formula could have also been for the Canonesses Regular of St. Mary Magdalene, Zaltbommel.

value.title: Karlsruhe, Badische Landesbibliothek, Lichtent. 69

details.value:
Written in a bastarda script predominantly by Sister Regula, except for:
• f.46ra (7 lines)
• f.222vb–223rb (two contemporary hands)
• f.51v (an addition around 1500).
Corrections and additions, mostly by the original scribe, are present.

Book of Holy Maidens and Women (f.1ra–223rb)
• Introduction: Discusses the four cardinal virtues symbolized by the four rivers of paradise (Ortus voluptatis).
• Legends: A collection of 57 legends of female saints, beginning with St. Mary Magdalene (Maria stabat ad monumentum foris plorans).
• Provenance: Compiled by Sister Regula, as noted in secondary literature (e.g., K. Kunze).
• Literature: The legend of Mary of Egypt has been edited by K. Kunze (1978).
2. Pseudo-Eusebius, Epistola ad Damasum de Morte Hieronymi, German Translation (f.223va–228rb, 267va–278rb)
• A medieval German adaptation of the Latin text (BHL 3866), attributed to Pseudo-Eusebius, concerning the death of St. Jerome.
• The German translation does not match other known Middle High German versions.
3. Pseudo-Jerome, Letter to His Mother on Virtues (f.229ra–240rb)
• An instructional and exhortative letter, in which “Jerome” advises his mother on virtuous living.
• The manuscript’s version is not mentioned in key reference works.
4. The Golden Pater Noster (f.240rb–243rb)
• An expanded meditation on the Pater Noster (Our Father) prayer, reflecting on its theological implications.
• Includes parallels with Patrologia Latina (PL 149, 569–576).
5. A Short Gloss on the Pater Noster (f.243rb–244ra)
• A brief guide on the meaning and spiritual significance of the prayer.
6. The School of Virtues (f.244ra–252vb)
• A didactic dialogue between a master and a novice (later referred to as a novitiate), discussing ascetic virtues and leading to eternal life.
7. Epistola ad Moniales (f.252vb–255ra)
• An exhortative letter to nuns, urging them to heed divine inspiration and embrace the love of Christ.
8. Dicta on the Gift of Tears and Prayer (f.255ra–255vb)
• Spiritual reflections and teachings attributed to Augustine, Basil, Paschasius, and Bernard.
9. An Epistle to an Abbess (f.255va–259ra)
• A letter emphasizing love and obedience, comparing divine love to the strength of death, and exalting Christ as the bridegroom of virgins.
Ascetic Instructions (f.259ra–262va)
• A text composed for the “entertainment of young cloistered nuns” by a learned priest.
• Focuses on ascetic ideals and encouragement, referring to the nuns as Christ’s chosen spouses.
• Likely written specifically for the Lichtenthal convent.
2. Another Epistle on Five Virtues (f.262va–264vb)
• Opens with Ponite corda vestra in virtute eius (Ps 47,14), emphasizing the virtues that adorn a faithful life.
• Encourages the practice of virtues to achieve eternal blessedness.
• Ends with a devotional note from the scribe, requesting a recitation of one Ave Maria.
• Mentions Liber Monasterii Lucida Vallis, linking it to Lichtenthal Abbey (often called Lucida Vallis in Latin).
3. On True Poverty (f.265ra–266ra)
• Draws on Matthew 12:1 to explore the virtue of poverty in imitation of Christ and his disciples.
• Provides a theological framework for embracing material poverty as a spiritual ideal.
4. A Consolatory Sermon by St. Bernard (f.266ra–267ra)
• Begins with Bonum est nos hic esse (Mt 17:4), using Bernard of Clairvaux’s alleged reflections to address monastic audiences.
• Discusses the joys and trials of cloistered life and the ultimate reward of eternal glory.
5. Poem on the Meaning of Suffering (f.267ra)
• A six-stanza poem offering solace to those enduring hardships, linking suffering to the promise of the Kingdom of Heaven.
• Contains irregularities in verse and stanza structure, reflecting its devotional rather than literary focus.
6. Return to Pseudo-Eusebius, Epistola ad Damasum (f.267va–278rb)
• This section resumes from f.223va, completing the translation of Pseudo-Eusebius’s text on the death of St. Jerome.

details.value: f.219v, written on a fragment in Lana’s hand: “Franciscus / et Claram” centered, then below, “Questo libro si è scrito per mane/ de Lana de i Galvagni,/ fiola che fu de miser zan / Bertolameo. (Iesu) Maria.”

Rome, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Varia 24 (574)
Lana dei Galvagni is not self-identified as a nun – but the contents of the ms. point to that conclusion – especially the “Regula perfecte religionis”. It was sent to a “Fra Giustino romano cappuccino predicatore” from Venice (f.218r). Lana states her name as “Lana de Galvagni fiola che fu de miser zan Bertolameo” (f.219v) – is this the Venetian Zuan? If so, this would again point to its production as Venetian. Lana wrote “Franciscus et Claram” on f.219v – was she possibly from a house of Clarissans? The ms. came from the Augustinian convent of Gesù e Maria in Rome

details.value: Anna Schott (ca. 1450-after 1521), daughter of the Strasbourg mayor Peter Schott (1427-1504) and sister of the jurist, theologian, and humanist Peter Schott (1460-1490), can be traced in Strasbourg as a Dominican nun of the convents St. Agnes and St. Margaret and St. Agnes (from 1475). She was extensively educated. During the fire of the Strasbourg city library in 1870, a manuscript written by her around 1500 (.Historia sanctorum") was lost (Schlechter, Schott, p. 467). In Schwarzach 19, it is the second known Anna Schott manuscript; it was considered lost (Cowie/Cowie (see Lit.), p.753).

details.value: Finissi di scrivere il detto libro negli anni del Signore mille quattrocento novanta Quattro, addì X d’aghosto. Iscritto con gran faticha e disagio la maggior parte di nocte al lume di lucerna. Prieghovi non ghuardiate alla rusticità della lettera, ma pigliate la sana e verace doctrina data dalla bocca della verità e della sua gloriosa madre virgho Maria alla nostra madre sancta Brigida. Priegho che chi llo leggie con diligentia lo tengha e cchi ll’acatta sì lo renda
Questo libro è delle suore e monache del Paradiso. Suor Cleofe.

I finished writing the said book in the year of the Lord one thousand four hundred ninety-four, on the 10th of August. Written with great effort and hardship, mostly at night by lamplight. I ask you not to judge the simplicity of the letter, but to take the sound and true doctrine given by the mouth of the Truth and his glorious mother, the Virgin Mary, to our holy mother, Saint Bridget. I pray that whoever reads it diligently may keep it, and whoever buys it may return it.
This book belongs to the sisters and nuns of the Paradiso. Sister Cleofe.

details.value: Since the text was almost certainly written by a nun named Sophia , it is very likely that the book decoration was also inserted in a nunnery, more precisely a Cistercian convent (see the calendar). Not the first, but perhaps the second owner was Margareta von Isenburg in the Marienborn monastery near Büdingen, which can provisionally be considered the place of origin. Judit 's entry on the endpaper and the document fragment provide the time frame.

details.value:
Quire signatures: b1 (27r), b2, etc., and aa1 (200r), aa2, etc.
Catchwords rare

1- and 2-line red and blue Lombard initials
    * Some with grotesque heads and simple pen-flourishing (fleuronné)
* Larger decorated initials (4–9 lines high) at:
    ff. 18r, 61v, 71r (unfinished), 197r, 238v
    * Split ornamental initials in color
    * Sometimes with leaves, flowers, occasionally gold
    * With pen-flourishing
* f. 228v:
    * Initial with acanthus tendril,
    * a drawn rabbit,
    * and a scroll (banderole)
* Painted historiated initials (some with gold):
    * f. 18v: Annunciation
    * f. 50r: Nativity
    * f. 166r: John the Evangelist
    * f. 172v: Massacre of the Innocents
    * f. 185r: Paul
    * f. 190v: Purification of Mary
    * f. 202v: Peter

details.value: Ich swester Dorothea uon Kippenheim ein conuent Swester deß wirdigen loͤblichen gotzhuß Sancti Johannis baptiste in vnderlinden zuͦ Colmar hab diß buͦch vß dem latin zuͦ tútzsch geschriben got zu lob vnd och zuͦ eren Sancto Sebastiano vnd den anderen lieben heilgen die doran stond vnd ich beger bemuͤticlich dz die alle got wellen fúr mich bitten die do werden leßen an dißem buͦch Amen); das ist nicht die in VL 2 (1980) Sp. 218 genannten Dorothea von Kippenheim OP (zu ihr die biographischen Notizen von moderner Hand 325r), sondern eine gleichnamige Schwester, die Anfang des 16. Jahrhunderts im Kloster Unterlinden lebte (VL 11 [2004] Sp. 380); rote Strichel und Überschriften, Lombarden rot, z. T. mit blauem Federwerk, blau, z. T. mit rotem Federwerk.
Collation fairly regular but with many cut folios.

I, Sister Dorothea von Kippenheim, a convent sister of the venerable and praiseworthy house of God, Saint John the Baptist in Unterlinden near Colmar, have written this book from Latin into German for the praise of God and also in honor of Saint Sebastian and the other dear saints mentioned therein. I humbly ask that all who read this book may be willing to pray to God for me. Amen.

Jahrhunderts im Kloster Unterlinden lebte (VL 11 [2004] Sp. 380); rote Strichel und Überschriften, Lombarden rot, z. T. mit blauem Federwerk, blau, z. T. mit rotem Federwerk.

(This is not the Dorothea von Kippenheim OP mentioned in VL 2 [1980], col. 218; rather, it refers to another sister of the same name who lived in the Unterlinden convent in the early 16th century [VL 11 (2004), col. 380].)

records.rec_Title: Gertrud Buchel, Nonnenwerth, Female

details.value:
Gertrud Büchel (also: Buchel) was an exceptionally well-educated nun at the Benedictine convent of Rolandswerth, where she worked as a skilled scribe and illuminator, and from 1507 as abbess. Johannes Butzbach dedicated his 1505 treatise "Von den berühmter Malern (De praeclaris picturae professoribus)" to her, an early work on art history from Germany.
Sources on Gertrud's life and work include the aforementioned writing by the Laach Benedictine Johannes Butzbach (1478-1516/17), as well as the necrology and the convent chronicle of Rolandswerth, and documents issued by Gertrud as abbess. Individual books produced by Gertrud herself provide direct evidence of her Latin education and craftsmanship.
Gertrude likely received her education at Rolandswerth Abbey, as girls were barred from Latin schools. Future nuns needed knowledge of Latin, liturgical texts, and the Gospels to perform their liturgical duties. According to the Bursfeld reformers, they were even expected to speak Latin fluently, thus achieving a high level of language proficiency. We know from Butzbach that Gertrude was very well-read. Interest in religious literature was pronounced in reformed nunneries. Copying books was considered appropriate manual labor for monks and nuns, a form of protection against idleness and a pious practice.
The Rolandswerth monastery historiography recounts that Gertrude acquired exceptional calligraphic and painting skills outside her own convent. She spent six months at the Augustinian canonesses' convent of Engelthal in Bonn, where she learned to write and illuminate manuscripts. Apparently, the Bonn canonesses operated a scriptorium of good reputation, though other evidence is lacking. Before the noble nun Gertrude was elected the fourth abbess of Rolandswerth after the reform, succeeding her biological sister Demodis, who died on November 22, 1507, the chronicle further reports that she worked as a scribe. Gertrude wrote the six large choir books on parchment that were still in Rolandswerth in 1700, including two graduals and four antiphonals. She decorated these manuscripts with large gold initials. She also wrote smaller prayer books, some of which still exist, while others were lost in the war.

148ra vnd durch meiner mü willen vnd arbaitt willen
wartt ich nicht anders Ions von den lewten neur allain daz si ir andechtige pet hincz dem aller-

details.value: Finito è il presente libro scripto per mano d’una monacha indegnamente consecrata nel monasterio del Paradiso, il cui nome sia scripto nel libro della vita, a dì quatordici di dicenbre M CCCC LXXVII. A llaude (et) gloria della somma (et)d eterna sapientia. Deo gratias. Poi ch’ài letto il libro (et) la visione coll’altre cose che qui sono scripte priega per me misera, peccatore. Dà il cuore a Dio intero (et) non diviso se gustar vuogli questo libro sancto (et) rendilo al monasterio del Paradiso

Finished is this present book written by the hand of a nun, unworthily consecrated in the monastery of Paradiso, whose name is written in the book of life, on the fourteenth day of December 1477. To the praise and glory of the highest and eternal wisdom. Thanks be to God. After you have read the book and the vision with the other things written here, pray for me, a miserable sinner. Give your heart entirely to God if you wish to taste this holy book, and return it to the monastery of Paradiso.

records.rec_Title: Clara Hätzlerin, Augsburg, Female

details.value:
Professional, laywoman scribe
Hatzlerin was a scribe in Augsburg who has nine signed surviving manuscripts. She lived with her brother, a notary, and was commissioned to produce books for wealthy citizens. The article concludes with a descriptive catalog of her nine known manuscripts. 
Clara Hätzlerin (* around 1430 in Augsburg ; † probably 1476 or the following year) was a hired clerk in the 15th century. She is the only woman documented who made handwritten copies of German codices for a fee . It can be proven in Augsburg tax books between 1452 and 1476. [1]
Clara Hätzlerin came from a family of notaries that was typical of Augsburg at the time. Her father Bartholomew is known to have been a so-called letter writer who, as a representative of rich citizens, regulated their legal rights. He is documented in tax books between 1409 and 1443 as well as through an entry in the Augsburg Missive Book and as a witness in a mortgage note from Marx Lang. [2] When Bartholomew died in 1444/45, Bartholomew's eldest son, who is documented as a notarius publicus between 1451 and 1496, took over the office and thus also the tax liability.
The most conclusive refutation is provided by Augsburg tax books, which show that Clara paid taxes in her father's house for 24 years, something she could never have done as a nun, since in this case her assets would have gone to the monastery. [4]
The profession of paid and professional writer is a phenomenon of the 15th century, a time in which the writing industry flourished and the need for everyday literature increased. The city of Augsburg played a pioneering role in this area, as it has a list of over 30 proven payroll clerks. Hired scribes were mainly laypeople who produced cheap copies of manuscripts for the public by copying them by hand and were no longer, as was usual up until then, members of the clergy who had specialized in the artistic design of magnificent manuscripts. In addition to Clara Hätzlerin, the calligraphers Heinrich Molitor and Heinrich Lengefeld and Konrad Bollstatter also belonged to this group of people. [5] It was quite common for professional writers to work part-time in public, legal or administrative writing. Clara Hätzlerin also worked in the law firm of her father Bartholomäus Hätzler and her brother of the same name. As a part-time job , she made handwritten copies of commissioned books. Some manuscripts from her pen, which are mainly practical manuscripts, have been preserved to this day.
Clara wrote her texts in a very readable and carefully crafted script , which is often cited by paleographers as the prototype of the 15th-century chancellery bastarda . Last but not least, the consistent naming of scribes at the end of all codices made it possible for them to be included in the DAmalS [6] project of the Institute for German Studies at the Karl Franzens University of Graz . Medievalists there try to identify the scribes' hands of a manuscript using databases and use the Hätzler's manuscripts as a paleographic comparison option.
To date, eight of the Hätzler's manuscripts are known. In the research literature the number nine is occasionally given when the two-part manuscript of “The Holy Lives” is counted as two works. These include legal books , hunting literature, a work on the subject of mysticism and magic and the collective manuscript “Song Book”. The eight codices date from the period between 1465 and 1473, were written in a script typical of Clara Hätzlerin, namely the Chancellery Bastarda , and could undoubtedly be attributed to Clara Hätzlerin as the scribe, as she signed most of the manuscripts herself . [2]

Christi sit dilectrix Walburgis, libri huius scriptrix,
Non bene finivi, quia scribere nescivi.
Si quis abstulerit, anathema sit.
Orate pro scriptrice unum paternoster.

When the book is finished, let there be praise to Christ.
In the year of the Lord 1467, on the day of Saint Agnes, Thursday.
May Walburgis, lover of Christ, be [remembered], she who is the female scribe of this book.
I have not finished well, because I did not know how to write properly.
If anyone should take [this book away], let them be anathema.
Pray for the female scribe one Our Father.

Hab got ir sel amen. Ich kartewsser obrlass vnd corrigirt es in cristminne im aduent 1455.

This little book on the Cantica canticorum was written by two sisters, Kunigund and Anna, and completed on the Saturday after the octave of the Visitation of Mary, in the year 1455. The first sister, Kunigund, died in the year of the Virgin and Martyr
May God have mercy on her, amen. I write and correct this in memory of Christ in the year 1455.

details.value: f. 145v: Explicit apparatus super arbore consanguinitatis et affinitatis compitus a domino Iohanne Andrea decreerum doctore et scriptus per me sororem Lauream de Bossis

Heavily decorated, miniatures, historiated initials.
The decoration consists of two large miniatures with a frontispiece on folios 4v and 5r, thus facing each other. The miniature on folio 4v (129 x 200 mm) depicts the Annunciation. Below the miniature is the evangelical inscription: ne timeas Maria invenisti gratiam, while above appears the monogram IHS; the miniature on folio 5r (133 x 205 mm) depicts the offering of the book by the author Giovanni d'Andrea to Pope Boniface VIII. Within the text, there are 6 rubricated initials, 413 filigree initials, 74 decorated illuminated initials, and 1 figurative initial, along with one decorated initial, and two figurative initials in the prologues on folios 4v-5r. In the gloss, there are 373 filigree initials and 77 illuminated initials. In the Apparatus, however, there are two filigree initials and one decorated illuminated initial. The manuscript's decoration is attributed to the copyist Laura Bossi, with the exception of the miniatures, which Giuseppa Zanichelli attributes to a Pavia artist from the last quarter of the 15th century who collaborated with the "master of the yellow backgrounds." Zanichelli attributes the name "Master of Laura Bossi" to this artist.

Sister Lijsbeth Witjens and Sister Magriet Raes have written in this book. After over eighteen years of writing, Sister Kathlinen van Molenbeke completed and ended it on the eve of Our Lady's Day of the 15th taps, on the eve of Saint Cecilia, in the year of our Lord 1489. At that time, she was approximately 51 years old. Please, from your heart, recite an Ave Maria for the three of them, so that God may grant them glory for their labor in eternity.
This book belongs to the cloister of the Roses Planted in Jericho within Brussels, near Saint Kathlinen.

details.value: Desen boeck wert gheschreven Int Jaer ons heren .xvc .x. van Suster Johannen Colijns doen sij out was .lvi. jaer. Ende sij schincten den convente In goeder minnen van Jericho opden viijsten dach In Julio alst viel haers incomst Jubileo Int Jaer .xv.c xi. Biddende haerer armer zielen ghetrouw te sine Op dat sij mach met christo leven ten fine. Amen. Desen boeck hout inne. xxxi. quarternen. ende daer es toe ghegaen .v. boecken panpiers ende .v. blaren

This book was written in the year of our Lord 1510 by Sister Johanna Colijns when she was fifty-six years old. And she donated it to the convent out of goodwill from Jericho on the eighth day of July, when her income fell on the Jubilee Year of the year 1511. Praying for her poor soul to be faithful so that she may live with Christ in the end. Amen. This book contains thirty-one quaternions and it took five reams of paper and five leaves.

details.value: INt Jaer ons heren M cccc lxxii tich. Op sinte peeters ende pauwels dach in junio. Begonste suster katherina van ghiseghem profes nonne in onsen cloester te iericho aen dit boec vanden tabernakel te scriuen. Ende sij volyndet int selue iaer iiii dage in april op sinte ambrosius dach. die viel opten sondach. Dit heeftse ter eren gods ende om gemeyn stichtinge met groeter nersticheit bearbeit in allen wtgesochten tijden als sij int gemeyn werck niet sijn en moeste. doense was out xxvi tich iaer. Bidt om die minne gods voer haer ewige salicheit. Dit boec behoert toe. den cloestere van onser lieuer vrouwen rose geplant in iericho. bynnen bruesele bi sinte katherinen. der ordenen sinte augustijns. soe wie dat vint geeft den relygiosen ioffrouwen weder om gods wille.

In the year of our Lord one thousand four hundred seventy-two. On the feast day of Saints Peter and Paul in June, Sister Katherina van Ghiseghem, professed nun in our cloister at Jericho, began to write this book on the tabernacle. And she completed it in the same year, on the fourth day of April, on the feast day of Saint Ambrose, which fell on a Sunday. She did this in honor of God and for the common edification with great diligence, working on it diligently at all chosen times when she was not engaged in communal work. She was twenty-six years old at the time. Pray for her eternal salvation out of love for God. This book belongs to the cloister of Our Lady Rose-planted in Jericho, within Brussels, near Saint Catherine's, of the Augustinian order. Whoever finds it, return it to the religious ladies for the love of God.

details.value: Dit boec es volscreuen op sinte symon ende yuden auont Int iaer ons heren m cccc en lxxiiii van suster lijsbetk vliechs. doen si out was li iear bidt voer haer om gode. Dit boec hoert toe int bloester tot onser lieuer vrouwen te yericho dat men heet te sinte katerinen.

Dit boeck hoert toe te onser lieuer vrouwen der Roosen gheplant in iherico dat men heet te sinte katherinen binnen bruesele. Inden iaer ons heren. m cccc ende lxxiiii soe heeft suster lijsbeth vlieghe desen boeck volscreuen ende met groeten arbeyde op sinte symon ende iuden auont volyndet ter eeren gods ende tot stichtinghen ende salicheit alre deuoter menschen doen sij out was. li. iaer. Bidt ghetrouwelijc om die minne gods voer haer. want sij seer neerstelijc ende vlietelijc vele iaren ghearbeit heeft in vele goeder boeken te scruene.

This book was fully written on the eve of Saint Simon and Jude in the year of our Lord 1474 by Sister Lijsbetk Vliechs when she was fifty-one years old. Pray for her to God. This book belongs to the monastery of Our Lady of the Roses planted in Jericho, known as Saint Catherine's.

This book belongs to Our Lady of the Roses planted in Jericho, known as Saint Catherine's within Brussels. In the year of our Lord 1474, Sister Lijsbeth Vlieghe completed this book with great effort on the eve of Saint Simon and Jude, for the glory of God and for the edification and salvation of all devout people, when she was fifty-one years old. Pray faithfully for her out of love for God, as she diligently and diligently worked for many years in writing many good books.

details.value: Hier ynt dat yerste boeck. gheheeten malogranatum. dat volscreuen wert op sinte nychasius dach. Int iaer ons heeren m cccc ende lxxxv van suster katherinen van molenbeke. als si out was xliiii iaer. dit heeft sij om die minne gods ghedaen ende tot ghemeynder stichtinghen. waer af ons heere haer loen wil sijn inder ewicheit Amen.
Dit boeck hoert toe den cloester der rosen gheplant in jherico binnen bruesel bij Sinte katherinen

Here ends the first book called "Malogranatum", completed on the day of Saint Nichasius, in the year of our Lord 1485, by Sister Katherinen van Molenbeke, when she was forty-three years old. She did this out of love for God and for the common good. May the Lord reward her for it in eternity. Amen.
This book belongs to the convent of the Rosary planted in Jericho within Brussels, near Saint Katherine.

It was completed by the grace of God by me, Sister Mariken Pompen, in the year of our Lord 1536, on the 19th of October. details.value: Hier beghint die prologe op die navolghende sermoenen die welke onse eerwerdige pater her jan storm hevet ghepredict in onsen cloestere te jhericho: doen hi ons commissarijs ende rector tsamen was. welke sermoenen onse werdige mater. doen sij noch inden staet der prelaturen niet en was. aensiende den swaren last ende arbeit des selven Eerbaren vaders crech minne ende devocie dese sermoenen te bescriven: op dat den arbeit des predicaers inder ewiger glorien met nyewen loene vergouden worde soe dicke als yemens devocie beweeght wert. uut aenhoerne oft selve te studeerne dese sermoene. Laet ons ghetrouwelijc bidden voer onsen eerwerdigen pater die den arbeit heeft ghedaen inder predicatien. ende voer onser ghemijnder mater: suster marie van pee god wil haer geven sinen ewegen vree die den arbeit heeft ghedaen om dit te bescriven ... soe hebic dit navolgende boec ghepijnt te vergaderen uut veel collacien die in onsen godshuyse gepredict sijn binnen vijf jaren ..."

Hier ynden die sermoenen ons Eerweerdeghen paters welke ic van velen een weynich vergadert hebbe tot mijns selfs orbore ende der gheendere dier in believen sal te studeren Ende sij waren volscreven int jaer ons heren. M. iii[c]. ende lxvi. op sinte laureis des gloriosen maerteleers dach voer vesperen
Dit boeck was volscreven Int jaer ons heren doemen screef.Dusent. vierhondert. seven ende tsestich. des sesten daeghs in septembri. op enen sondach

Here begins the prologue to the following sermons, which our venerable father, Master Jan Storm, preached in our convent at Jericho, when he was both our commissary and rector. These sermons our worthy mother—while she was not yet in the office of prioress—out of compassion for the great burden and labor of that honorable father, was moved by love and devotion to have them written down, so that the labor of the preacher might be rewarded in eternal glory with renewed grace each time someone’s devotion is stirred to hear or to study these sermons. Let us therefore devoutly pray for our venerable father, who performed the labor of preaching, and for our worthy mother, Sister Marie van Pee—may God grant her His eternal peace—who undertook the labor of writing this down. … Thus I have taken pains to gather this following book from many sermons that were preached in our house of God over the course of five years.

Here end the sermons of our Venerable fathers, which I have gathered a few of for my own edification and for those who wish to study. And they were completed in the year of our Lord, 1366, on the feast of Saint Laurence, the glorious martyr, before vespers.
This book was completed in the year of our Lord when it was written. Fourteen hundred and sixty-seven, on the sixth day of September, on a Sunday.

This was preached on the separation of the apostles in our monastery of Jericho by a learned man and priest from the Society of Jesus, and composed and written down by a worldly lady from his words, who, at my request, lent it to me, and it has been transcribed by Sister Katherina Moleman, hoping for improvement.

details.value: Ghescreven gheset ende volbracht metter gracien gods van enen armen sondigen mensche welcs name ic wilde dat bekent ware ende onvutdoenliken gescreven in dat boec des ewighe levens ende op dat dat gescien mach soe biddic alle den ghenen die dit of sijn uutscrift sullen sien oft horen lesen voir hem willen bidden Int Jair ons heren dusent vierhondert ende eenen vijftich als die gracie vanden gulden jare te mechelen was

Written, set, and completed with the grace of God by a poor sinful person whose name I would like to be known, and indelibly written in the book of eternal life, and so that this may happen, I ask all those who will see or hear or read this or its copy to pray for them. This little book was written in the year of our Lord one thousand five hundred and eighty-six. It was begun in the same year, on the twenty-fifth day of July, and completed on the eighteenth day of September in that same year. It was written by Sister Katherijn van Eyck, living at the Begarden, in the convent, for the use of the community, and she desires to become a sharer in all that is good.

details.value:
Esther Inglis (Esther Anglois, Esther Kello) was born in 1571, one of three children of Nicholas Langlois and his wife Marie Prescot, who fled to London from France about 1569 as
Hugenot refugees. They had settled in Edinburgh by 1574 and apparently appeared on the poor roll for the years 1578 - 1580. At about this time Langlois was appointed Master of the French School, which position he retained until his death in 1611. Esther married around 1596 Bartholomew Kello, a clerk in Holy Orders, however she retained an anglicized version of her maiden name throughout her career. She died in 1624.

records.rec_Title: Dorothea von Hof, Constance, Female

details.value: Dorothea von Hof was the daughter of the merchant and guild representative Heinrich Ehinger. At the age of 16, she married Jerg (Jörg) von Hof, who served as mayor of Constance from 1499. After subscribing to the church, she made a pilgrimage to Einsiedeln at the age of 19. There, she donated clothing and jewelry, but was not clothed herself . Von Hof was later close to the Dominican nuns of St. Gall and is mentioned several times as a benefactor in the convent chronicle of St. Catherine's Abbey . However, there is no evidence of how the benefactor was connected to the abbey. After 15 years of childless marriage, the couple drew up a joint will in 1489. She died on February 27, 1501, and was buried in St. Stephen's Cathedral.

details.value: Do man zalt von der geburt unsere heren Christi 1483 an s. Silvestertag han ich Dorothe von Hof dis buoch ungeschriben und bin davor ze herbst an s. Frenentag im 1482 iar alt gesin 24 iar und ist gesin nün iar an s; Pallus bekert im 83 iar, das Jerg und ich elich zesamen kamen. Liebe überwint alle alle ding. Deo gratias. Item und do ich alt bin gesin 19 iar uf s. Verenatag, do gieng ich uf des hl. crütztag nächst darnach genden Einsideln uf ain engelwiche und Satz do den sturtz uf und let etliche weltliche claider und clainet hin, das ich yr nit me truog.

In the year of our Lord’s birth 1483, on St. Sylvester’s Day, I, Dorothea von Hof, wrote out this book. And in the previous autumn, on St. Fridolin’s Day in the year 1482, I was 24 years old. And it was nine years since St. Paul’s Conversion Day in the year ’83 that Jörg and I were joined together in marriage. Love overcomes all things. Deo gratias.

scribe, Dorothea von Hof, née Ehingerin
Dorothea von Hof (1458-1501)
From the possession of Margarete Ehingerin, née Neidhart (died 1513), married since 1482 to the Constance patrician Hans Ehinger (1456–1505), son of Heinrich Ehinger and Margarete von Kappel; cf.the alliance coat of arms Ehinger/Neidhart 2r and the ownership entry 357r: This book belongs to Margreth Ehingerjn in Mergstat. Contrary to earlier opinions, it was therefore not the older Margarete Ehinger, née von Kappel (died 1490?), but rather her daughter-in-law who owned this manuscript (cf.Gebauer [2010] p. 37 f.[with family tree]); she was thus likely also the sister-in-law of the scribe, Dorothea von Hof, née Ehingerin. Regarding three other manuscripts from the possession of the older Ehinger generation, see Nos. 36.0.2. (Einsiedeln Stiftsbibliothek, Codex 710), No. 43.1.55. (Einsiedeln, Stiftsbibliothek, Codex 283), and No. 59.2.5. (St. Gallen, Kantonsbibliothek, VadSlg. Ms. 343 c–d).

records.rec_Title: Anna Ebin, Pillenreuth, Female

details.value:
Anna Ebin or Eybin, a fifteenth-century Augustinian nun, and provost of her convent in Pillenreuth (near Nuremberg) from 1461-1476, was a prolific scribe and compiler of devotional books. Although only four books have survived in which her hand has been identified, in one of these books she is said to have written “gar und vil puecher dem convent […] die ungezelt sind” (very many books for the convent that are countless).

Anna Eybin (d. 1485), canoness in the Augustinian Convent in Pillenreuth (near Nuremberg), also served as provost of the house from 1461 to 1476. She was known in her community for her writing, scribal, and compiling activity.

records.rec_Title: Diemut, Wessobrunn, Female

details.value: One of the most remarkable medieval women writers, the German nun Diemut (d. c. 1130) is known to scholars primarily as a scribe who during her lifetime was likely the chief copyist for her reformed community at Wessobrunn, which she provided with a host of religious writings. These fill dozens of extant manuscripts, many of which bear her name. Her extraordinary work remains a monument to the literary accomplishments of medieval women.

details.value: f.195: Dit boec heeft ghescreven Suster alijt lambert dochter op sommighefeest daghen intjaer ons heren M iiiic ende lxxvia Bidt voer haer om gods willen (cop.). Dit boec hoert toe den regulierissen s' marie magdalenen in amsterdam woenende indie nes opt spoey (autre main contemporaine).

Leiden, Bibliotheek der Rijksuniversiteit, Letterk. 219
Contains: 
(ff. 1r-106v) Collaties / Johannes Brinckerinck. 
(ff. 106v-107r) Second letter / Gerlach Peters. 
(ff. 107v-111v) Een corte leer hoe hem een mensche hebben sel. With excerpts from Jan van Ruusbroec’s Van den blinkenden steen and his Spieghel der salicheit and from Jan van Leeuwen.. 
(ff. 111v-116r) Een exempel van der armoeden. Dutch translation of Meister Eckharts Wirtschaft. Discussion between a woman, a beggar (sometimes identified as Master Eckhart) and a learned man about poverty of the soul. 
(ff. 116r-119r) Vander reynicheit. Dutch translation of a dictum on purity attributed to Jerome. 
(ff. 119r-122v) Van de heilighe sacrament / Meister Eckhart. Excerpts of Master Eckhart’s Die Rede der Underscheidunge (chapters 20 and 23), translated into Dutch. 
(ff. 122v-125r) Rhymed text on the differences between nature and soul, including an excerpt of Jan van Ruusbroec's Vanden twaelf beghinen. 
(ff. 125r-126v) Een gheystelec wijnghelaech. 
(ff. 127v-129v) Vanden missen. 
(ff. 129v-130v) Hoe goet dattet is die misse ghehoert. 
(ff. 129v-133v) Contains four exempla, of which the last two on Edmund, archbishop of Canterbury. 
(ff. 133v-191r) Van die passie ons heren. 
(f. 191r) Pseudo-Palm tree treatise.

Eugenia, France, Female, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 7560, Full manuscript, scribe of Eugenia, France, Female

value.title: Eugenia, France, Female, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Latin 7560, Full manuscript

details.value:
Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, BnF Latin 7560, Des annotations et corrections interlinéaires sans doute de la main de la copiste : f.4r, 5r, 33r-34r, 39r, 42r, 44r, 46v-54r ; et d’autres mains : f.41r-43v, 47r-47v. Des annotations marginales de diverses mains : au f.1r, la cote Colbert, la cote Regius répétée deux fois, la cote actuelle, une ligne d’un chant religieux (« Nunctio uere quia misit dominus angelimi »), et des neumes (orisci catalans et neumes aquitains ; on en trouve aussi au f.54v) ; d’autres annotations à connotation religieuse sont à noter aux f.6r, 42v et 54v ; un certain nombre d’annotations sont illisibles ou effacées (f.11r, 22r, 40r et 54r) ; on peut également mentionner un astérisque au f.45r, un « y » au f.49r et, d’une main moderne, « 307 » sur le f.54v. 
 Comme l’indiquent C. Jeudy (1974, p. 129-130) et B. Bischoff (2014, p. 128-129) dans leur notice respective, le manuscrit a été copié dans le troisième quart du IXe siècle en France, dans un scriptorium d’influence insulaire, par une copiste du nom d’Eugenia, qui donne son nom dans une souscription rédigée en lettres grecques (mais en langue latine) au f.54r (voir H. OMONT, 1905, p. 15 pour la transposition). Il a peut-être été copié dans le Sud de la France ou en Catalogne, ou du moins s’y est trouvé très vite après sa copie, car la main légèrement postérieure à la première (fin du IXe siècle) qui ajoute les carmina des f.54r et 54v est caractérisée par des traits wisigothiques et des neumes d’Aquitaine et orisci catalans ont été notés sur les f.1r et 54v vers la même période.

details.value: Katarina Gudmundsdotter (Gudmundi), Vadstena, Palaeography analaysis, Low

Linköping City Library, T 229, This manuscript was written in Vadstena Abbey, in the nuns scriptorium. The parchment was payed by sr Birgitta Gudmundi and it was completed at S Michaels eve 1517. It was written by one of the nuns, keeping her identity secret in the colophon on f.37v. It contained music and was intended for use in the church. There are closely related manuscripts in both Uppsala and Stockholm Libraries, either written or decorated by the same nun/nuns. The nuns had taken influence from their sisters i the Netherlands in the design of the large pen-flourished initials. One of the nuns who most frequently painted her large decorated initials in the same style as here was Christina Hansdotter Brask, but she seem to have hade successors. A very similar design can be found in KB A 12, UUB C 431, C 443, C 484, RA E 9002. Some of these are by Christina Hansdotter Brask and from the same period as this manuscript. The present mss is however executed by a much more stable hand than the Brask mss from the same period. A more suitable candidate is Katarina Gudmundsdotter, whose palaeography is in accordance with the scribe of this mss.

Le nom de l'écrivain be peut pas être déterminé ici de manière tout à fait objective. Dans la deuxième partie, le nom du scribe est certain, mais l'époque n'est pas assez précise. Cependant en 1486, Anna Fickesdotter devint prieure et cela aurait probablement été mentionné d'une manière ou d'une autre si le manuscrit avait été écrit après cette années. Mais il ne fait aucun doute que la main est la même dans les deux parties. Kristina Johansdotter Brask a écrit le directorium chori.

 Written in North-east France or possibly Cologne, as script and ornamentation in the type developed by the nuns of Chelles suggest; the MS has close affinity with the group of three MSS of St Augustine (Cologne, Dombibliothek 63, 65, 67) written by nuns for Hildebald, Archbishop of Cologne (785–819). Belonged to St Faron, Meaux, till the French Revolution, then to Gosselin, later to Remusat, at whose sale it was bought by Messrs Payne, the London booksellers, in 1833.

 Written in North France, probably in the convent that produced the three Cologne manuscripts written by nuns for Archbishop Hildebald of Cologne (785–819) and also the Paris manuscript Lat. 18282 (CLA 5.674). Belonged to Pithou whose autographed notes are in the manuscript. Later the property of Colbert in whose collection it was number 1863, and number 3887.14.14 in the Royal collection.
This manuscript's script and decoration is very similar to the Chelles' manuscript of Köln, Erzbischöfliche Diözesan- und Dombibliothek, Cod. 63, 65, 67

 Le ms. Français 1176 est un des vingt-cinq manuscrits entièrement copiés de la main de Christine de Pizan. Selon l’ Album Christine de Pizan, ce manuscrit est le plus ancien témoin du texte, daté de 1405. 
 
 Corrections de la main de Christine de Pizan : additions indiquées dans la marge et rapportées dans l'interligne (f.58) ; additions avec signes de renvoi (f.20v, 43, 63) ; au f.76, préparation de la rubrique en écriture cursive. Nombreux mots, souvent déjà exponctués, barrés de rouge. Au verso de la 3e garde de parchemin, table de l'ouvrage ajoutée à l'encre rouge de la main de l'auteur.
One hand was identified as Christine's autograph by G. Ouy et C. Reno

details.value:
Maria Dies de Oña, Burgos, Colophon, High, Dallas, Bridwell Library, Southern Methodist University, BRMS 155, Produced, signed, and dated by the Spanish nun Maria Dies de Oña, this early sixteenth-century Spanish manuscript gradual contains the “propers” and choral chants for the Mass for Cistercian Use, according to the pre-Tridentine liturgical calendar. Although a complete volume, it is not a complete work as it contains approximately only the first third of the liturgical year, from the first Sunday in Advent to Palm Sunday. Given the size and format of this volume, the complete gradual for the entire liturgical year would have been represented by three or four volumes.

Produced by a female religious copyist for use by the female monastery of San Salvador de Oña in Burgos, this substantial volume is almost entirely composed of chant and does not include the long spoken portions of the Mass. Minor leaf repairs, occasional corrections, marginal additions, and instructions for following the text indicate that this manuscript was used on a regular basis.

f.1 posessionmark: "Miner hertzliben sch. Kunigunda von mir schw. Maria Cleopha Duocherin im gotzhuss zuo sant Clara in Filingen, butt dich, min hertzlieben schw(ester), wellest gott och fu"r mich bitten, das selbe will ich och thun, diewil ietz leb, damit sind gott befolchen, den 15. tag abrilis 6011 ( = 1611). f.1
(Possession note):My dearest Sister Kunigunda, from me, Sister Maria Cleopha Duocherin, in the convent of Saint Clare in Villingen: I beg you, my dearest sister, please also pray to God for me — that I will also do, as long as I live. With this, may we both be entrusted to God, on the 15th day of April, 1611.
(In another hand below)
This belongs to the convent of Saint Peter in Schwyz.

[Apparamment il faut comprendre que Sustef a préparé le livre pour Fye. Au f.9v°, elle donnait les obits de son père, d'un frère et d'une sœur (1467-1477); plus tard (?) elle (?) ajoutait ceux de l'oncle Ansse (1468; sans doute le père de Fye), de deux autres frères (1468, 1481) et les noms d'une sœur et de Suster elle-même (ces deux étant encore en vie). Une autre main (celle de Fye?) a noté le décès de ces deux dernières (1509, 1510) ainsi que d'une autre personne de la famille (1519).]

details.value:
Maria Horn, Boppard, Colophon, High, Fulda, Landesbibliothek, Ms. Aa 125, The origin in a Franciscan convent is evidenced by:
	•	The feast of the stigmatization of St. Francis (135r) and the rubric on f.150r referring to von unßerm werdigen vader Franciscus (“our worthy Father Francis”).
	•	The suffrage for Severus, unserm Patrone (“our patron”) on f.162r, situated within the liturgical year sequence between November 11 and November 21, suggesting Boppard (Archdiocese of Trier).
In 1489, Franciscan sisters from Besselich settled in Boppard, known for their manuscript production (cf.J. Marx, Geschichte des Erzstifts Trier, vol. 2, part 2, 1862, p. 423, and K. Schlegel, Besselich am Mittelrhein, 1980, p. 19).

details.value: Christina Kamrer, Nuremberg, Colophon, High, Gera, HB 7623, In the period after the introduction of the reform, Engelthal received a German martyrology from the Nuremberg St. Catherine's Monastery, which Sister Christina Kamrerin completed on October 28, 1518. She wrote it for the prioress Birgitta Haller and the convent. The manuscript is now in the Gera City Archives (HB 7623) and was made known by Antje Willing: The Library of the St. Catherine's Monastery in Nuremberg. Synoptic Representation of the Book Lists Vol. 1 (2012), p. LXXXII (see also http://www.handschriftencensus.de/10308 with a link to the archive description by Paul Sparmberg).

records.rec_Title: Elisabeth von Kirchberg, Female

details.value:
Little is known about Elisabeth besides that which has been gleaned from her two texts, a Vita of Irmgard von Roth, and the Kirchberg sister-book. According to the Irmgard-Vita, she entered the Dominican monastery of Kirchberg at age four-and-a-half, and may have been of Jewish heritage. She had been a nun for forty-two years, and had been Irmgard's close confidante for twenty years when she began to write.
      The process by which the Irmgard Vita came to be written was rather complicated, has similarities with the composition of the Vita of Heinrich Seuse and Mechthild von Hackeborn's Liber specialis gratiae, and is detailed at the end of the Vita. Elisabeth wrote about Irmgard's experiences in secret; at first she recorded them on a wax tablet, then she transferred them to parchment for a permanent record. Irmgard sensed that Elisabeth might be engaged in such an activity, and her suspicions culminated in a nocturnal visit to Elisabeth's bed in which Irmgard searched for the manuscript. After Elisabeth received a promise from Irmgard that she would not destroy the text, she produced it for her. At this point, Irmgard took an active interest and role in the writing process, and the two women corroborated closely on a final version of the Vita.
      Like the Vita, there are two different versions of the sister-book. The shorter, more detailed version contains twenty-three vitae, is extant in a fifteenth-century manuscript, and was edited as the sister-book of Kirchberg bei Sulz. The longer contains sixty-four abbreviated vitae, is extant in a seventeenth-century manuscript, and was edited as Kirchberg bei Haigerloch. Walter Blank contends that both versions are independent copies of the same original, now lost. Due to continuities of style and content between the two redactions of the Irmgard-Vita--there is little doubt that Elisabeth was responsible for both renditions of the Vita--and the corresponding versions of the sister-book, Siegfried Ringler believes that Elisabeth wrote both editions of that text as well.

details.value: Loppa von Spiegel, Cologne, Script comparison, Medium, London, Victoria and Albert Museum, Inv.-Nr. 8997 I, An Antiphonal contains the choral parts sung during the celebration of the Divine Office or Mass celebrated by a monastic or other community. This type of choirbook was usually written in large format so that the whole choir could read the music at once. This example was made at the convent of St Klara in Cologne by one of the nuns, Sister Loppa de Speculo. Another surviving leaf records that Sister Jutta paid for the book while Loppa carried out the writing, lining (putting in the staves for the music), notation and illumination 'in the year 1350, when there was a great plague everywhere'. This was one of a series of books produced in the convent. The Abbess, Heylwigis von Beechoven, who had ruled the convent since 1344, is portrayed kneeling by the historiated initial of the Descent of the Holy Ghost on the Virgin and Apostles associating her prayer with this crucial event, when the Holy Spirit came to earth and the mission of the Apostles to spread the Christian revelation began. The prayer of her convent was thus part of the mission.

details.value: Ms. Munich CLM 29400 / 8 Unidentified nun-scribe A, Chelles, , Low, Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 29400 / 8, Written in Northeast France in the centre which produced the Cologne manuscripts of Augustine for Archbishop Hildebald (795–819), apparently the convent of Chelles. The fragment was used as a fly-leaf in a printed book (Asc. 837) which probably belonged to the small Augustinian house at Bernried in Bavaria: an entry saec. XVI referring to the obit of 'Johan Ducziner Brobst zu Berñriedt' (†15 August 1535) is seen on the recto.

details.value:
Ms. Nuremberg Cent. III 41 Unidentified hand A, Nuremberg, Hand identification, Medium, Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Cent. III 41, Three volumes of a Bible that was originally four volumes, but was originally planned to be six volumes or six volumes ( MBK III,3, p. 599f.): Cent. III,40 is referred to in old entries (1 r , 285 v ) as daz ander puch der bibel , Cent. III,41 (front cover, 258 va ) as Daz dritt puch der bibel, Cent. III,43 (front cover, 354 v ) as Daz VI puch der bibel. In the city library since 1538.
two hands: Kunigund Niklasin (1 ra –5 vb , 19 ra –109 rb , 135 ra –258 rb ) and another scribe (7 ra –18 vb , 109 va –134 rb )
corrections by another hand

20 slips of paper sewn to the lower margins contain instructions for illustrations, which are repeated on a sheet pasted to the inside front cover.

details.value:
Kunigund Schreiberin, Nuremberg, Unclear, Low, Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Cent. IV 14, 2 hands: 
1st hand: f.1ra–202ra,
2nd hand: f.205ra–307vb.
Later additions by two further hands:
1st: f.301r–v,
2nd: f.307vb–308ra.

On the inside of the front cover: a small parchment slip glued in, containing a table of contents written by Kunigund Niklasin, reading:
“Item in this book are found first the 24 harps… then about Saint Catherine of Siena.”

On f.1r: Swester Kungund Clos Schryberin (Sister Kunigund Clos, scribe); see also IV,6.

Brought into the convent by Kunigund Schreiberin (MBK III, 3, p. 615).

Ursula Geiselherin, Nuremberg, Script comparison, Medium, Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Cent. IV 30, The ms. bore the signature E LXIII in Nuremberg's St. Catherine's Monastery .
Continuation in Nuremberg, Stadtbibl., Cod. Cent. V, 5
written in book cursive by the hand of Ursula Geiselherin; a second hand appears on f.s 185rb-189ra, 217vb-219rb; corrections and additions by a third hand.

Written by Ursula Geiselherin based on an exemplar from the Klarakloster (Poor Clares) in Nuremberg.

The exemplar is preserved in Berlin, germ. f.1276 (see Degering I, p. 171), formerly Cheltenham, Phillipps 19491 (see Priebsch, Deutsche Handschriften in England I (1896), p. 127, no. 131).

The copy made at the Katharinenkloster is in two volumes; Volume II = Cent. V, 5.

details.value:
Kunigund Schreiberin, Nuremberg, Colophon. Is this Kunigund Niklasin?, Low, Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Cent. IV 37, Contains addenda written on f.129v-131v in the monastery of St. Katharina Nuremberg, including a text on f.130-131v with a note by the Kunigund scribe
Is this Kunigund Niklasin?

Gothic cursive script by several hands:
	•	Hand 1: fols. 1r–93r and 127r–129v
	•	Hand 2: fols. 93r–124v
	•	Hand 3: f.129v
	•	Hand 4: fols. 130r–131v, the hand of the scribe Kunigund, as seen on f.131v:
“Küngünt Schreyberin scripsit do pit got für mit einem avemaria dez begert sy daz irgotgnedig sey.”
(“Küngünt the scribe wrote [this]; she asks God with a Hail Mary that He may be merciful to her.”)
Hands 3 and 4 are additions, written in the Katharinenkloster.

details.value:
Gertrud Tetzel, Nuremberg, Colophon, High, Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Cent. VII 11a, Parchment: 1, 180, 189-190, 198, 207-208, 219-220.
book cursive script by two different hands:
 1. 2r-24r and 180r-262r by the hand of Gertraud Tetzlin;
 2. 25r-179r by the hand of Klara Keiperin

On 1r, an old table of contents, but the texts listed there are now in a different order in the manuscript, and some are missing; the manuscript was later rebound:
	•	“Item in the book, first, many beautiful sermons on how one should adorn and prepare the heart for God” (now 180r-251r)
	•	“Item, how one should prepare oneself for the Holy Sacrament” (154r-179v)
	•	“Item, The Twelve Deaths” (25r-153v)
	•	“Item, Saint Bernardino’s sermon on the Passion of Christ”
	•	“Item, On the Ten Commandments” (now missing)
	•	“Item, finally, about a holy virgin named Lydeweyg” (252r-262r).

 1. f.1r-7v
 2. f.8v-260r
 3. Additional supplements in numerous places by a younger hand.

details.value:
Chelles Poss 1, Chelles, This manuscript's script and decoration is very similar to the Chelles' manuscript of Köln, Erzbischöfliche Diözesan- und Dombibliothek, Cod. 63, 65, 67 (see E.A. Lowe, CLA, vol. 2, no. 238)., Low, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Douce 176, Can't be consulted (restricted)
Written in North-east France or possibly Cologne, as script and ornamentation in the type developed by the nuns of Chelles suggest; the MS has close affinity with the group of three MSS of St Augustine (Cologne, Dombibliothek 63, 65, 67) written by nuns for Hildebald, Archbishop of Cologne (785–819). Belonged to St Faron, Meaux, till the French Revolution, then to Gosselin, later to Remusat, at whose sale it was bought by Messrs Payne, the London booksellers, in 1833.
This manuscript's script and decoration is very similar to the Chelles' manuscript of Köln, Erzbischöfliche Diözesan- und Dombibliothek, Cod. 63, 65, 67 (see E.A. Lowe, CLA, vol. 2, no. 238).

details.value:
JC Sacramentary, Chelles, Extracted from the binding of an incunable (early printed book): a copy of Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum Historiale from the press of Johannes Mentelin, Strasbourg 1473 (now Douce 306).
Ziegler, Sakramentar Gelasianum, n. 18 associated them with Chelles, McKitterick argues they form a paleographical group with Bodleian, Vat. Reg. lat. 316 (R. McKitterick, 'Nuns' Scriptoria in England and Francia in the Eighth Century' Francia 19 (1992) 1–35 at p. 11) , Low, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Douce f.1, Can't be consulted (restricted)
pre-Caroline script, 'the immediate precursor of the so-called Corbie a-b'
Written in Chelles, doubtless in the same scriptorium as Vatic. Regin. Lat. 316 (CLA 1.105). The leaves were removed from the binding of an early printed book, Douce 306, containing Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum Historiale from the press of Johannes Mentelin, Strasbourg 1473.

details.value: Christine of Pizan, Paris, One hand was identified as Christine's autograph by G. Ouy et C. Reno., Medium, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, BnF Français 835, Les manuscrits de Christine de Pizan ont été écrits par trois mains bien reconnaissables : P, R et X (Christine de Pizan elle-même). Le ms Français 835 a été transcrit, dans sa majeure partie par R, identifié à P. de Cruce : cf.Delsaux, « Profil d’un copiste des manuscrits originaux de Christine de Pisan : P. de La Croix, alias la main R », article à paraître dans Scriptorium. P a copié les ff.441vb, l. 26 à 44vb. La main X a fait quelques corrections : mouche ou restauration sur laquelle l’auteur a réécrit, à l’encre noire, les mots manquants au f.100 : cf.G. Ouy et C. Reno, « Identification des autographes de Christine de Pizan », dans Scriptorium, 34, 1980, p. 221-238.

details.value: Henrieta of Lathilliaco, Lathilliacum, Colophon, High, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, BnF Latin 11969, Hugo Ripelin, Compendium theologicae veritatis, written between the lines and on the margins of a codex containing biblical texts from the 12th century. The space intended for the gloss, which was left blank, was occupied by the new text. The dimensions of the manuscript (ff.195) are 320x215 mm, the space for the original text is 208x90 mm for 18 lines on a full page. Many of the sheets were partially cut, presumably to make parchment. In 1354, before the new text was added, the codex had belonged to Nicasius, curate of 'Casiacum' (Chezy-sur-Marne, Aisne), as can be deduced from the ex libris on f.195v.The manuscript was later transferred to Saint-Germain-des-Prés (ex libris of the 16th century on f.195v and of the 18th century, with the signature 116, on the unnumbered sheet preceding f.1).

details.value: Regina Sattler, St. Gallen, Colophon, High, St.Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek , Ms. Sang. 603, Manuscrit composite du XVe siècle, en provenance du couvent dominicain Sainte-Catherine à Saint-Gall. Le codex composé de cinq fascicules reliés, en langue allemande, contient en plus d'un traité sur la Passion (« Les quarante bouquets de myrrhe de la Passion du Christ »), l'histoire de la fondation du couvent dominicain de Sainte-Catherine à Diessenhofen, le livre des sœurs de Diessenhofen et de Tösser, les légendes d'Elisabeth de Hongrie, de Marguerite de Hongrie, d'Ida de Toggenburg et de Louis de Toulouse, ainsi qu'un court extrait du Liber specialis gratiae de Mechthild von Hackeborn en traduction allemande. (fas)

details.value: Birgitta Andersdotter, Birgittine nun in Vadstena (Sweden) from 1491 to 1532, was closely connected to the ruling elite of her time, the Sture family. She corresponded with them, composed their family chronicle, and produced a manuscript for one of its members. She also paid for the production of manuscripts for the sisters’ convent in Vadstena Abbey, collaborating with a younger nun-scribe.

value.title: Barbara von Rottenburg, Reuthin, Female, Stuttgart, Württembergische Landesbibliothek, Brev. 63, Main parts

details.value:
Barbara von Rottenburg, Reuthin, Script comparison, Medium, Stuttgart, Württembergische Landesbibliothek, Brev. 63, Writer of the main parts: Sister Barbara von Rottenburg in the Dominican monastery Maria-Reut(h)in (Fiala/Irtenkauf p. 84)
Based on the documents used for binding, this (collective) manuscript originates from the Dominican convent of Reutin. According to G. Piccard’s watermark analysis, it was not begun before 1515 and was completed by around 1529.
The main scribe of its primary sections is Sister Barbara von Rottenburg of Reutin (Gand No. 175), who identifies herself in a manuscript she authored (Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 31, f.64r). She is considered the primary scribe of Reutin from around 1488 to 1534. Her works include:
 • Cod. theol. et phil. qu. 77 (1488-1492),
 • Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 31 (1492),
 • Cod. brev. 27 (1511),
 • Cod. brev. 73 (1521),
 • Cod. theol. et phil. qu. 49a-b (1524),
 • Cod. brev. 49 (1529),
 • Cod. theol. et phil. oct. 33 (1534).

details.value:
Barbara von Rottenburg, Reuthin, Colophon, High, Stuttgart, Württembergische Landesbibliothek, Brev. 73, several hands: Hd. 2 = Barbara von Rottenburg
The manuscript is composed of partially incomplete prayer booklets written by various hands at different times. The initial section was written in 1496 at the Benedictine Monastery of Lorch: “56v Written in Lorch in the year 1496 by Clemens of the convent brothers of Lorch” (likely Clemens Aurifabri, prior in 1490; see Württembergische Geschichtsquellen, Vol. 12, 1910, p. 86).
The second hand is attributed to Sister Barbara of Rottenburg from Reutin (see Cod.brev.63), suggesting Reutin as the manuscript’s library of origin. Her work is dated to 1521 (83v).

details.value:
Ms. Württembergische Landesbibliothek Brev. 73, Unidentified Hand 4, Stuttgart, , Low, Stuttgart, Württembergische Landesbibliothek, Brev. 73, several hands: Hd. 2 = Barbara von Rottenburg
The manuscript is composed of partially incomplete prayer booklets written by various hands at different times. The initial section was written in 1496 at the Benedictine Monastery of Lorch: “56v Written in Lorch in the year 1496 by Clemens of the convent brothers of Lorch” (likely Clemens Aurifabri, prior in 1490; see Württembergische Geschichtsquellen, Vol. 12, 1910, p. 86).
The second hand is attributed to Sister Barbara of Rottenburg from Reutin (see Cod.brev.63), suggesting Reutin as the manuscript’s library of origin. Her work is dated to 1521 (83v).

value.title: Angela Varnbühler, St. Gallen, Female, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), Main sections
Angela Varnbühler, St. Gallen, Female

details.value:
Angela Varnbühler, St. Gallen, Script comparison, Medium, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch"), Ce manuscrit, qui dans la recherche scientifique antérieure a souvent été appelé « Chronique », est le « Konventsbuch » de St. Katharina à Saint-Gall (61r:...und sol dis also in des convents buoch gesetz werden...). On y trouve des entrées chronologiques concernant les intérêts économiques du couvent. Le manuscrit a été établi au cours de la réforme au moment où le couvent passait de propriété privée à une propriété commune. Ainsi, ce livre permettait à la direction du couvent de St. Katharina de rendre compte auprès de la communauté des possessions gérées. Il permettait également aux sœurs de connaître l’état de leurs biens initialement déposés au couvent. Le manuscrit contient des contributions concernant les activités de construction, l’équipement, le scriptorium, les contentieux, les donations, mais aussi des entrées relatives à certaines soeurs, directeurs de conscience ou ouvriers, ainsi que, épisodiquement, des entrées concernant l’histoire du couvent.
 The chronicle contains reports and notes from a wide variety of areas of contemporary convent history: Angela Varnbühler 's investing hand begins (ex post) with her election as prioress in 1476, and continues with a list of the conventuals as well as reports from the implementation of the first Steps to reform the monastery. Regula Keller, St. Gallen, Unclear, Medium, Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, No inventory number, Main hand and accounting entries written by Prioress Anna Krumm, e.g., fols. 1r–2r [1v blank], ljrv, lxiijr–lxviv, and throughout
 • Alternating with the hand of Angela Varnbühler, in semi-cursive; both using brown ink
 • f.lxxiiijv: a 7-line entry in almost black ink by Elisabeth Schaigenwiler
 • Additional hands from around 1450, including some otherwise unknown female scribes

Numerous marginal annotations by Regula Keller in the first half of the 16th century (ca. 1530 and after), using a very fine quill
 • Examples:
 • f.1r: “The estates were sold during the adversities of the Lutheran times by the people of St. Gallen”
 • f.4v: “The estate was also sold in the turbulent Lutheran times by the people of St. Gallen”
 • f.11r: “The estate was sold by the people of St. Gallen as they authorized us”
(see also fig. 25)

details.value: Cecilia Sparnecker, Germany, Colophon, High, Würzburg Universitätsbibliothek, M.ch.f.4, A collection of manuscripts, written primarily on paper, which can be localized to Bamberg. The first part of the manuscript contains a German mirror of salvation. Erasmus Sternhals is identified as its writer in a colophon. The work was probably made for the Bamberg canon Georg von Löwenstein. This is indicated by the depiction of a kneeling canon and several coats of arms on f.56r. The German-language biography of the Holy Bishop Otto, which is bound in afterwards, also refers to Bamberg. It was written down by two Bamberg Poor Clares and completed in 1483. The third work in the collection is a life of Saint Catherine, dated 1488 and also written by a woman.

records.rec_Title: Catherine of Bologna, Female

details.value: OSC. Italian Poor Clare from Bologna. Daughter of Giovanni Vigri of Ferrara and Benvenuta Mammolini. She received a courtly education at the court of the princes of Este in Ferrara, where he was for a while a personal servant of the duke's daughter Margarita. Around 1427/28, she came under the spiritual influence of Lucia Mascheroni, who led a local female religious community that initially followed the Augustinian rule, but was in the process of becoming a house of Observant Poor Clares. During this period, Caterina experienced a religious crisis, fell victim to ‘diabolical’ illusions. Once a member of the now Clarissan community, Caterina became responsible for the training of novices. In 1456, she was instrumental in creating a new convent of Observant Poor Clares in Bologna, where she obtained the position of Abbess until her death on 9 March 1463. Under her abbatiate, the Bologna Observant Clarissan monastery became a renowned hub of religious culture. Throughout her life, Caterina experienced visions and revelations, and at the same time obtained saintly reputation. She also became renowned for her religious art (including paintings and an illustrated breviary) and her spiritual writings in Italian and Latin, which included the Rosarium Metricum de Mysteriis Passionis Christi Domini et de Vita B. Marie Virginis, and Le armi necessarie alla battaglia spirituale (1483), composed for female novices. Caterina was canonised in 1712 by pope Clement XI.

records.rec_Title: Jane Segar, Female

details.value: This manuscript contains The Divine Prophecies of the Ten Sibills, written and illuminated by Jane Segar, sister of the Elizabethan herald and officer of arms Sir William Segar (b. c. 1554, d. 1633) and the courtier and painter Francis Segar (b. 1563, d. 1615). Jane presented the volume to Elizabeth I (r. 1558-1603) in 1589, probably as a New Year's gift, and prefaced the work with a prose dedication to the Queen.

details.value: In the Nonnberg necrology (archive MS 6/106 V, fol. 87r) she is recorded with her date of death on 21 September as Hilaria monialis nostrae congregationis Pfaffinger S. E. She was the aunt of the later abbess Regina Pfaffinger (1505–1514) and sister of Monteflor (Genteflor) Pfaffinger, documented in 1478 as steward to Duke Ludwig IX of Bavaria-Landshut (Lang, pp. 58f.). She also copied MS 23 B 24, fols. 1r–105r.
