value.title: Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cgm 6940

details.value:
According to the colophon (202vb), Fascicle I was written in 1493 by two sisters of the Poor Clares’ convent in Söflingen:

“This book was written in the year when one counted from the birth of Christ 1493 by two sisters of the Order of Saint Clare of the convent at Söflingen, and the scribes request that one pray to God for them, whether they be living or dead, with a Pater noster or Ave Maria or Requiem aeternam. 1493.”

In another script (loopless Bastarda), probably by a different contemporary hand, the sisters’ names are added:

“The names of these sisters (is crossed out) are Cordula von Reischach (the following d crossed out) and Cristina Keckin of Nuremberg.”

details.value: f.Iv: Gedenckt der lieben unser geislich muter Anna Ebyn die daz puch und gar und vil pu/e/cher dem convent hat geschriben die ungezelt sind (librarian's entry). Also, on 1r, librarian has written "Daz puch ist der ffrawen zu Pillennrewt und sol allczeit pey dem clostr beleyben. In the 4th item (14v-24r), Joh. von Marienwerder's 37 Zeichen der Gottesliebe der Dorothea von Montau, Anna Ebin announces "Aber an eim roten puch da etlich heyligen an steen (=Wolf cod. 17.9.Aug.4o, see Ringler VL 2nd ed 2, 295 and MTU 72 s. 55-57) hab ich dy geschriben ... alz ez meister Nycloz prediger zum newen spital zu Nurmberg Dorothee peichtigers schulgesell beschryben hat. (15r). For 9th item, Schwesternbuch von Weiler, colophon reads "Geendet am eritag nach der h. trinitat in die Marci und Marcelliani (=18 June) anno domini M. CCCC. LIIII. im covent zu Bildenrew/e/t. At end of 17th item (145r-174v), Vita of H. Eufrasia, dt. von Kaspar KreSS, "Geendet am freytag nach dem achten tag dez obersten in die sancte Prysce ... anno domini M. CCCC. LX. (=18 Jan)... Pitet got fu"r dye schreyberin und auch fu"r den dew"tschmacher diser legend eins gelerten pryster sanct Benedicten ordens zu sancto Egydigio (!) zu Nu"rmbeg genant mgr. C. Kr. (=Kaspar KreSS). A SECOND HAND COPIED Item 22 (252v-274v) shows that she consciously copied this as a "buchlein" -- in sections. For Bonaventura, De quinque festivitatibus pueri Jesu (dt), she says "Also hat ende das puchelein wi Yesus Xc kind ist worden und entfangen geportn geislich etc. 1461

details.value: A tres excellent Redoubtee & puissant et tres princesse. Ma dame ysabel Royne de France ...- ... Escript le ve jour d'octombre. l'an de grace mil iiij C et/ cinq. Vostre treshumble obeissant Creature/ cristine de Pizan. Prennez en gré s'il vous plaist cest escript / De ma main fait aprés mienuit une heure / Noble seigneur pour qui je l'ai escript / Prennez en gré / Quant vous plaira mieulz vous sera rescript / Mais n'avoye nul autre clerc a l'eure / Prennez en gré s'il...

To the most excellent, revered, powerful, and most noble princess,
My lady Isabel, Queen of France…

Written on the eve of October, in the year of grace 1405.

Your most humble and obedient servant,
Christine de Pizan.

Please accept this writing, if it pleases you,
Made by my own hand after midnight, at one o’clock.
Noble lord, for whom I have written it,
Please accept it.
When it pleases you, it can be copied more finely.
But I had no other clerk at the time—
Please accept it…”

value.title: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 580

details.value: « A tres excellent Redoubtee & puissant et tres princesse. Ma dame ysabel Royne de France ...- ... Escript le ve jour d'octombre. l'an de grace mil iiij C et/ cinq. Vostre treshumble obeissant Creature/ cristine de Pizan. Prennez en gré s'il vous plaist cest escript / De ma main fait aprés mienuit une heure / Noble seigneur pour qui je l'ai escript / Prennez en gré / Quant vous plaira mieulz vous sera rescript / Mais n'avoye nul autre clerc a l'eure / Prennez en gré s'il...» (f.53r)

Selon Christine Reno et Inès Villela-Petit, ce manuscrit serait une commande du duc de Berry et l’Epitre à la reine ne figurait pas dans le projet initial. L'Epitre à la reine a été identifié comme un autographe par Charity Cannon Willard.

details.value: Das puch ward auSS geschriben an der helligen marter tag Johannes vnd Paulus tag als man zalt von Christus gepurt MCCCC. vnd ym L(X)XVII jar (erste X getilgt). Item das puch hot geschriben swester Hrabra Pfinczigin in Bilenrewt sancti Augustini ordinis regularium cananicarum czu lob vnd ere der ho"hsten trinitat vnd wer das nu"czt der gedenk ir gen got ym leben vnd todt was in got vermant etc.

This book was completed on the feast day of the Holy Martyrs John and Paul, according to the reckoning from the birth of Christ, 1500, and in the year L(X)XVII (the first X erased). Furthermore, this book was written by Sister Hrabra Pfinczigin in Bilenrewt, of the Order of Saint Augustine, Regular Canons, for the praise and glory of the Most Holy Trinity, and for the remembrance of her and her service to God in life and death, may she be united with God, etc.

Part of C08 was written in the years 1473–1486, when Margareta Claesdotter was abbess. The name of the scribe cannot be determined here in a fully objective manner. In the second part, the name of the scribe is certain, but the dating is not sufficiently precise. However, in 1486 Anna Fickesdotter became prioress, and this would probably have been mentioned in some way if the manuscript had been written after that year. There is, however, no doubt that the hand is the same in both parts. Kristina Johansdotter Brask wrote the directorium chori.

details.value: A treshaute et puissante Princesse Elizabeth Roine d'Angleterre et cetera, Madame, combien que ie soye peu exercée ... De votre Majestie La treshumble, tresobeissante et tresaffectionnée servante a Jamais, Esther Langlois, Fille Françoise. Explicit: de pouvoir a Jamais vous faire treshumble service. Huius ipsius Libelli Prosopopoeia, Filia me scripsit mandante vtroque Parente/ Exilii calamo taedia discutiens.
Crown atop an unidentifiable device, hidden in the gutter on f.i only.
Collation beginning with f. ii: 12 24 34(replacement leaf attached to stub of original 3rd leaf) 42 5-124 136 142(+ a leaf pasted to 2nd leaf)

To the most high and powerful Princess Elizabeth, Queen of England, etc., Madam, although I am little practiced… From Your Majesty’s most humble, most obedient, and most affectionate servant forever, Esther Langlois, a French daughter.”

Explicit: “To be forever able to render you most humble service. The personification of this very little book — my daughter wrote me, at the command of both parents / driving away the tedium of exile with her pen.”

value.title: San Marino, Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens, mssHM 26068

details.value: Incipit: A treshaute et puissante Princesse Elizabeth Roine d'Angleterre et cetera, Madame, combien que ie soye peu exercée ... Huius ipsius Libelli Prosopopoeia, Filia me scripsit mandante vtroque Parente/ Exilii calamo taedia discutiens.

Discours de la Foy copied (but possibly not written?) by the calligrapher Esther Inglis in Edinburgh, 1591, for Queen Elizabeth.
There are more manuscripts written by this scribe after 1600, cf.PXL_20241029_151037781.MP.jpg
2-line initials in black, most with flourishing, begin stanzas.

details.value:
Prayer book:
 • 57r–71r: Passion prayers beginning “Protect me at all times and especially at my last departure…” including (on 59r) a list of saints predominantly of Dominican origin.
70r: Morning prayer addressed to Eternal Wisdom: “O most beautiful, most radiant, eternal Wisdom…”
 • 71v–83v: Prayers to saints including Mary Magdalene, (76r) Anna, (78r) George, (79r) Nicholas, (80r) Dorothea, (80v) Barbara, (81v) Margaret, (82v) Catherine. At 83v, the date mentioned earlier is repeated.
 • 88r–100v: Prayer by St. Bernard when Jesus descended to him from the Cross: “Hail, Jesus, the salvation of the world…”
 • 101r: Blank.
 • 101v: Rubric for the Rosary of Christ, incomplete.
 • 142r–153v: Exhortation for the contemplation of the sovereignty of God, German, ,

Sessinghaus, Scholastica

Scholastica was elected abbess of Kloster Vinnenberg around July 19, 1547, by Bishop Franz von Waldeck, succeeding Hillegund Hoyer. During her term, the monastery church underwent two devastating fires in 1550 and 1568. She compiled a calendar and index for the monastery around 1560. She died sometime before March 26 1572, when Johann von Hoya, Bishop of Münster, appointed her successor Dorothea Peicks. (from himml: https://haf.vhmml.org/person/832310079740)

details.value: f. 25r: Es ist zu wissen das die legend der heiligen wirdigen junckfrawn sant Margrethn nicht beslissung hat vmb des willen das si noch nicht erhaben ist ... Pittet got für vnsern erwirdigen getrewen liben vater vikari Jorg Valder der dise legend mit müe aus latein zu deüczsch pracht hat. Auch pitt ich euch mein allerherzigistn libsten muter vnd swester das ir got pittfür die schreiberinn s(wester) Agnes Pabnbergerin wann ich euch das mit ganzer begird meins herzen geschribn hab das ir mein dapei gedenkt zu got vnd der junckfrawn Maria mit einem avemaria. (Darunter von anderer Hand: gern gern.)

It should be known that the legend of the holy, worthy virgin Saint Margaret has no conclusion, because she has not yet been elevated [to sainthood]…
Pray to God for our venerable, faithful, dear father, Vicar Jörg Valder, who with effort has brought this legend from Latin into German.
I also beg you, my most beloved mother and sister, to pray to God for the scribe, Sister Agnes Pabnbergerin, for I have written this for you with the whole desire of my heart, so that you may remember me before God and the Virgin Mary with an Ave Maria.
(Underneath, in another hand: Gladly, gladly.)

A single added f.at the end of Edinburgh University Library, MS 59 that may with certainty be attributed to Mary.
The insertion of a final f.to compensate for one that had got lost at the end of a quire (the catchword ‘iudicare’ is found on f.115v) would support de Hamel’s thesis that it was Mary’s job as chantress to repair manuscripts that had missing text.

details.value:
Composed of three parts: I 1r-21vb ; II 22ra-72v ; III 73r-150v.
The three parts of the codex were written in the Benedictine nunnery of Lamspringe in the early third quarter of the 12th century

value.title: Lamspringe, Benedictine, Lamspringe, Lower Saxony, Germany,-1138

details.value: Rubricated, red Lombards, marginal corrections and additions framed in red, scriptural quotations underlined in red. Section majuscules in black, depending on the letter form stroked, dotted, or filled in red. At the beginning of the individual books, column-staff initials with white staff stem outlined in red, clasps, and red column filling, colored grounds and frames. In detail: 73r (preface to book I), initial I over 9 lines, through the slit in the letter stem winds a dragon outlined in red; the letter is framed left blue, right green, each with red dots. 78r (book I), initial F over 10 lines on a framing ground blue on the left and green on the right with red dots, surrounded by a red wavy line. The vertical shaft of the F is formed of two spirally interlaced staffs outlined in green; one ends above in a leafy curved branch and below in a serpent’s head; the ends of the second are identical but reversed. From the upper serpent’s head grows the body of a winged dragon forming the upper crossbar of the letter; from its mouth protrudes a human foot. The second crossbar of the F is a simple column-staff separating two inner-field motifs: in the upper part, the filius regis named in the text, in pen drawing as a crowned bust in speaking gesture with an open book; in the lower part, a dog-like beast of prey, from whose jaws grows a vine with knobbed and herb leaves as well as half-palmettes. Enlarged illustration in Härtel, 48. 98v (preface to book II), initial P over 16 lines, plain form with a knobbed-leaf vine in the field and a contour-following half-palmette vine; letter framed in gold color, only under the stem blue, as also the ground of the inner field. 99r (book II), similarly framed initial I over 9 lines, whose letter body is formed by two symmetrically intertwined serpents. 129v (preface to book III), initial E over 6 lines, framed in gold, inner field blue above and in front, green below, and at the clasp of the crossbar two axially symmetrical spiral vines with vegetal outgrowths. 129v (book III), initial D over 9 lines, framed in gold, inner field blue on the left, green on the right, with the crowned half-figures of Sponsus (left, with red scroll) and Sponsa (right), enlarged illustration in Härtel, 49. 137r (preface to book IV), initial P over 12 lines, analogous in design to the above, though here the ground is three-colored (gold, blue, green), and a bird additionally sits on the vine in the inner field. 137v (book IV), initial V over 11 lines with three-colored ground and framing (gold, blue, green); the inner field is occupied by the forepart of a lion shown from the side, looking backward, whose hindpart with tail wound through the hind legs projects far left into the side margin. From its mouth grows a vine with knobbed leaves and half-palmette.

details.value: Collation: vol. 1: i2 (ff.1-2); ii8+1 (ff. 3-11); iii-vi8 (ff. 12-43); vii8+4-1 (ff. 49-52 including 2 unfoliated leaves after f. 50; 1 originaly blank leaf excised after f. 50**; a quire of 4 leaves is inserted in the main quire of 8 leaves between ff. 48 and 51); viii-xii8 (ff. 53-92); xiii2 (ff. 93-94); xiv-xxiii8 (ff. 95-173); xxiv4 (ff. 174-177); vol. 2: xxv-xxix8 (ff. 178-217); xxx4-1 (ff. 218-220; 1 leaf excised after f. 219); xxxi16 (ff. 221-236); xxxi-xxxiii8 (ff. 237-252); xxxiv2 (ff. 253-254); xxxv4-1 (ff. 255-257); xxxvi-liii8 (ff. 258-398; including 2 unfoliated leaves after f. 374 in quire l and 1 unfoliated leaf after f. 398 in quire liii).

value.title: London, British Library, Harley MS 4431

details.value:
Bound in two volumes with continuous foliation: vol. 1: ff. 177(+ 8 unfoliated flyleaves: 3 paper leaves and 2 ruled parchment leaves at the beginning and 3 paper leaves at the end; + 2 unfoliated ruled parchment leaves after f. 50); vol. 2: ff. 220 (+ 8 unfoliated: 4 paper flyleaves at the beginning and 3 paper and one parchemnt at the end; + 2 unfoliated ruled parchment leaves after f. 374).

Catchwords and bifolium signatures. Bifolium signatures start in quire ii (ff. 3-11).

2 half-page miniatures in gold and colours (ff. 3r, 290r). Numerous smaller miniatures in gold and colours, the width of one column. Large initials in gold and colours with ivy and foliate motifs, sometimes with a full border with acanthus and flowers (f. 3r), with gold ivy and flowers (ff. 4r, 390r), or with a partial border (f. 2v), or with a few foliate ink tendrils. Initials in colours and gold, sometimes with foliate ink tendrils. Paraph marks and line-fillers in red, blue and gold. Cadels with scrolls wrapped around the ascenders.

Miniatures attributed to the Master of the Cité des Dames and workshop and to the Master of the Duke of Bedford.

details.value: Desen boeck heft ghescreuen. Ende met groeten aerbeyt vergadert onse gheminde mede suster. suster lijsbeth mols. Ende dat inden tijt dat sij aen die schiue diende. Ende sij heeft begheert dat desen boeck altoes op den choer sal ligghen. omtrint oft voer die priorinne op dat een yeghelijc daer in mach vinden na sijn beliefte. Ende sij bidt ende begheert zeere oetmoedelijc uwer alder deuoet ghebeth voer haer arm ziele. die v oec wilen inden last der priorinscap onweerdich ghedient heeft. xxxiii Requiescant in pace Amen
Mostly quaternions but varies a lot. Many folios cut off.

This book has been written and, with great effort, compiled by our dear fellow-sister, Sister Lijsbeth Mols, at the time when she was serving at the writing desk. And she has requested that this book should always lie in the choir, either near or before the prioress, so that everyone may find in it according to their devotion. And she prays and most humbly asks for your most devout prayers for her poor soul, who also once served—unworthily—in the burden of the prioress’s office.
May they rest in peace. Amen.

Bilingual – Latin and Middle Dutch – psalter (Den Haag, Koninklijke Bibliotheek, MS 133 C 1) - The psalms are supplemented by both a prayer in Dutch and one in Latin, and by a Latin commentary which is derived from Ludolf von Sachsen’s Expositio super psalterium.15 According to the renowned Flemish philologist Jan Deschamps, Elisabeth did not translate the Latin texts into Middle Dutch herself; supposedly she used a Brabantine redaction of a West-Flemish translation of the psalter, which was made at the end of the thirteenth or the beginning of the fourteenth century. Nevertheless, the fact that Elisabeth gathered texts from different sources and put them together shows that she must have had excellent Latin.16

details.value: Cum ageretur a partu virginis annus vicesimus secundus post mille quingentos scripsit librum hunc soror Magdalena Buxtehuden hic regulari professione Christo dicata. Sumptus provenere ex diversis fidelium elemosinis. Exoretur deus pro omnibus qui manus hoc porrexere adiutrices.

When the 22nd year after the birth of the Virgin’s Son was being counted (i.e., in the year 1522), this book was written by Sister Magdalena Buxtehuden, here consecrated to Christ by religious profession.
The costs were covered by various offerings from the faithful.
May God be entreated on behalf of all who extended helping hands in this work.

St. Anne's Priory, Augustinian, Lübeck, Germany, 1502-
1532

details.value: lue and red initials span two or three lines/staves with interlocking divided color fields, inner and outer palmette fleur-de-lis, partly on a green background on folios 1r, 2r, 39r, 188r, and 204r. On folio 237v, an L initial spans two lines/staves with a drawing of St. Joseph and the inscription " Sanctus Josephus ." On folio 254r, an A initial also spans two lines with the inscription " Ave Maria gratia plena. Dominus tecum. Benedicta . " Rubricated, red and blue Lombards as well as black Cadellen with leaf and tendril decoration as contour accompaniment and in the inner fields.
Above each line of text is a staff consisting of four red staves with C and F clefs and Gothic chant notation. Some sections include instructions for chorus and organum

details.value:
A split-border initial. Five Lombard silhouettes. Two sketches.
Initial and silhouette Lombards: At the beginning of Gilbertus Crispinus, a cleft initial with single and five-nailed clasps (81v; 3.6 cm). From one clasp arises a palmette shoot filling the central field, another as the initial stem end. The ends contain seeded palmettes and buds. The leaf backs are hatched. At other highlighted text beginnings, Lombards with simple stem-accompanying silhouette decoration (1r, 10v, 58r, 59v, 60r; 2.0–3.9 cm). The Lombard on 10v is indicated in the stem as a cleft initial.

Sketches: On 10r in the upper right corner, a hastily drawn head (en face) with a hood-like headdress (by a later hand; 5.5 cm). On an inlaid strip of parchment, a pen drawing of a hand chained around the neck (contemporaneous hand; 3.6 cm).

Colors: The initial letter is drawn in red, the initial stem columns are filled in green. The tendril in the center is green, the initial stem end is red. The Lombardic strokes are red and green with silhouette decoration in the contrasting color.

details.value:
Ornate sentence and initial capital letters. 3 initials.
Decorated sentence and initial capitals: Some sentences with rubricated sentence capitals, which in the final arrangement or as letter replacements have feather-like curved leaves (profile leaves, cf. 53v), dot decorations (cf. 67v), mythical creature heads (cf. 73r) and buds (cf. 33v).

Initials: At the beginnings of three books, cleft-ribbed initials with cross- or flower-decorated clasps (1v lib. I, 43v lib. 3, 77v lib. 4). In the inner fields, spiral tendrils run in a dynamic pattern, arranged axially symmetrically as a herbaceous plant on 1v. The terminal decoration consists of bulbous leaves, palmette leaves, and profiled palmette leaves with veining/hatching. The tendril/bud variant with the palmette integrated into the flow and the backward-curving bud at the end (1v) is particularly striking. Large bud primordia are present in the tendril forks. A large, winged dragon with a circularly decorated body and a twisted palmette tail serves as a tail substitute on 1v. 5.4–8.0 cm.

details.value:
6 initials. 1 miniature. Two marginal drawings.
Miniature: On 1v, at the beginning of the Bede text, a colored pen drawing of a scribe working at a lectern (framed). In his hands he holds a knife and a pen. On the lectern are an open book and inkwells. Kneeling, a monk/cleric (possibly a provost of Lamspringe) holds the shaft of the lectern in his arms. Within the frame, around the drawing, is the inscription: Ut huius sancti Hieronimi beatitudinis particeps apud dominum efficiatur, prefiguratus felix Petrus idcirco, quantum humana possibilitas permittit, eius doctrinis et meritis divina gratia preveniente incessanter adheret . 13.1–7.6 cm – framed field.

Initials: The initials at the beginnings of the texts around Bede (2r, 2v, 4r, 48v, 90v, and 129v) are cleft-frame initials with loosely curved spiral tendrils and five-pointed nailed clasps. The terminals are decorated with bulbous and palmette leaves. The latter sometimes show seeds, veins, and hatched leaf spines. The tendril forks have plastic (cf. 4r) and linear compressions. On 90v, the initial stem ends in a mythical creature's head. 2.2–5.4 cm.

Marginal drawings on the lower edges of the leaves: 136v a palmette plant. 139r, a colored pen drawing of a man in a cloak (a nobleman), holding a branch in his right hand. Beside him, a two-headed bird with branches in its beaks. Above, the inscription Filius columbae .P. porta[n]s [?] ramum oliviae (Gen 8:11) scilicet viscera misericordiae (Lc 1:78). Next to the bird, the inscription Vox turturis (with neumes). On the upper edge of leaf 35r, a head with a Phrygian cap (blind drawing). 139v: 3.0 × 4.4 cm (entire image area).

Colors: The initials are drawn with a red pen. Details (clasps and leaves) are washed in yellow. Garments are painted with light washes (orange and green). The valleys of folds are in a darkened local color, the highlights are left unpainted in parchment. The flesh tones are parchment-colored with circular red cheeks. The edges of the garments, the shaft of the lectern, as well as the cushions and bench are ornamentally decorated in orange and washed in yellow. The miniature and border drawing on 139r are in the same color scheme.

details.value: The vertical letter stems are decorated with generously lobed, only slightly veined leaf appliqués and show gold pollen against a red background as split filling. The terminal strokes are trefoils or half-palmettes with barely segmented edges and no veins. The initials are surrounded by broad green borders with red outlines, which also enclose the terminal strokes of the letters. The spandrels between the frame and the initial, as well as part of the letter background, are colored blue, while the figures depicted in the figural initials are set against a gold ground. Despite general similarities with the figural initials of the Hamersleben Psalter (Cod. Guelf. 1075 Helmst.), the details of the initial design show that, contrary to the prevailing scholarly opinion (e.g., Wolter-von dem Knesebeck, Lamspringe , 474f.), the Hamersleben Psalter probably did not serve as a direct model. However, there is no doubt that the illuminator of Cod. Guelf. 905 Helmst. was familiar with the iconographic program of the Hamersleben Psalter and was inspired by it; see, in more detail, the forthcoming catalogue of illuminated manuscripts, HAB 1 . Specifically included are: 27r historicized initial D for Psalm 26 over 8 lines (approx. 6.8 x 6 cm): Christ, recognizable by the cruciform halo, in a blue tunic heightened with white and a red pallium, heals a young man clothed in a yellowish-brown garment. This serves as a word illustration for Psalm 26:1 ( Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea).The scene depicted probably represents the healing of the man born blind at the Pool of Siloam (John 9:1–41), during which Christ proclaims himself the Light of the World (John 9:5). Since the scrolls held by both figures in their left hands are blank, a definitive identification is not possible. 41r Historicized initial D to Psalm 38 over 8 lines (approx. 6.8 x 65 cm): A youthful, golden-nimbed saint in a frontal half-figure, wearing a blue tunic heightened with white and a red pallium, his right hand half-raised in a gesture of speech, holding a book with red fittings in his left. A more precise identification is not possible based on the attributes; it is evidently a word illustration for Psalm 38:2 ( Dixi custodiam vias meas ut non delinquam in lingua mea posui ori meo custodiam ). 53v Historicized initial Q to Psalm 51 over 7 lines (6 x 6.5 cm): The youthful Christ (half-figure) with a cruciform halo, yellowish-brown tunic, and red pallium addresses Satan in a speech-like gesture. Satan is depicted as a wolf-like animal with grayish-brown fur, pointing to three stones represented as round spheres, which Christ is to transform into bread. Both figures hold blank scrolls, so that the exact source of the scene of the first temptation (Matthew 4:3–4 or Luke 4:3–4) can no longer be determined. The choice of representation is probably motivated by Psalm 51:3 ( Quid gloriaris in malitia qui potens in iniquitate ). 54r Historicized initial D to Psalm 52 over 5 lines (approx. 4.5 x 5.5 cm): Bust of a gold-crowned king with a green undergarment and a red cloak fastened at the right shoulder with a clasp, his right hand half-raised in a speaking gesture, holding a book with red fittings in his left. It is not entirely clear how the depiction relates to the traditional insipiens shown (Psalm 52:1). 68r Figurative initial S to Psalm 68 over 9 lines (approx. 7.5 x 6 cm): Design differs from the historicized initials; the frame consists of a red (top), green (right), brown (bottom), and blue (left) strip. Against a gold background stands a two-legged, red-and-blue winged dragon (lindworm), whose coiled body, colored in three stripes of green, pink, and brown, forms the letter. 85v Initial E to Psalm 80 over 7 lines (approx. 5.5 x 5.5 cm): In a slightly right-turned half-figure, a golden-nimbed, crowned king (David?) with a green undergarment and a red cloak fastened at the right shoulder with a clasp, holding a golden orb in his right hand and a golden scepter with a blue lily-like crown in his left. 102r Initial CPsalm 97, over 7 lines (approx. 5.8 x 5 cm): Half-figure of a haloed woman with long, flowing hair, a crown-like diadem, and a blue undergarment and red outer garment, holding both hands half-raised in an orant gesture. 104r Initial D , for Psalm 101, over 8 lines (approx. 6.5 x 7 cm): Ascension of Christ according to the type of the vanishing Christ, who has risen so far from the centrally located altar-like stone that only his legs and the lower part of his blue tunic with white highlights and his red pallium are visible. The scene is observed by four figures depicted as busts, with golden halos: above, two blue-clad angels holding empty scrolls; below, on the left, Mary in red; and below, on the right, the youthful beloved disciple John. The chosen scene corresponds thematically to Psalms 101:17 and 101:20. For the depiction, see A. Worm , Steine ​​und Fußspuren Christi auf dem Ölberg. Zu zwei ungewöhnlichen Motiven bei Darstellungen der Himmelfahrt Christi, in: Zeitschrift für Kunstgeschichte 66 (2003), 297–320, here 303f. with fig. 9. 118r Initial D to Psalm 109 over 6 lines (approx. 5 x 6 cm): A youthful, red-robed, tonsured cleric in frontal half-length, holding a green palm frond in his right hand and an olive-green bound book in his left. The depiction with the martyr's attribute of the palm frond could be interpreted as a word illustration for Psalm 109:2 ( virgam virtutis emittet dominus ex Zion ). At the beginning of each psalm (59r is the initial for Psalm 58, cut out) and at the beginning of each month in the calendar (abbreviated KŁ ), red-outlined gold initials feature stem-accompanying, sometimes deviating from the outline, vegetal and geometric silhouette ornaments in a lively, varied palette of green, red, and blue; in the calendar, only the latter is used. The silhouettes, mostly lobed in simple teardrop or bud shapes, transition into large, curved palmettes. The inner fields contain vegetal (plants, leaves) and geometric elements (medallions, etc.). Some letter bodies are partially or completely replaced by dragon-like mythical creatures or their heads, which spew out silhouette ornaments or initial stems. Details of the fleuronnée and silhouette design can already be found in the older products of the Lamspringe scriptorium, which belong to the so-called "Scriptrix" group; cf. Cod. Guelf. 723 Helmst. The text is consistently rubricated and features alternating red and blue uncial capitals.

details.value:
A split-border initial. Five Lombard silhouettes. Two sketches.
Initial and silhouette Lombards: At the beginning of Gilbertus Crispinus, a cleft initial with single and five-nailed clasps (81v; 3.6 cm). From one clasp arises a palmette shoot filling the central field, another as the initial stem end. The ends contain seeded palmettes and buds. The leaf backs are hatched. At other highlighted text beginnings, Lombards with simple stem-accompanying silhouette decoration (1r, 10v, 58r, 59v, 60r; 2.0–3.9 cm). The Lombard on 10v is indicated in the stem as a cleft initial.

Sketches: On 10r in the upper right corner, a hastily drawn head (en face) with a hood-like headdress (by a later hand; 5.5 cm). On an inlaid strip of parchment, a pen drawing of a hand chained around the neck (contemporaneous hand; 3.6 cm).

Colors: The initial letter is drawn in red, the initial stem columns are filled in green. The tendril in the center is green, the initial stem end is red. The Lombardic strokes are red and green with silhouette decoration in the contrasting color.

Signatures on the foot of the last verso page of the following gathers: (8v): Ius , (32v): IIIIus , (40v) : Vus , (48v): VIus , (64v): VIIIus and (80v): Xus , otherwise lost due to trimming.
single column (1v, 25rv, 49rv, 83rv, 114v two columns)

Rubricated, the rubrics are written in uncial mixed with rustic capitals. In addition, larger red and green uncial capitals alternate as a display script in the first lines of text. At the beginning of each book, split-bar initials with a white, red-outlined bar (decorated with alternating red and green dots), nailed buckles, and red gap filling, accompanied by foliate tendrils in the center, their vegetal elements highlighted in relief by red dashes. The cushion background of the initials is alternately green and blue in sections; smaller areas are also highlighted in gold, as are the buckles and some of the terminal bulbous leaves. 2r, initial S over 13 lines with green gap filling. The letter ends are formed as dog or dragon heads, from which tendrils with half-palmettes grow, filling the center and featuring palmettes or acanthus-like profile leaves as terminal motifs; two further, similarly decorated tendrils are attached directly to the letter body with buckles. 26r, initial QOver 14 lines, with a red gap fill, blue background of the outer frame, inner field filled with green and gold (padded ground). The figure, extending diagonally across the entire width of the text area, is designed as an elongated, two-legged dragon with red-gold outlines and a green-red dotted body, whose tail terminates in a vegetal ornament (a fan-like trefoil consisting of two conical leaves and a central acanthus leaf). The creature's neck is coiled in a knot around the letter stem; from the mouth of its head, which extends into the inner field, emerges a double, axially symmetrical tendril with half-palmette and bud leaves, filling the inner field and extending beyond it to the left. 50r, initial P over 16 lines against a green-blue padded ground. The stem of the letter grows downwards from the mouth of a frontally depicted lion's head and consists of two parallel gold border bands, which terminate at the bottom in a braided knot and terminate in two tendrils with terminal red bulbous leaves. The stem is filled with a frieze-like ornament consisting of slanted red half-palmettes and green acanthus leaves in alternating sequence. The head of the letter consists of a red-filled cleft strip into which a dog-like creature, rearing up on its hind legs against the stem, extends its head. From the creature's mouth grows a short-stemmed tendril adorned with various leaf shapes. 84r, initial P over 16 lines against a green-blue cushioned background, cleft fillings gold with a red diamond grid. The head of the P terminates in a tendril adorned with half-palmettes and bulbous leaves, which fills the central field. A tendril winds its way to the bottom of the initial, upon which sits a stylized bird whose beak bites the border. From the upper joint grows a short, outward-curving tendril with a downward-pointing dog's or dragon's head, from whose mouth emerges a cone-shaped golden figure decorated with a red lattice and green dots. 114v, initial Q over 9 lines on a green field, the inner field alternating green and blue, the cleft fillings red, the buckles gold. The cauda, ​​formed as a vegetal cleft border, shows a gold cleft filling with a red diamond lattice and flower, terminating in a strongly lobed half-palmette. The inner field is filled with two axially symmetrical half-palmette tendrils, the ends of which are curled in a volute-like fashion and also wrapped around the letter stem; both are fastened with buckles. Such split-border initials with varying colored backgrounds and diverse vegetal tendril forms are characteristic of the codices of the "Scriptrix Group"

details.value:
Easter Orationale , hymnic meditations on liturgical texts of the Easter season, predominantly in Latin and Low German
Rhymed prayers and songs in Low German: (36v ) Easter Hallelujah, O du ware balsem vat …; (100v ) Easter Song, Also hillich is desse Dach …; (230v ) Easter Song, Nu help uns dat heyligher graf …; (335v ) Easter Poem, Nu wil wy keren ghans al unsen flith … (edited by Irtenkauf , pp. 109-111). Sometimes also language mixing, e.g. (309 v -320 r ) Easter song, Salve centies millesies milies gloriosissima … festa dies paschalis … with longer Low German parts.

details.value:
With the exception of the ninth quire (fol. 81–90) and the final quire of unit B (fol. 195–204), catchwords are by the main scribe.
At the beginning of the fifth quire (fol. 41r), and continuously from the seventh quire onward (fol. 61r), alphanumeric quire signatures in grey ink are visible, partly heavily trimmed. Legible are: ninth quire (fol. 81r): f; tenth quire (fol. 91r): l; eleventh quire (fol. 101r): m; twelfth quire (fol. 111r): n; thirteenth quire (fol. 117r): o; fourteenth quire (fol. 127r): p; fifteenth quire (fol. 137r): q; sixteenth quire (fol. 147r): r; seventeenth quire (fol. 157r): s; eighteenth quire (fol. 167r): ß; nineteenth quire (fol. 175r): t; and twentieth quire (fol. 185r): v.

simply decorated red Lombards of two to six lines, with guide letters by the scribe (?); not executed on fol. 38va. Red headings by the scribe in texts 1, 2, and 4. Rubricated throughout. Proper names, numerals, Latin and partly also German expressions, for example crúcʒ, kúngin, drÿvaltikait, liechtmiſſ, and engel[l], and from fol. 127r onward headings, are underlined in red. Line fillers in red ink. Title names in red ink on fol. 183r. Red paragraph markers and speaker labels in the dialogues by the scribe. In the second text, Christus und die minnende Seele, corresponding to the image programme, 19 blank spaces measuring 4.9–8.7 × 6.3–8 cm were left for unexecuted illustrations, with image captions, on fol. 3vb, 5rb, 6va, 7ra, 8ra (caption on fol. 7vb), 9ra, 9va, 10rb, 11ra, 11vb, 12va, 13ra, 13vb (caption fol. 13va), 14va, 15ra, 15vb, 17ra (caption fol. 16vb), and 17rb. In addition there are three image captions without blank spaces on fol. 16rb, 17vb, and 19ra.

value.title: Pütrich convent, Franciscan, Munich, Germany

details.value:
Illustrations: 8 pasted-in miniatures with scenes of the Christ Child, mostly colored pen drawings:
	•	1v, parchment, 7.8 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child at a nun’s window in a convent; inscription: “Ich ste vor der tur, tue mir auf und laß mich ein du allerliebste mein” (“I stand at the door, open for me and let me in, my dearest”).
	•	46r, parchment, 7.1 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child in a golden robe with a flower crown; from the backpack, scrolls with: lieb, frid, rainigkeit, diemutigkeit, gedult (love, peace, purity, humility, patience); inscription: “Ich Jhesus clarpring mit mir vil guetter jar und ain krenczlein das haist vergißnitmein” (“I Jesus bring with me many good years and a little wreath called ‘Forget-me-not’”).
	•	194v, paper, 4 × 6.2 cm: Christ Child in a tub between two plants, no inscription.
	•	206r, paper, 7.6 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child in a tub, with an angel beside him; inscription: “Ich hab vil zu hayß gepadet und bedorft daz man mich labet” (“I have wandered much in heat and need, that one may refresh me”).
	•	217r, parchment, ca. 6.3 × 5 cm: Christ Child with harp under flowers; above, in the scribe’s hand: “Ich Jesus wyl dyr wol und sues hofyern, das du dem fyeber mugst entpßyechen” (“I Jesus wish well and sweet joy to you, that you may withstand fever”).
	•	230r, parchment, 6.6 × 5 cm, tempera miniature on gold ground, differing from the other miniatures: a saint pouring medicine from a vessel into a sack for a nun; inscription: “Ich pin ein guoter arczt, wan ich gyb erczeney für den aussacz” (“I am a good doctor, for I give medicine for the plague”).
	•	261r, paper, 8 × 5.5 cm: Christ Child with backpack among vines; inscription: “Ich pin Jhs daz kindlein undprin (!) vil guter jar in meinem körblein” (“I am Jesus the little child, bringing many good years in my little basket”).
	•	264r, parchment, 6.5 × 6.1 cm: Christ with a lamb; inscription: “Durch die tieff meiner wunden hab ich das verloren schaff wider funden. Venite ad me” (“Through the depth of my wounds I have found again the lost sheep. Come to me”).

Three further miniatures are missing (glue traces on 51v, 244v, 275r). The images were originally planned to be part of the text. Cf. B. Hernad, Eine kuriose Christus-Darstellung in München, Zs. f. Kunstgeschichte 49 (1986), pp. 579–583, this manuscript p. 581.

“This book was commissioned to be written by the venerable in God, Lady Anna Gurr, abbess of the venerable convent at Neuburg, and it was completed on the feast of St Quirinus the holy martyr in the year of the Lord 1501, in the first year [of her abbacy].”

Anna Gurr († 1517) was abbess of the Benedictine convent of Neuburg an der Donau until 1509; see P. Lindner, Monasticon episcopatus Augustani antiqui, Bregenz 1913, p. 132 no. 180.
After the dissolution of their convent in 1554, the Neuburg nuns partly moved to Kühbach; thus the ownership note on fol. 1r is probably to be dated after 1554:
“This book belongs to Anna Rinckhamerin, nun of the convent at Kühbach.”

value.title: Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Will.II, 19. 8o

details.value:
Nuremberg, Stadtbibliothek, Will.II, 19. 8o
Bound between 1448 and 1457 from two parts of different origins: Part I f. 1-120, brought by Kunigund Schreiber to the Monastery of St. Catherine in Nuremberg; Part II f. 121-259, brought by Katharina Tucher to the Monastery of St. Catherine in Nuremberg.

Red, often extensive headings, red lombard initials, pen flourishing. Often red ornamental curls at the upper and lower margins.
five pasted-in coloured woodcuts:
– fol. 44v, Schreiber II 817: Christ Child with flowers. 90 × 79 mm. Colours: carmine, vermilion, blue, ochre, and grey-brown. Upper Rhine, c. 1480. The Nuremberg copy not recorded by Schreiber.
– fol. 94r: Creation of Adam. Adam half reclining, half sitting diagonally to the right foreground; on the left God the Father with long hair and beard, wedge-shaped nimbus, long belted garment, reaching for Adam’s hands and eyes. In the background rocky terraces, one large and two small trees; in the foreground tufts of grass and two more small trees. Double frame 68 × 57 mm, trimmed without margins. Colours: strongly opaque green, blue, violet, and pink, with reserved highlights on God’s garment and Adam’s body. Not in Weinberger or Schreiber.
– fol. 98r: Man of Sorrows in half-figure with the instruments of the Passion, standing in the tomb; in front a pope and a cardinal in adoration. Christ, bearded head inclined to the left, with wedge-shaped nimbus, holding scourge and rod in crossed hands. Perspective tomb with four recesses; behind it a T-shaped cross with three nails, pillar of scourging, tongs, ladder, sponge on a reed, lance, hammer, and the thirty pieces of silver (?). In front of the tomb garments with three dice, a chalice and a cup (?). Double frame 71 × 61 mm, trimmed without margins. Colours: blue, violet, green, light ochre and grey-brown; nimbus and metal details silver, oxidised. Composition similar to Schreiber II 876, where Pilate and a mocker appear instead of pope and cardinal.
– fol. 101r, Schreiber I 721: Death of the Virgin. 67 × 57 mm. Colours: violet, blue, green, ochre, pale yellow; nimbi partly silver, oxidised.
– fol. 104r, Schreiber I 356: Carrying of the Cross. 67 × 56 mm. Colours: blue, green, light to medium brown; nimbi and metal details silver, oxidised.

details.value:
On the pastedown: Dis bůch het uns geton schriben die erwirdig junckfrow Johanna von Mersperck in dem jor do man zalt von Christi gebůrt m° cccc° xxviij. 
Johanna (Jeanne) von Mörsberg may be regarded either as the scribe of this manuscript or as its commissioner, since tůn schriben can also mean “to have [something] written.” A Poor Clare at the convent of Gnadenthal in Basel, she became, in 1430, a penitent at St Mary Magdalene in the convent “An den Steinen,” where she died in 1450 (?) (Degler-Spengler).

value.title: Gnadental Monastery, Basel, Poor Clares, Basel, Switzerland

Woodcut illustrations:
4v : Pasted woodcut: Annunciation of Mary.
5v : presumably a woodcut that was formerly pasted in.

details.value: Hie ist volendet di legend von sand Franciscen. Die hat geschriben Elspet von Amberk in dem iar, do man zalt von Christes geburt tausent und driͦu hundert unn in dem xxxvii iar. So hat Katerina von Purchhausen geschriben di legend von sancto Antonio unn diu was in dem lxvii iar alt, da si di legend schreip. Unn di legend wurden peid geschriben unn erleuht unn vol praht nah sand Bartholomeus des naehtes tages. Swer di legend les, der pit got fur si, unn ůch fur di, di daz permeid unn daz pinten habent verrihte, daz uns got allen helfe zu den erlichen scharen des lieben herren sand Franciscen unn der werden fr owen sand Chlaren. Amen.

Here is completed the legend of Saint Francis. It was written by Elspet of Amberg in the year when one counted from Christ’s birth one thousand three hundred and in the thirty-seventh year [i.e. 1337]. And Katerina of Burghausen wrote the legend of Saint Anthony, and she was sixty-seven years old when she wrote the legend. And the legends were both written and illuminated and fully completed on the day after the feast of Saint Bartholomew. Whoever reads the legends, let him pray to God for them, and also for those who carried out the parchment-making and the binding, that God may help us all to the honourable company of the beloved lord Saint Francis and the worthy lady Saint Clare. Amen.

details.value: 126r Schreibervermerk. In Rot. Hie ist volendet di legend von sand Franciscen. Die hat geschriben Elspet von Amberk in dem iar, do man zalt von Christes geburt tausent und driͦu hundert unn in dem xxxvii iar. So hat Katerina von Purchhausen geschriben di legend von sancto Antonio unn diu was in dem lxvii iar alt, da si di legend schreip. Unn di legend wurden peid geschriben unn erleuht unn vol praht nah sand Bartholomeus des naehtes tages. Swer di legend les, der pit got fur si, unn ůch fur di, di daz permeid unn daz pinten habent verrihte, daz uns got allen helfe zu den erlichen scharen des lieben herren sand Franciscen unn der werden fr owen sand Chlaren. Amen.
Quire signatures in red at the end of the quires: i–xviii.

Rubricated; red headings and line fillers, red paragraph marks; on fols. 3v–4r also blue.
Saints’ names usually outlined in red; occasionally written in alternating red and black majuscules (fols. 2r, 4r, 72r) or in red and blue (fols. 21v, 82v, 90r), as are the incipits on fols. 4r, 78r, and 88r.

On fols. 3v–4r one-line initials; from fol. 75r onward, two-line red and blue Lombard initials, some with shaft cut-outs, contour strokes, extensions, or pen flourishing (fleuronné).

In the Legenda maior, at the beginning of the prologue and of individual chapters, as well as on fols. 129v, 138v, and 152v in the Vita Antonii, and on fol. 170r at the beginning of the Indulgentiae, there are 3–5-line red-and-blue ornamentally split initials with pen flourishing and one- to two-sided flourishing bars.

Figural decoration includes:
– fol. 25v: a red quadruped and a blue bird;
– fols. 45v and 129r: a red bird.

Fol. 4r: seven-line blue historiated initial heightened with white vegetal and ornamental motifs on a red ground; within the field, Francis as a mounted knight on a gold ground; above him God holding a scroll inscribed Francisce quis potest.

Fol. 77v: miniature in a red and green frame with yellow vines: the Stigmatization of St Francis.

Opaque painting in red, green, blue, yellow, pink, brown, grey, black, white, and gold.

details.value:
Rosalie Green, Michael Evans, Christine Bischoff, and Michael Curschmann(ed.) (1979) The Hortus Deliciarum of Herrad of Hohenbourg (Landsberg, 1176-96): A Reconstruction. Warburg Institute/E.J. Brill
Fiona J. Griffiths (2007) The Garden of Delights: Reform and Renaissance for Women in the Twelfth Century. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press.

The Hortus deliciarum is a Christian encyclopedic manuscript, produced between 1159 and 1175 by Herrade of Landsberg (also known as Herrade of Hohenbourg) and the nuns of the convent of Hohenbourg Abbey (Mount Sainte Odile). The original manuscript was destroyed in the fire at the Strasbourg Library on 24 August 1870.

It is the earliest known encyclopedia produced by a woman. Written in Latin, the work summarizes both theological and secular knowledge of its time.

The original manuscript, which had been transferred to the Strasbourg Library during the French Revolution, was destroyed in the 1870 fire during the Franco-Prussian War. The miniatures are known to us through partial copies made by Christian Moritz Engelhardt and by Auguste de Bastard d'Estang. In most cases, the original captions were ignored during the copying process (see the section “Reconstruction of the original”).

details.value: Two Merovingian saints from Hesbaye, who were successively abbesses of Aldeneik on the Meuse. According to their Vita, the two sisters had received a careful education: they had learned to read, to sing, to paint, and to write—activities which, their biographer notes, even strong men would have found arduous. They later settled in the family monastery, where they devoted themselves, among other things, to passementerie work to embellish ritual garments. They also copied, again according to their biographer, the Gospels, a psalter, and other sacred writings.

details.value: Eleven leaves are missing: fols. 35, 36, and 49; one leaf between fols. 106 and 107; five between fols. 108 and 109; and two between fols. 156 and 157. Fols. 105 and 106 have been cut and pasted back together. There is an inserted folio 21bis.

Nine miniatures of column width (on fols. 1, 90v, 106v, 107v, 108, 149v, 154, 157), executed by the Master of the Pastoure and the Master of Jeanne Ravenelle (see the Album Christine de Pizan). Five of the original illuminations are missing. Initials attributable to the ‘lozenge-lily’ filigree artist, with cadel initials and paragraph marks. Rubrics precede the Virelays, the Epîtres sur le Roman de la Rose, the Enseignements à son fils, the Oraison Notre Dame, and Les quinze joies de Notre Dame.

details.value: Les Enluminures attributed it to this scribe

It is possible that although the manuscript was decorated by Elsbeth Töpplin, it may have been copied for use at a house for friars (or monks), since the rubric on f. 30v in the Gospel reading for Holy Thursday mentions “fratribus” (the brothers).  An alternative and probably more likely explanation is that this was copied from an exemplar for Friars without updating the rubrics to reflect feminine use, even though it was used by the sisters at the convent of St. Mary Magdalene.

multi-colored rubrics in purplish-red, blue, orange-red, green and blue, red and green line fillers, one-line blue, purplish red, green and orange-red initials, initials equivalent to one-line of text and music in blue, orange-red and green (outlined in red or green pen), eight colored initials equivalent to one-line of text and music (parted red and green, red, blue, or pink) with decorative pen flourishes and infilling in red, blue and green, on ff. 18v, 20, 21v, 23, 24v, 25v, 26, 28, two 2-line gold initials, heavily edged in black with white dots, infilled and on multi-colored grounds on ff. 28, 30v, four parted red and blue initials, with gold balls and floral motifs within the initials, equivalent to one-line text and music, with extensions, with red, blue and green pen work, five similar parted red and green or red and blue initials, infilled with contrasting colors with yellow highlights, edged in black with white dots, terminating in large extensions of flowers or leaves, ff. 1, 2v, 3v, 6 and 12, and SEVEN HISTORIATED INITIALS:  f. 7v, the baby Jesus, ff. 10 and 13v, the face of Christ, f. 15v, the Virgin, crowned, and child, f. 18, Christ as Man of Sorrows, upper torso depicted peeking out from alongside a cadel initial, f. 18, Virgin crowned, f. 27v, 7-line “I” with extensions, showing the standing Christ teaching, all with thick burnished gold, halos, crowns and other ornaments, in very good condition with wide margins, occasional small stains in the margins.

value.title: Wolfenbüttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, Cod. Guelf. 480 Helmst.
Lamspringe, Benedictine, Lamspringe, Lower Saxony, Germany,-1138

details.value:
On the lower margin of fols. 8v, 16v, and 24v, quire signatures in Arabic numerals I–III (III on 24v); on the lower margin of the last verso of the next seven quires, quire signatures in minuscule letters a–g. The quires from fol. 96 onward mostly have red catchwords.
Parchment: coarse and often irregular, with many holes and stitched repairs, most of them outlined in red; places difficult to write on are marked in red or filled with red wavy lines.

•	1v: an initial I spanning 13 lines, shaped like a chalice that widens upward like a funnel or flower, with four budding “knob-leaf” offshoots attached to the body with buckle-like bands (identical in Cod. Guelf. 475 Helmst., 175v). From the leafy chalice emerges the haloed St Augustine (bust) with crozier, book (?) and mitre (illustrated in Cohen-Mushlin, 166 no. 145). Executed only as an outline drawing; the depiction resembles the fully finished initial in Cod. Guelf. 204 Helmst., 3v.
	•	27r: inhabited column-bar initial D over 5 lines, in uncial form, with a tail ending in knob-leaf forms. In the inner field, Bede appears as a haloed tonsured monk (bust), writing with a pen in his right hand while holding a penknife/correcting knife in his left to steady the leaf. Also only outlined.
	•	On 25v, 88r, and 106r, space was left for initials; on 126r an initial O is outlined as a red circle.

The initials were probably executed—like those in Cod. Guelf. 475 Helmst.—by the scribe and illuminator Ermengarde.

Item daz ist das erst puch daz
man hat abgeschriben von dem puch das vns die frawen zu sant Clarn geliehen haben vnd daz selb puch hat
geschriben junckfraw Anna Winterin vnd das gegenwärtig puch swester Vrsula Geiselherin vnd wart ge-
schriben da man zalt nach Cristi gepurt M CCCC vnd in dem LXI jar nach vnsers hochgelobten wirdigen
vaters sant Dominicus tag (nach 5. Aug. 1461).
On blank leaves at the end: three-mount (Dreiberg), Briquet 11911; three-mount similar to Briquet 11878 variant.

This is the first book that was copied from the book which the ladies of St Clare lent us; that book was written by the maiden Anna Winterin, and the present book by Sister Ursula Geiselherin, and it was written in the year of Christ’s birth 1461, after the feast of our highly praised worthy father Saint Dominic (after 5 August 1461).

details.value: Mostly watermarks already known from other St Catherine manuscripts: 	•	Characteristic ox-head types in various forms, including: 	•	Ox-head with eyes and nostrils, with staff and “Z” (e.g. fol. 3), as in Codd. sang. 363 and 1916 (here: right eye placed higher, right ear hanging downward, right cheek indented). 	•	Mitre-like mark (fol. 4), as in Codd. sang. 363, 406, 1916. 	•	Small crown (from fol. 19 onward), as in Cod. sang. 1066. 	•	Female head (from fol. 106 onward), as in the Urbar register booklet. Watermarks not previously attested in other St Catherine manuscripts: 	•	Small, somewhat misshapen ox-head (fols. 66–69), visible especially on fol. 67, somewhat similar to Piccard II/2 (1966), VII, no. 226 (Basel, Strasbourg 1489), though that model has a staff with star as subsidiary mark (possibly here not visible?); not recorded in Briquet. 	•	Chalice (fol. 135; clearly visible fols. 155 and 167), very similar to Briquet no. 4546 (Sion 1490; Lucerne 1492; Freiburg im Breisgau 1494). 	•	Toward the end: large crown (lower part visible fol. 175; upper part fol. 180). Watermarks allow only approximate chronological placement (1480s), not precise dating.

value.title: Wil, Dominikarinnenkloster St. Katharina, Chronik ("Konventsbuch")

details.value:
Principal compiler’s hand: Angela Varnbühler
	•	Initially writes in her characteristic, disciplined, formal Bastarda.
	•	From 1481 onward alternates with the hand of Elisabeth Muntprat.
	•	Over the years she continues to add entries passim.
	•	Her script develops into a more right-leaning, less formal semi-cursive.
	•	Her last autograph entry concerns the year 1505 (written at age 64).
	•	In the final years before her death (1509), she no longer writes herself but dictates to a fellow sister (entries fol. 106r [1505], 109r [1506], 113r [1507]). Entries mentioning “mine[m] lieben vetter hansen varnbueler” are certainly not in her hand.

Additional identifiable scribal hands
	•	Cordula von Schönau (fols. 70v–71v)
	•	Justina Blarer (fols. 86r; 87r–88v; 96v–97r; 111v–114v; and elsewhere)
	•	Sapientia Wirt
	•	Elisabeth Schaigenwiler (fols. 132v–143v)
	•	Regula Keller (fols. 102r–v; 115v ff.; 152r–v; 154r–157r; 158r–161r; 160r–v; 162v–164r; 169r ff.; 175v; 185r)

details.value: (f.126r) Hie ist volendet di legend von sand Franciscen. Die hat geschriben Elspet von Amberk in den iar, do man zalt von Chistes geburt tausent und driuhundert und in dem xxxvij iar. So hat Katerina von Purchhausen geschriben di legend von sancto Antonio. Und diu was in den lxvij iar alt, da si di legend schreip. Und di legend wurden peid geschriben vnd erleuht und volpraht nah sand Bartholomeus des na’htes tages. Swer di legend les, der pit got fur si, und fur [durchgestrichen] vᵒch fur di, di daz permeid und daz pinten habent verrihte, daz uns Got allen helfe zu den erlichen scharen des lieben herren sand Franciscen und der werden frowen sand Chlaren. Amen.

(f.126r) Here ends the legend of Saint Francis. This was written by Elspet von Amberk in the year counted from Christ's birth as one thousand three hundred and thirty-seven. Then Katerina von Purchhausen wrote the legend of Saint Anthony. She was sixty-seven years old when she wrote the legend. The legends were completed, illuminated, and perfected after Saint Bartholomew's day at night. Whoever reads the legend, pray to God for her, and for [crossed out] also for those who have sponsored and arranged it, may God help us all to the honorable company of the beloved Saint Francis and the venerable lady Saint Clare. Amen.

details.value:
Schwesternbuch, Sisters' book
The designation “Schwesternbuch” is misleading.

It does not correspond to what scholarship usually calls a “Sisters’ Book,” namely:

“a seemingly chronicle-like compilation of numerous short vitae of deceased sisters of a particular convent, produced by members of the subsequent generation of sisters” (Ringler, 1980, p. 4).

The St Gall Schwesternbuch shares with that genre:
	•	a chronicle-like character (Part I)
	•	gradual textual expansion
	•	didactic and edifying function (Part II)

However, it should not, as has unfortunately happened in older scholarship, be misinterpreted—especially in its second part—as a document presenting exemplary traditions of spiritual life at St Katharina, St Gall.

That literary type arose in the first half of the 14th century as a female counterpart to the Vitas fratrum (see Meyer, Katharinental, 1995, p. 23).

details.value:
The third sexternion (quire of six bifolia) forms a separate booklet in a smaller format, on paper with a watermark not known from other St Katharina manuscripts (e.g. fol. xliiij). This watermark cannot be identified in Piccard (Wasserzeichen, 1961–1997) or Briquet (Filigranes, 1907).


The first four sexternions are marked by Angela Varnbühler with signatures:
	•	fol. xiijv: “the first sext[ernion]”
	•	fol. xiijr: “the second”
	•	fol. xxvijr: “the third”
	•	fol. xlvr: “the fourth”

details.value:
Produced, signed, and dated by the Spanish nun Maria Dies de Oña, this early sixteenth-century Spanish manuscript gradual contains the “propers” and choral chants for the Mass for Cistercian Use, according to the pre-Tridentine liturgical calendar. Although a complete volume, it is not a complete work as it contains approximately only the first third of the liturgical year, from the first Sunday in Advent to Palm Sunday. Given the size and format of this volume, the complete gradual for the entire liturgical year would have been represented by three or four volumes.

Produced by a female religious copyist for use by the female monastery of San Salvador de Oña in Burgos, this substantial volume is almost entirely composed of chant and does not include the long spoken portions of the Mass. Minor leaf repairs, occasional corrections, marginal additions, and instructions for following the text indicate that this manuscript was used on a regular basis.

details.value: 27v: Ora deum pro me peccatrice soror Maria Horns

The origin in a Franciscan convent is evidenced by:
• The feast of the stigmatization of St. Francis (135r) and the rubric on f.150r referring to von unßerm werdigen vader Franciscus (“our worthy Father Francis”).
• The suffrage for Severus, unserm Patrone (“our patron”) on f.162r, situated within the liturgical year sequence between November 11 and November 21, suggesting Boppard (Archdiocese of Trier).
In 1489, Franciscan sisters from Besselich settled in Boppard, known for their manuscript production (cf.J. Marx, Geschichte des Erzstifts Trier, vol. 2, part 2, 1862, p. 423, and K. Schlegel, Besselich am Mittelrhein, 1980, p. 19).

details.value: Thässen bok aer skriffuet uppå thz perman som systr birgitta iohannis gudmundi aategudh alzwallogher the siälena miskwnne bidhin kära systra för henne oc glömen ey mik sum skreff oc wrt thenna bok lyktat oppa sancte michaells affton anno domino MDXVII gudh till hedher oc edher almaent oppa badha chora till hugnat.

This book is written on the parchment owned by Sister Birgitta Johannis Gudhmundi. May God, all-merciful, have mercy on her soul. Dear sisters, pray for her and do not forget me, who wrote this book, which was completed on the eve of Saint Michael, in the year of our Lord 1517, to the honor of God and for the spiritual benefit of you all, both in the choir and beyond.

details.value: f.37v: “Thässen bok aer skriffuet uppå thz perman som systr birgitta iohannis gudmundi aategudh alzwallogher the siälena miskwnne bidhin kära systra för henne oc glömen ey mik sum skreff oc wrt thenna bok lyktat oppa sancte michaells affton anno domino MDXVII gudh till hedher oc edher almaent oppa badha chora till hugnat”.

This manuscript was written in Vadstena Abbey, in the nuns scriptorium. The parchment was payed by sr Birgitta Gudmundi and it was completed at S Michaels eve 1517. It was written by one of the nuns, keeping her identity secret in the colophon on f.37v. It contained music and was intended for use in the church. There are closely related manuscripts in both Uppsala and Stockholm Libraries, either written or decorated by the same nun/nuns. The nuns had taken influence from their sisters i the Netherlands in the design of the large pen-flourished initials. One of the nuns who most frequently painted her large decorated initials in the same style as here was Christina Hansdotter Brask, but she seem to have hade successors. A very similar design can be found in KB A 12, UUB C 431, C 443, C 484, RA E 9002. Some of these are by Christina Hansdotter Brask and from the same period as this manuscript. The present mss is however executed by a much more stable hand than the Brask mss from the same period. A more suitable candidate is Katarina Gudmundsdotter, whose palaeography is in accordance with the scribe of this mss.

details.value: large ox head with staff and diagonal bar, without eyes or nostrils, with very small ears; the line continues upward past the ears. It is quite similar to Gerhard Piccard, Wasserzeichen II (1966), no. 253, though that example is dated later (1504–1506, Augsburg). At least two variants of the motif appear in this manuscript (see fols. 116–117, where the ears and skull differ).

details.value: According to Stooker & Verbeij 1997, no. 364 produced by the sisters of the common life of the Brandeshuis or the Kerstekenshuis in Deventer, or the S. Ursulenhuis, which was created in 1470 from the merger of these houses. Origin based on comparison of hands from Deventer: SAB, 101 D 2 KL, 101 D 5 KL, 101 D 6 KL and 101 F 4 KL. See also Rademaker-Helfferich, who also identifies these hands with each other and dates the manuscripts 101 F 4 KL and 101 D 6 KL to around 1485, so in the period after the merger. - According to BNM, f.47r-247v from the same hand as Deventer, SAB: 101 F 4 KL etc. and according to Rademaker-Helfferich and BNM f.3r-6r same hand as Deventer, SAB: 101 D 9 KL, copied in 1474 by a sister in the S. Ursulenhuis, 101 F 15 KL, copied in 1459 in the Brandeshuis and 101 F 3 KL, copied in 1464 by a sister in the Kerstekenshuis or Brandeshuis, the predecessors of the S. Ursulenhuis., Low

details.value: Quese oretur pro scriptice Gni, cognoscaturque propter deum si quid invenitur incorrectum. Nam omnia intelligere corrigere non potui. Exemplarium incorrectum valde habui. Laus domino Christo, qui me liberavit ab isto.

May one pray for the female scribe Gni, and may it be recognized, for God’s sake, if anything incorrect is found. For I was not able to understand and correct everything. I had a very faulty exemplar. Praise be to the Lord Christ, who has freed me from this.

details.value:
The original binding was replaced in the Benedictine monastery of Clus, after the codex was supplemented there around 1510, by a late Gothic wooden-board binding with an undyed sheepskin cover (flesh side outward).
This is remarkable insofar as the Augustinian canonesses of Marienberg belonged not only to a different monastic observance, but also to a different reform association—the Windesheim Congregation of the Augustinian Canons—and were in fact supervised and visited by the prior of the neighboring Augustinian canons’ house of Hamersleben, who was also responsible for the standardization of liturgical books according to Windesheim requirements, as Cod. Guelf. 501 Helmst. shows. The correction work of the Benedictines of Clus on this codex is a striking example of collaboration among reformed religious across the boundaries of their own association.

Überlingen, Leopold-Sophien-Bibliothek, Ms. 22

details.value:
On the flyleaf fol. I there is a watermark that cannot otherwise be detected in the manuscript and probably comes from the bookbinder’s stock: ox head with staff and diagonal bar (|| 60 mm), very similar, if not identical, to Ravensburg paper Piccard Ox Head V 353 (southwestern Germany [including Constance], 1498–1506) and Briquet 15258 (Schaffhausen 1506).

Codicological units A and B:
(1) Double tower with three battlements and one window per tower, without countermark, clearly visible on fol. 2 and 202–204, identical with Piccard, Tower IV 32, and Piccard online no. 101207 (Biberach, Sigmaringen 1504, 1505).
(2) Ox head (|| 57 mm) with single-contour staff and cross, eyes and nostrils, very similar, if not identical, to Piccard Ox Head VII 83 (southwestern Germany [including Constance and St. Gallen], 1501–1510).

Codicological units C and D: letter P, broken, double-contoured, with countermark, above it a four-leaf clover (only fragmentary) on fol. 278, within a bifolium inserted into the eighth quire [fol. 278–279, different paper, medium-strong ribbing], identical with Piccard Letter P IX 676, fragment (Constance 1505). The same watermark is also found in the manuscripts Überlingen, Leopold-Sophien-Bibliothek, Mss. 1 (Regina Sattler) and 16 (1504, Cordula von Schönau), as well as Freiburg im Breisgau, Archiepiscopal Archive, Hss. 27 (1506/1507, Regina Sattler and Cordula von Schönau) and 28 (Regina Sattler and Cordula von Schönau).

For the production process of Ms. 22 (= Ü), Simone Mengis assumes that Cordula von Schönau, after completing the first two codicological units A and B in Constance, sent the blank fascicles to St. Gallen, where Regina Sattler wrote units C and D. However, two passages in the codices Freiburg im Breisgau, Archiepiscopal Archive, Hs. 28, and Überlingen, Leopold-Sophien-Bibliothek, Ms. 5, likewise written by the two convent sisters, where the hands of the two scribes change in the middle of a sentence, show that Cordula von Schönau and Regina Sattler were active, at least temporarily, in the same place. Even though Regina Sattler’s stay in the Zoffingen convent is not documented by charters, this place, according to the dates 1504 and 1506/1507, the identity of the paper with that of units C and D of Ü, and the bindings of several manuscripts written individually or jointly by the two Dominican nuns, cannot have been the Dominican convent in St. Gallen, but only the Dominican convent of Zoffingen in Constance, where Cordula von Schönau is demonstrably present from 1497 onward.

Iustina a lupffen, Female, Heidelberg, Universitätsbibliothek, Pal. germ. 807, f. 1-63

details.value:
363 prescriptions for various illnesses, in no particular order. Recipe contributors, people on whom the remedies were tested, and informants are not named.

1. Fols. 1v–2v: 16 prescriptions concerning which herbs are used or applied.
2. Fol. 3v: Note: all the entries written in this book are crossed out, not because they are wrong or objectionable, but because they are all written elsewhere in another book. The lines are marked so that what is written here should not be written again. Marginal note: “Note.”
3. Fols. 4r–7v: 28 recipes for diseases of the mouth, throat, and teeth.
4. Fols. 8r–10v: 17 plague recipes. Heading: “For the pestilence.”
5. Fols. 11v–12v: 10 recipes for erysipelas / “rose.”
6. Fols. 13r–15v: 24 recipes for various illnesses: fever, dysentery or “red belly,” abdominal pain, poisoning.
7. Fols. 16r/v: 9 recipes for coughs and chest ailments.
8. Fols. 17r–18v: 16 recipes for diseases of the body and abdomen.
9. Fols. 18v–23r: 29 recipes for various illnesses: headache, dizziness, hallucinations, stomach problems, liver problems, abscesses, blood purification, stroke.
10. Fols. 24r–29v: 40 recipes for women’s illnesses.
11. Fols. 30r–31v: 15 recipes for jaundice and dropsy.
12. Fols. 32r–34r: 19 recipes for various illnesses: stone, stroke, epilepsy, fever, and other conditions.
13. Fols. 34v–35r: 11 recipes for the ears.
14. Fol. 35v: 6 recipes for the eyes.
15. Fols. 36r/v: 6 recipes against wounds.
16. Fols. 37r–38r: 15 recipes against various illnesses, including worms in the stomach, colic, rage, and heart pain.
17. Fols. 38r–39v: 17 recipes for teeth and gums.
18. Fols. 39v–44v: 36 recipes for various diseases, including cancer or boils, fistulas, scabies, spots, etc.
19. Fols. 45v–47v: 12 recipes for wounds.
20. Fols. 48r–53r: 35 recipes for various illnesses and cosmetics.
21. Fols. 54r–56v: 11 recipes for edema, sores, ruptures, and scabies.
22. Fols. 57v–58r: Sage tract, not in Hlawitschka. Heading: “How one should make the water of virtues, this drink of youth…”
23. Fols. 58r–62r: 10 recipes for various illnesses, especially stomach, head, and wounds.
24. Fols. 62v–63r: Index. Alphabetical list of indications in Latin and German, referring to fols. 4–61, equivalent to modern fols. 1–58.
25. Fol. 63r: At the upper margin, beginning of a recipe: “For the swelling under the…” It breaks off.

Fols. 3r, 11r, 23v, 45r, 53v, 55v, 57r, 58v, and 63v are blank.

details.value: f. 184v: “Item dit boeck hoert tot die nonnen in beverwijck ende heest ghescreven suster maritghen claes dodjter op heilighe daghen Int jaer ons heren dusent vijf hondert ende xvi” (This book belongs to the nuns in Beverwijck and was written by sister Maritghen Claes’s daughter on the holy days in the year of our Lord one thousand five hundred and sixteen).

In total, seventeen manuscripts in Dutch collections are either known or suspected to have been made in Beverwijk, but most were made by the Canons Regular of St. Mary (Sion) in Beverwijk (cf. Byvanck database in Online Resources). It would be especially interesting to compare our manuscript with two Books of Hours in Dutch, one copied by brother Gherijt van Castrinchem at the convent of St. Mary in Beverwijk in 1498 (Leiden, University Library, MS B. P. L. 2747; see CMD-NL, vol. 2, no. 543 and Online Resources), and another copied in 1489, most likely at Beverwijk, and decorated with miniatures, as well as penwork flourishes that are very similar to those in our manuscript (Hague, KB, MS 79 K 5; sold by Les Enluminures in 2000). In addition, there are manuscripts which were copied elsewhere, but were acquired by the Beverwijk convent, including a Book of Hours for the use of Utrecht copied at a Charterhouse near Utrecht (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Douce 57).

value.title: Marienborn Convent in Beverwijk

details.value: alphanumerical leaf signatures in tiny writing in brown ink (mostly cropped),

The beautiful penwork ornamentation decorating sixty-five pages in this book include forms typical of the pen-flourishes made in North Holland at the end of the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. These include the “U-bends,” “eye-leaves,” pointed lines in bundles (often in violet ink in our manuscript), and the Haarlem “sunbursts”; for comparison, see contemporary manuscripts made in Haarlem and North Holland, as described by Hülsmann and Nieuwstraten, 1992. There are also wonderful pearl borders, stylized roses and aubergines; see f. 91v in our manuscript. The penwork flourishes in our manuscript are very similar to those in a Book of Hours in Dutch copied in 1498 by brother Gherijt van Castrinchem at the convent of St. Mary in Beverwijk (Leiden, University Library, MS B. P. L. 2747; see a reproduction from the Manuscrits datés conservés dans les Pays-Bas in Online Resources).

rubrics red, capitals touched in red, 2- and 1-line initials alternately red and blue, fifty-four puzzle initials of 3- to 4-lines high with very fine penwork ornamentation extending to the margins in red and violet inks, enhanced with red, blue, green and yellow paint, eleven large puzzle initials of 5- to 6-lines high of the same style with the penwork extending to all margins, minor stains and signs of use, in overall excellent condition.

records.rec_Title: Admont Abbey, Benedictine, Admont, Austria, 1074

details.value: Abbot Wolfhold founded a convent for the education of girls of noble families; Gottfried of Venningen educated thirteen monks later chosen abbots of other monasteries. Abbot Henry VII (1275-97) began restoration work on the community, Engelbert (1297-1331)completed the restoration.

St. Hemma, Countess of Friesach and Zeltschach, founded community after entering convent at Gurk, leaving lands for the building of a monastery near the salt works of Hall. Foundation, however, was not begun until 1072, more than a quarter of a century after the Saint's death. Abbey church was consecrated by Gebhard von Helfenstein, Archbishop of Salzburg, in honour of St. Blasius in 1074. Gebhard also brought twelve monks from Salzburg to start community. In the following century, a school and community of women emerged from a less formal gathering of religious women around the parish church of S Amandus.
The associated nunnery ceased to exist during the Reformation.

details.value: Kloster unserer lieben Frau zu Lichtenthal; Lucida Vallis; Lucidevallis

The convent of Lichtenthal had an extensive library (see Manuscript sources). It possessed several Psalters, Breviaries, Graduals, Sermons, and lives of the saints. Several works were produced by a "Margaretha dicta Regula" during the course of the fifteenth century, including a Diurnal, Breviary, Solioquies of Bonaventura, Book of holy maids and women, Evangeliar., Leben der Altväter, Paradisus anime, The spiritual rosegarden, and Legend aurea.

records.rec_Title: Lamspringe, Augustinian, Lamspringe, Lower Saxony, Germany, 845-1138

details.value: Lamspringe; sanctus Adrianus monasterium (873); ecclesia sancti Adriani lamesprinche (1149); ecclesia in Lamesprigge (1169); monasterium beatorum Adriani et Dyonisii martirum in Lammespringhe (1338)

The Herzog-August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel possesses 18 manuscript volumes, which belonged to the library of the convent. These are primarily theological and spiritual works, written from the tenth to the sixteenth century. Other documents are located in the HauptStaatsarchiv in Hannover.

A book from the convent (preserved in the Herzog-August-Bibliothek) mentions the nun Ermengarde (c. 1178/1205) as the scribe and as the painter of a miniature of S. Augustine. It is thus likely that the convent did possess a scriptorium (Römer, 370). There are 18 extant books from the convent, 12 stem from the twelfth century. Of the twelve, there are four works of Augustine, two of Gregory the Great, two from Venerable Bede, and one each by Hieronymus, Clemens, John Chrysostomos, and Hugo of S. Victor. Römer ascribes these works to the influence of provost Gerhard (1178-1205) (Römer, 335).

Augustinian canonesses; end of 12th century, changed to Benedictine convent
Augustinian; Benedictine by 1138
